short_explanation: Organic farming is the system defined by cutting out synthetic herbicides and pesticides and relying on manures, composts and biological pest control instead.
explanation_text: The four systems in the options sit on a spectrum of how much external input is used. Organic farming follows a certification standard: no synthetic fertiliser, herbicide or pesticide, with organic manures, green manuring, crop rotation and biological control taking their place. Natural farming (Fukuoka, and in India Zero Budget Natural Farming) goes further and also drops ploughing, weeding and purchased inputs of any kind. Biodynamic farming is organic plus the Steiner preparations and a sowing calendar. A stem that says only 'less herbicides, less pesticides' is describing the input-substitution idea at the heart of organic farming.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Natural farming does not merely reduce herbicides and pesticides, it eliminates all external inputs along with tillage and weeding; the stem describes reduction, not elimination.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Bio-intensive agriculture is about maximising yield from a small area through deep beds, close spacing and composting; its defining feature is land-use intensity, not chemical reduction.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Biodynamic farming is organic farming plus Steiner's preparations and a lunar planting calendar, so it would be identified by those extras, not by the two statements given.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 'Green farming' is not a recognised farming system in Indian agricultural literature.

common_traps: Natural farming and organic farming are close neighbours. The test is whether inputs are reduced and substituted (organic) or dropped altogether along with tillage (natural).

short_explanation: Nandini sits on Ginni's immediate left. Sana was born in Jaipur, Ginni sits second to Sana's right, and Nandini — born in Bangalore — is the neighbour of Sana who falls between the two, which puts her on Ginni's left.
explanation_text: Three clues lock this corner of the circle. Sana is the Jaipur person. Ginni, born in Mumbai, sits second to her right, so exactly one seat separates them. Nandini, born in Bangalore, must sit next to the Jaipur person, and the only free seat next to Sana on that side is the one between Sana and Ginni. Since everyone faces the centre, a person's left is the clockwise side, so Nandini — one step clockwise from Ginni — is on Ginni's immediate left.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Sana is two seats from Ginni, with Nandini between them, not next to her.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Reeta, born in Bihar, sits directly opposite Sana, which puts her well away from Ginni.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Shubhi sits three seats to Nandini's left, on the far side of the circle from Ginni.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Gudia sits on Ginni's immediate right, not her left.

common_traps: Everyone faces the centre, so left and right are the reverse of what they look like on the page. Ginni's left is the clockwise side of the circle.
key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.1-Q.5. Reading round the circle in the direction of each person's right hand (facing the centre, that is anticlockwise seen from above): Sana, Nandini, Ginni, Gudia, Reeta, Kavya, Shubhi, Rekha, back to Sana. Cities in the same order: Jaipur, Bangalore, Mumbai, Manali, Bihar, Goa, Amritsar, Chandigarh. This seating is the only one the clues allow.

short_explanation: Oyster mushroom (Pleurotus species) is the one keyed here: its shell- or fan-shaped cap spreads into an umbrella as it ages, with prominent gills running down the short stalk.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Shiitake has a brown, domed cap on a central stalk; it is grown on hardwood logs or sawdust, not the mushroom this stem points to.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Enoki grows as slender white threads with tiny caps and almost no visible gill spread.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Portabello is the fully mature white button mushroom, so it does open out with dark exposed gills; the source key still reads oyster.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: White button is harvested closed, before the veil breaks, so its gills are not exposed at all.

key_note: The stem is loosely worded. 'Ages well and opens into a gilled umbrella' also describes Portabello, which is simply a mature Agaricus bisporus; the paper's key is oyster. Worth a source check before publication.

short_explanation: Counting from Sana towards her left, Rekha comes first and Shubhi second, and Kavya is next after them — so two persons sit between Kavya and Sana on that side.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Three is the count on the other side of the circle, going from Sana's right through Nandini, Ginni and Gudia to Reeta, not to Kavya.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: One would mean only Rekha stands between them; Shubhi is also in the gap.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Four overshoots — only three seats lie between Sana and Kavya going the other way round.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Kavya and Sana are not neighbours; Rekha and Shubhi separate them.

common_traps: The question fixes the direction — count only towards Sana's left. Going the other way round gives a different number.
key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.1-Q.5. Reading round the circle in the direction of each person's right hand (facing the centre, that is anticlockwise seen from above): Sana, Nandini, Ginni, Gudia, Reeta, Kavya, Shubhi, Rekha, back to Sana. Cities in the same order: Jaipur, Bangalore, Mumbai, Manali, Bihar, Goa, Amritsar, Chandigarh. This seating is the only one the clues allow.

short_explanation: Kavya was born in Goa. Reeta, born in Bihar, must have the Goa person as an immediate neighbour, and Reeta's two neighbours are Gudia — already placed in Manali — and Kavya, so Goa falls to Kavya.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Jaipur is Sana's, stated directly in the clues.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Bangalore is Nandini's, stated directly in the clues.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Amritsar is left for Shubhi, the only person still unassigned once Kavya takes Goa.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Bihar is Reeta's, stated directly in the clues.

key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.1-Q.5. Reading round the circle in the direction of each person's right hand (facing the centre, that is anticlockwise seen from above): Sana, Nandini, Ginni, Gudia, Reeta, Kavya, Shubhi, Rekha, back to Sana. Cities in the same order: Jaipur, Bangalore, Mumbai, Manali, Bihar, Goa, Amritsar, Chandigarh. This seating is the only one the clues allow.

short_explanation: Blue Revolution is the drive to raise fish production through aquaculture, begun with the Fish Farmers Development Agency in 1970 and now carried by the Blue Revolution scheme and PMMSY.
explanation_text: India's colour-coded revolutions each name a commodity push: Green for foodgrains, White (Operation Flood) for milk, Yellow for oilseeds, Blue for fish. The Blue Revolution's content is planned fish culture — pond and tank aquaculture, inland and brackish-water farming, hatcheries, and later mariculture — rather than simply catching more fish from the sea. The umbrella scheme 'Blue Revolution: Integrated Development and Management of Fisheries' ran from 2015-16 and has since been subsumed under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020).

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Fisheries is the wider sector, including capture from rivers and seas; the Blue Revolution is specifically the culture-based push inside it.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Marine life is a biological category, not a production programme.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Ocean resources cover minerals, energy and shipping as well, which the Blue Revolution does not address.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Water resources belong to irrigation and river-basin policy, not to the fish production drive.

common_traps: 'Fisheries' looks equally right. The keyed distinction is that the Blue Revolution is about farming fish, so aquaculture is the narrower and more exact answer.
key_note: A candidate who reads 'Blue Revolution = fish production' can defend option B; the paper treats aquaculture as the precise term.

short_explanation: The first milk secreted after calving is colostrum — thick, yellow, rich in immunoglobulins, vitamin A and protein, and the calf's only source of passive immunity. 'Plasma milk' is not a term used in dairy science.
explanation_text: Secretion after parturition moves through three stages. Colostrum is drawn for roughly the first three to five milkings: it carries 15-20 per cent protein, most of it immunoglobulin, against about 3.5 per cent in normal milk, and the calf must receive it within the first six hours while the gut can still absorb whole antibodies. Transition milk follows for a few days as the composition shifts. Mature milk is the stable secretion that follows and is what is sold.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Colostrum is in fact the first milk drawn after calving, and this explanation proposes it as the correct option against the paper's key.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Mature milk is the stable secretion that appears after the first week, not the first milk.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Transition milk comes after colostrum, as composition moves toward mature milk; it is second, not first.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Colostrum is indeed yellow, but 'yellow milk' is a description, not the name of the secretion.

common_traps: Colostrum, transition milk and mature milk run in that order. Only colostrum answers 'first'.
key_note: The key marks 'Plasma milk', which is not a term in dairy science. The first milk after calving is colostrum, option B, on every standard reading; this looks like a key-entry error in the source.

short_explanation: Reeta sits between Gudia and Kavya, so she is the immediate neighbour of both.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Rekha sits opposite Gudia, as far from her as the circle allows.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ginni is Gudia's other neighbour, but Kavya is two seats away from Ginni.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Shubhi neighbours Kavya on the other side, but not Gudia.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Nandini sits between Sana and Ginni, next to neither Gudia nor Kavya.

key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.1-Q.5. Reading round the circle in the direction of each person's right hand (facing the centre, that is anticlockwise seen from above): Sana, Nandini, Ginni, Gudia, Reeta, Kavya, Shubhi, Rekha, back to Sana. Cities in the same order: Jaipur, Bangalore, Mumbai, Manali, Bihar, Goa, Amritsar, Chandigarh. This seating is the only one the clues allow.

short_explanation: Rekha sits third to Ginni's left. Stepping to the left from Ginni gives Nandini, then Sana, then Rekha.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Shubhi is third to Ginni's right, not her left — the same count taken in the wrong direction.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Reeta sits second to Ginni's right.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Kavya sits third to Ginni's right.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Sana is second to Ginni's left, one seat short.

common_traps: Counting three seats the wrong way round lands on Shubhi, which is why she is offered. With everyone facing the centre, left runs clockwise.
key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.1-Q.5. Reading round the circle in the direction of each person's right hand (facing the centre, that is anticlockwise seen from above): Sana, Nandini, Ginni, Gudia, Reeta, Kavya, Shubhi, Rekha, back to Sana. Cities in the same order: Jaipur, Bangalore, Mumbai, Manali, Bihar, Goa, Amritsar, Chandigarh. This seating is the only one the clues allow.

short_explanation: A disc harrow does its work through a gang of concave steel discs that rotate as they are pulled, cutting and turning the topsoil.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A spring tooth harrow works with curved spring steel tines that vibrate through the soil; nothing rotates.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A soil surgeon is a deep-working chisel-type implement, used to break hardpan rather than to harrow.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: An acme harrow has V-shaped blades set on a frame and is dragged, not rotated.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A blade harrow (bakhar) scrapes with a horizontal blade to cut weeds just below the surface; it has no discs.

short_explanation: An agri-silvipastoral system is the agroforestry combination that carries all three components together — trees, crops and pasture for livestock — on the same unit of land.
explanation_text: Agroforestry systems are named from the components they combine. Silvi- stands for trees, agri- for crops, pastoral for grass and livestock. So agri-silviculture is trees plus crops, silvopasture is trees plus pasture and animals, and agri-silvipasture is all three. The three-component system is typical of smallholder farms that need grain, fodder, fuelwood and timber from one holding, and it spreads risk across the year.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The agri-silvicultural system is trees with crops only; it leaves out the livestock component the stem names.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: An agri-pastoral system is crops with pasture and animals but no tree component.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Timber-coppice management is a silvicultural regeneration practice, not an agroforestry combination.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Ranching is extensive livestock grazing on rangeland, with neither the tree nor the crop component managed.

short_explanation: Even with both statements the box above H cannot be named: the two clues fix H four places above L with F just above L, but they still allow four different stacks, and in one of them H is the top box with nothing above it at all.
explanation_text: Statement I never mentions H, so on its own it can say nothing about H's neighbour. Statement II fixes L three boxes below H but names nothing else. Put them together and the picture is tight: L somewhere, F immediately above L, H four places above L, and B four places from F. Work through the places L can occupy in a stack of eight. If L is first, second or third from the bottom, B lands immediately above H and the answer would be B. But L can also be fourth from the bottom, which pushes H to the very top of the stack and forces B down to the bottom — and then no box sits above H. Two different outcomes survive, so the data are not sufficient.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I names only B, F and L. It never refers to H, so it cannot locate anything above H.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II places H four boxes above L but identifies no other box, so the position immediately above H stays nameless.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Neither statement alone reaches an answer, so "either alone" cannot hold.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Together they narrow the stack but do not settle it — the arrangement with H on top leaves no box above H, which contradicts the arrangement in which B sits there.

common_traps: It is easy to build one stack that works, see B above H and stop. The trap is the stack that puts H at the very top, where the question has no answer at all.
key_note: Only four of the eight boxes are named, so any question about an unnamed position is a warning sign in this format.

short_explanation: Community forestry is the model run by the community, for the community, on land the community holds or manages — the villagers are the decision-makers, not just the beneficiaries.
explanation_text: Social forestry, recommended by the National Commission on Agriculture in 1976, is the broader programme of raising trees outside reserved forests for fuelwood, fodder and small timber; it includes farm forestry, extension forestry on roadsides and canal banks, and community woodlots raised by the forest department on village common land. Community forestry is the strand within it where the village institution itself plans, protects and shares the produce. The distinction the stem tests is ownership of the decision, and this is also what separates Joint Forest Management, where the department and the village share control, from full community control.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 'Village forestry' is not a defined programme term; the recognised name for community-run woodlots is community forestry.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 'Collective forestry' is not used in Indian forestry policy.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 'People's farms' names no forestry system.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Social forestry is the wider umbrella, much of it raised by the forest department on public land, so it does not capture 'by the community'.

common_traps: Social forestry is the umbrella; community forestry is the community-controlled strand inside it. The phrase 'by the community' is what rules out the umbrella term.

short_explanation: Neither statement settles the fourth floor alone, but together they force R onto it, so both statements together are needed and are enough.
explanation_text: Statement I alone leaves three shapes alive — S on the ground floor with P on the fourth, S on the third with P on the sixth, S on the fifth with P on the fourth — and the fourth-floor tenant differs between them. Statement II alone barely constrains anything. Combine them: T sits immediately above R and T must be on an odd floor, so R is on an even floor; Q and P are on even floors too, so R, Q and P fill the second, fourth and sixth in some order. Q is not on the top floor. S is odd and three floors from P, which forces P to the sixth and S to the third. That leaves the second and fourth for R and Q, and R and Q must be two floors apart — which they are either way — but T = R + 1 must be odd and free, so R takes the fourth with T on the fifth, Q the second, and U the ground floor.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement I alone allows P, Q or an unnamed person on the fourth floor depending on where S sits, so it does not answer the question.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement II alone fixes no floor at all — it only relates T to R, R to Q, and says P is on an even floor.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Since neither statement alone answers the question, "either alone" fails.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Taken together the statements do reach a single arrangement, with R on the fourth floor.

key_note: The fixing move is combining "T is on an odd floor" from statement I with "T is immediately above R" from statement II — that is what makes R even and starts the chain.

short_explanation: Three strands run in parallel: the leading number climbs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; the letter climbs B, C, D, E, F; the trailing number falls 25, 24, 23, 22, 21. The third term is therefore 4D23.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 4D26 has the right number and letter but the trailing number rises to 26 instead of falling to 23.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 5D21 jumps the leading number to 5 and drops the trailing number to 21 — both belong to later terms.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 5D20 breaks two strands: the leading number should be 4, the trailing number 23.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 3D22 repeats the leading number 3 from the previous term instead of advancing it to 4.

common_traps: The letter D is in four of the five options, so the letter alone settles nothing — check the two numbers.

topic_name: Operational land holdings and farm size classification
short_explanation: A marginal farmer is one operating less than 1 hectare; the Agriculture Census places small farmers at 1 to 2 hectares above that.
explanation_text: The Agriculture Census classes operational holdings into five sizes: marginal below 1 hectare, small 1 to 2, semi-medium 2 to 4, medium 4 to 10, and large above 10. This matters well beyond statistics, because scheme eligibility is written on it — small and marginal farmers get the higher subsidy slab under SMAM, are the priority group for KCC and interest subvention, and made up the original PM-KISAN target group. As of the 2015-16 Census marginal holdings alone were about 68 per cent of all holdings but barely a quarter of the operated area.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Less than 2 hectares is the combined 'small and marginal' band used in scheme eligibility, not the marginal class by itself.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 2.5 hectares is not a class boundary in the Agriculture Census.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 0.5 hectare is not a census boundary; sub-half-hectare holdings are reported within the marginal class.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 4 hectares is the top of the semi-medium class, not the marginal one.

common_traps: 'Small and marginal' together means below 2 hectares, which is why option B feels right. Marginal on its own is below 1 hectare.

short_explanation: Sahiwal is the highest milk-yielding indigenous cattle breed, giving roughly 2,000-3,000 kg in a lactation, well above the other Indian milch breeds.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Gir is a strong milch breed and second on yield, but Sahiwal is placed above it in standard breed comparisons.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Red Sindhi is a milch breed of the same Zebu group with a lower lactation yield than Sahiwal.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Hallikar is a draught breed of Karnataka, prized for bullocks and a poor milker.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Khillari is a Deccan draught breed, again kept for work rather than milk.

short_explanation: W is X's grandparent on the father's side, but nothing in the clues fixes whether W is male or female, so the exact relation cannot be determined.
explanation_text: Trace the line. P is Q's wife and Q fathers only R and S. T is P's daughter-in-law, and since R is unmarried, T is married to S. T's two children are U and V. U is X's aunt, so U is a sister of one of X's parents; U's only sibling is V, so V is X's parent. V is W's daughter-in-law, which makes V's husband W's son — and V's husband is X's father. So W is the father's parent: X's paternal grandfather or paternal grandmother. The clues never state W's gender.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Paternal grandfather is possible but not established — W's gender is never given.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Paternal grandmother is equally possible and equally unestablished.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The maternal side is ruled out: V, X's mother, is W's daughter-in-law, so W belongs to the father's side.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Same problem — the link to W runs through X's father, not X's mother.

common_traps: "Daughter-in-law of W" tells you V married into W's family, which puts W on X's father's side. It does not say whether W is the grandfather or the grandmother.
key_note: Gender-undetermined puzzles usually hinge on one person whose sex is never stated and never implied by a gender-specific word such as wife, son or daughter-in-law.

short_explanation: Chokla, of the Rajasthan semi-arid belt, produces the finest carpet wool in India and is the standard reference breed for carpet-grade fleece.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Baluchi is a coarse-wool and mutton sheep, not the fine-carpet-wool breed.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Keezhakaraisal is a Tamil Nadu hair sheep kept for meat, producing no usable wool.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Mecheri is another Tamil Nadu meat breed, valued for its skin rather than fleece.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Ramanathapuram White is a southern meat breed with hair rather than wool.

key_note: Chokla is sometimes called the 'Merino of Rajasthan' in breed literature, which is the phrase to recognise.

short_explanation: V is P's granddaughter. P's son S married T, V is T's child, and V is female because she is described as W's daughter-in-law.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: V is female, so father is impossible; in any case V is a generation below P's children.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: V's mother is T. V stands two generations below P, not one above.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Uncle is the wrong generation and the wrong gender.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Grandson would be right in generation but wrong in gender — being a daughter-in-law makes V female.

common_traps: Grandson is the same relation with the wrong gender, and the only word fixing V as female is "daughter in law of W".
key_note: Same family tree as Q.9: P and Q are the grandparents, R is unmarried, S and T are the parents, U and V are their children.

topic_name: Linear row — single row, one direction
short_explanation: S sits fifth to U's left. In the finished row S is third from the left end and U is eighth, so counting leftwards from U — Q, X, T, P, S — S is the fifth.
explanation_text: Two clues open the row. Yellow sits immediately left of pink and R likes yellow, while W sits immediately to R's right — so W is the pink one, sitting next to R. Three persons separate X from pink, and X must be on an even place from the left, which puts R first, W second and X sixth. One person sits between W and P, so P is fourth. Two persons sit between X and V, and brown must be immediately left of V, which forces V to the far right end with brown eighth. Blue sits just right of T, and T likes orange; the only fit is T fifth with X sixth in blue. Q, who likes black, cannot sit immediately right of W, so Q takes the seventh place with S third, black and red land three apart on the seventh and fourth, U is eighth in brown and V ninth in green.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Second to U's left is X, not S.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: U sits to S's right, so S cannot be to U's right at all — the direction is reversed.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Third to U's left is T.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

common_traps: The question asks for S's position relative to U, not U's relative to S. Start the count at U and move left.
key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.11-Q.14. From the left end the row runs R, W, S, P, T, X, Q, U, V, and their colours in the same order are yellow, pink, grey, red, orange, blue, black, brown, green.

topic_name: Soil classification systems and soil orders
short_explanation: Indian soils are classified under USDA Soil Taxonomy, the comprehensive system that sorts soils into orders such as Inceptisols, Entisols, Alfisols, Vertisols and Aridisols on measurable diagnostic horizons.
explanation_text: Soil Taxonomy classifies on properties that can be measured in the field and laboratory — diagnostic surface and subsurface horizons, moisture and temperature regimes — rather than on assumed origin, which is why it travels across countries. India's soils map onto eight of its orders, with Inceptisols the largest share, followed by Entisols, Alfisols and Vertisols. The older Indian usage of alluvial, black, red and laterite soils is a descriptive grouping that sits alongside it, not a competing formal system.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: There is no classification called 'soil genealogical'; heredity language does not apply to soils.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Classification purely by origin was the older genetic approach, superseded because inferred origin cannot be measured consistently.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 'Soil-spatial classification' is not a recognised system; spatial spread is mapped, not used as the class rule.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Soil structure is a single physical property, one of many inputs to classification, not a system in itself.

topic_name: Linear row — single row, one direction
short_explanation: Q's two neighbours are X on the left and U on the right, and X is the one offered here.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: V sits at the right end with U between V and Q.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: S sits in the left half of the row, four places from Q.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: R is at the far left end, as far from Q as the row allows.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: W sits second from the left, next to R, not next to Q.

key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.11-Q.14. From the left end the row runs R, W, S, P, T, X, Q, U, V, and their colours in the same order are yellow, pink, grey, red, orange, blue, black, brown, green. Q, who likes black, sits seventh with X on his left and U on his right.

topic_name: Soil types and their distribution in India
short_explanation: Alluvial soils cover the largest area in India, about 43 per cent of the land, spread across the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains and the coastal deltas.
explanation_text: After alluvial soils come black (regur) soils at roughly 15 per cent of the area on the Deccan trap, then red soils on the crystalline peninsular shield, then laterites in high-rainfall tracts. Alluvium's dominance follows from the rivers: repeated deposition by the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and peninsular rivers builds deep, fertile, potash- and lime-rich profiles that are low in nitrogen and organic matter. This is the soil base of the wheat and rice belt, which is why area under alluvium tracks the country's foodgrain map so closely.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Laterite soils are confined to high-rainfall tracts of the Western Ghats, Odisha, Jharkhand and the north-east, a small share of the area.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Red soils are extensive across the peninsula and rank third or fourth, but well behind alluvium.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Forest soils are restricted to hill and mountain slopes under tree cover.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Peaty and marshy soils occupy small waterlogged pockets in Kerala, coastal Odisha and the Sundarbans.

topic_name: Linear row — single row, one direction
short_explanation: T likes orange and sits fifth; V likes green and sits ninth at the right end. X, Q and U fill the gap, so three persons sit between them.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Four would need one more person in the gap than the row provides.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Two undercounts — X, Q and U all lie between the orange and green seats.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: One is the count only if you stop at X and ignore Q and U.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The orange and green seats are four places apart, so they are not neighbours.

key_note: Solved from the direction block shared by Q.11-Q.14. From the left end the row runs R, W, S, P, T, X, Q, U, V, and their colours in the same order are yellow, pink, grey, red, orange, blue, black, brown, green.

topic_name: Soil classification systems and soil orders
short_explanation: Aridisols, the soils of dry regions, are low in organic matter and plant nutrients while accumulating salts including boron, because there is too little rainfall to leach them out of the profile.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ultisols are deeply weathered and leached soils of humid regions — acidic and nutrient-poor, but with bases washed out rather than boron accumulated.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Inceptisols are young soils with weakly developed horizons and no boron build-up; they are India's most extensive order.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Mollisols have a thick, dark, base-rich surface horizon and are among the most fertile soils, the opposite of the stem.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Histosols are organic peat soils, very high in organic matter.

topic_name: Linear row — single row, one direction
short_explanation: U sits eighth and V ninth, at the right end of the row, so U and V are the neighbouring pair.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: P is fourth and Q seventh — three places apart.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: S is third and T fifth, with P between them.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: W is second and T fifth, well apart.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: T is fifth and Q seventh, with X between them.
