option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 10 mm is well above the threshold and is used in intensity classification.

short_explanation: The United Nations, on India's proposal, declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, with FAO as the lead agency.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 2019 was the International Year of Indigenous Languages.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 2020 was the International Year of Plant Health.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 2021 was the International Year of Fruits and Vegetables, the nearest agricultural neighbour to this one.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 2025 carries other UN designations, not millets.

common_traps: 2021 was Fruits and Vegetables and 2020 Plant Health. The agricultural years run close together and are easy to swap.

short_explanation: A domestic bank that falls short of its priority sector lending target must place the shortfall with NABARD in the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund, which then lends it to state governments for rural infrastructure.
explanation_text: RIDF was set up in 1995-96 precisely to put this shortfall to work. Scheduled commercial banks are required to lend 40 per cent of adjusted net bank credit to the priority sector, with sub-targets for agriculture, small and marginal farmers, micro enterprises and weaker sections. Where a bank misses the target, the allocated amount goes into RIDF, held with NABARD, and is drawn by state governments to build irrigation projects, rural roads and bridges, watershed works and rural markets. The deposit earns a lower return than normal lending, which is what makes the target bite.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The amount does not go to the central government's account; it is a deposit that returns to the bank with interest.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: NABARD does administer the fund, so this is the near-miss option; the stem asks for the fund, which is RIDF.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Shortfall deposits go to RIDF with NABARD, not to the Reserve Bank, though the RBI sets the targets and allocates the shortfall.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The options describe different destinations, so they cannot all be right.

common_traps: NABARD is the institution that holds the fund; RIDF is the fund. The question asks which fund, which rules out the institution.

short_explanation: Contour farming is the practice meant here — ploughing, sowing and laying rows along the contour of a slope so that each furrow holds back runoff instead of channelling it downhill.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Terracing cuts the slope into level steps supported by risers; it is earthwork, not a way of aligning rows.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 'Slopy farming' is not a term used in soil conservation.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 'Hilly farming' describes where farming happens, not the conservation practice.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

common_traps: Contour farming aligns with contour lines, meaning across the slope. Reading 'along the slope' as up-and-down inverts the practice.
key_note: The stem says 'along the lines of slopes', which reads ambiguously. Contour farming runs across the slope, along the contour lines; ploughing up and down the slope is what it is designed to avoid.

short_explanation: Inarching, or approach grafting, joins a rooted stock plant to a shoot of the mother tree while both stay on their own roots until the union takes; the paper keys guava, which is commercially propagated this way.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Mango is the crop most texts name first for inarching, which makes this the strongest competing answer.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Litchi is normally propagated by air layering (gootee), not inarching.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Sapota is propagated by approach grafting on khirni rootstock in many texts, so it too is a defensible option.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Banana is propagated by suckers or tissue culture; grafting is not possible in a monocot.

key_note: Inarching is used in mango, sapota, guava and jackfruit, and standard horticulture texts most often cite mango. The key reads guava; because more than one option is defensible the item needs a source check.

short_explanation: Tipping is a tea operation: young shoots are cut at a set height to build a flat plucking table across the bush so that harvesting is even.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Coffee is managed by capping, handling and pruning of verticals, not by tipping.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Jute is harvested whole at flowering; there is no plucking table to build.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Gram is sometimes nipped at the top to encourage branching, but the operation is not called tipping.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Wheat receives no such canopy operation.

short_explanation: The paper keys bank finance for a combine harvester at a 40 per cent subsidy on cost limited to Rs 24 lakh; capital subsidy on farm machinery is routed through the Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation with the bank as the financing channel.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 10 per cent is far below any mechanisation subsidy slab.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 20 per cent understates the assistance available on high-value machinery.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 50 per cent is the slab for small and marginal, SC/ST and women farmers on many implements, but the cost ceiling here does not match a combine harvester.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 60 per cent exceeds the highest slab under the mechanisation scheme.

key_note: Subsidy rates and cost ceilings on farm machinery change with each SMAM circular and vary by state and category of farmer. I cannot corroborate this exact pair of figures; verify against the current operational guidelines before publication.

short_explanation: Sugarcane converts solar energy to biomass most efficiently of the crops listed — a C4 plant with a long growing period and a dense canopy, reaching around 2 per cent conversion against well under 1 per cent for most crops.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Jowar is also a C4 crop with good efficiency, but its short duration and lower biomass leave it behind sugarcane.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Millets are efficient per unit of water but produce far less biomass per unit of land.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Rice is a C3 crop and loses a share of fixed carbon to photorespiration.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Sunflower is C3 and short-duration, with much lower total conversion.

common_traps: C4 crops — sugarcane, maize, sorghum — outrank C3 crops here. Duration matters too: a long-season crop intercepts light for more of the year.

short_explanation: Wind erosion is keyed as the dominant degradation process in India's semi-arid zone, where sparse vegetation, loose sandy soils and a long dry season leave the surface open to strong seasonal winds.
explanation_text: Soil degradation in India is dominated overall by water erosion, which affects the largest area nationally. Wind erosion is concentrated in the arid and semi-arid west — western Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat and Haryana — where it moves sand, buries fields and strips fine particles and organic matter from the surface. The control measures follow the process: shelterbelts and windbreaks, sand dune stabilisation, stubble mulching and keeping the ground covered through the dry months, rather than the bunding and terracing used against water erosion.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Water erosion is the dominant process nationally and in the humid and sub-humid zones, but not in the dry western tracts the stem asks about.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Rill erosion is a form of water erosion, not a separate dominant factor.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Sheet erosion is also a form of water erosion, the first stage before rills develop.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

common_traps: Rill and sheet erosion are both water erosion; listing them separately makes the answer look crowded when only two processes are really on offer.
key_note: Water erosion dominates India's degraded area overall, so a candidate reading the stem without the semi-arid qualifier can defend option B.

short_explanation: Elephant grass is Napier grass, Pennisetum purpureum, a tall perennial fodder grass grown for cut-and-carry feeding and widely used as the hybrid Bajra-Napier.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Bermuda grass (doob) is a low, creeping pasture grass, quite unlike the tall Napier.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Wheat grass refers to young wheat shoots used as a health food.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Lemon grass is an aromatic grass grown for its essential oil, not for fodder.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

topic_name: Crop production statistics and leading states
short_explanation: Potato occupies the largest area of the vegetables listed, at roughly 2 million hectares, and is also India's largest vegetable crop by production.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Tomato covers under a million hectares.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Onion is second on this list by area, at about 1.4 million hectares.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Okra is grown on a few hundred thousand hectares.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Brinjal covers roughly 0.7 million hectares.

topic_name: Soil types and their distribution in India
short_explanation: Black soil is self-ploughing: its montmorillonite clay swells when wet and shrinks on drying, opening deep cracks in summer through which surface material falls and the profile is churned.
explanation_text: This shrink-swell behaviour is why black soils are classed as Vertisols, from the Latin for turning. Practically it cuts both ways. The cracking gives a degree of natural tillage and lets the first rains enter deep, but when wet the soil becomes sticky and almost unworkable, so the tillage window is narrow and the crop is often sown on residual moisture. High clay and lime content give black soils their moisture retention and their suitability for cotton, which is why the Deccan trap region became India's cotton belt.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Red soils are light, porous and low in clay, and do not crack in this way.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Forest soils vary with slope and litter cover and have no shrink-swell character.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Alluvial soils are loamy and friable, easy to till but not self-churning.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Desert soils are sandy with almost no clay, so nothing swells or cracks.

short_explanation: The Union Budget 2020-21 announced a 16-point action plan for agriculture, irrigation and rural development, alongside an allocation of about Rs 2.83 lakh crore for the sector.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 5 points is an arbitrary figure; the budget speech set out sixteen.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 9 points is arbitrary here.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 11 points is arbitrary here.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 20 points is arbitrary; no twenty-point agriculture plan featured in this budget.

key_note: The plan covered model laws on land leasing and agricultural marketing, water-stressed district planning, solar pumps under PM-KUSUM, warehousing on Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority norms, Krishi Udaan and Kisan Rail.

topic_name: Irrigation projects and command area classification
short_explanation: A minor irrigation scheme is one with a culturable command area of up to 2,000 hectares; medium runs from 2,000 to 10,000 hectares and major above 10,000.
explanation_text: The classification is by culturable command area, the land that the scheme can actually irrigate, and it decides how a project is planned, funded and reported. Minor irrigation covers both groundwater structures — dugwells, shallow and deep tubewells — and small surface flow and lift schemes, and is counted through the Minor Irrigation Census. Most of India's irrigated area is served by minor irrigation, groundwater in particular, even though major projects draw more attention and money.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 100 hectares is far below the limit and matches no class boundary.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 200 hectares is not a boundary in this classification.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 500 hectares is not a boundary; it is sometimes quoted for micro-level schemes.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 10,000 hectares is the boundary between medium and major schemes, not the minor ceiling.

common_traps: 10,000 hectares belongs to the medium-major boundary. Picking it means moving one step up the classification.

short_explanation: The National Council of Applied Economic Research is keyed as knowledge partner to the Committee on Doubling Farmers' Income, the Ashok Dalwai committee constituted in 2016.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: NABARD supports rural credit and refinance and contributed to the discussion, but the key names the research institute.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: ICAR is the research and education body for agriculture, not the committee's knowledge partner.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: AVRDC is the world vegetable centre, with no role in this committee.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The options name different bodies, so they cannot all be right.

key_note: The Dalwai committee's fourteen-volume report is the durable content here — the seven sources of income growth it identified. I cannot corroborate the knowledge partner from memory; verify before publication.

short_explanation: Catadromous fish live in fresh water and migrate to the sea to breed — the eel is the standard example.
explanation_text: The two migration terms are mirror images and are told apart by where breeding happens. Anadromous fish, such as hilsa and salmon, live in the sea and run up rivers to spawn. Catadromous fish, such as the freshwater eel, do the reverse: they grow in rivers and lakes and go down to the sea to spawn. The root helps — ana- is upward, so upriver to breed, and cata- is downward, so downriver to the sea.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Anadromous is the exact reverse — sea-dwelling fish that ascend rivers to spawn, like hilsa.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Indian major carps breed in rivers and do not go to sea at all.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Goldfish is an ornamental freshwater species with no such migration.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Shrimp is not a fish, and the penaeid species run the opposite way, breeding offshore.

common_traps: Anadromous and catadromous differ by one syllable and point in opposite directions. Fix the pair on hilsa going up to breed and eel going down.

short_explanation: Ranikhet disease, the Indian name for Newcastle disease, is the most serious viral disease of poultry, capable of wiping out a flock; it is controlled by regular vaccination with the F, Lasota and R2B strains.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Duck plague is a serious viral disease but affects ducks, not poultry generally.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Inclusion body hepatitis affects poultry but is far less destructive than Ranikhet.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Foot and mouth disease is a disease of cloven-hoofed animals such as cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat and pig; birds do not get it.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Fowl cholera is bacterial, caused by Pasteurella multocida, so it fails the 'viral' part of the stem.

common_traps: The stem asks for a viral disease. Fowl cholera is bacterial and FMD is not a poultry disease at all, so both can be dropped at once.

topic_name: Plant nutrients, their functions and deficiency symptoms
short_explanation: Potassium drives sugar synthesis and movement in sugarcane: it activates the enzymes of photosynthesis and carries sugars from leaf to cane, which is why cane is a heavy potash feeder.
explanation_text: Potassium is the nutrient of quality rather than of bulk growth. It regulates stomatal opening, activates enzymes including those of starch and sugar metabolism, and drives phloem loading so that photosynthates move to the storage tissue. In sugarcane that shows up directly as juice sucrose content and recovery percentage; potassium deficiency gives thin canes, marginal scorching of older leaves and poor juice quality. Nitrogen, by contrast, builds vegetative growth, and excess nitrogen late in the season actually depresses sucrose.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Calcium builds cell walls and keeps membranes stable; it is not the sugar translocation nutrient.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Iron is a micronutrient needed for chlorophyll synthesis, required in traces.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Nitrogen drives vegetative growth and cane tonnage; applied late it lowers sucrose rather than raising it.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Sodium is not an essential nutrient for sugarcane and has no such role.

common_traps: Nitrogen gives tonnage, potassium gives sugar. Reaching for nitrogen because it is the big fertiliser is the usual slip.

topic_name: Crop diseases and their causal agents
short_explanation: Groundnut rosette is caused by a virus complex transmitted by the aphid Aphis craccivora, producing stunted plants with bunched, chlorotic or mottled leaves.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Fungi cause tikka leaf spot, rust and stem rot in groundnut, none of which give the rosette symptom.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Bacterial wilt affects groundnut in some regions but causes wilting, not rosetting.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Iron deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis of young leaves without the bunching and stunting.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Calcium deficiency in groundnut shows as pops and unfilled pods, since calcium is taken up by the developing pod.

common_traps: Rosetting looks like a nutrient disorder because the leaves are chlorotic and bunched, which pulls candidates toward the deficiency options. The aphid vector is the clue that it is viral.

short_explanation: Once the arrangement is fixed, only floors 2 and 7 are left for Ramesh and Ishant, and those two floors belong to the Odisha man and the Bihar man; nothing says which friend is on which, so Ramesh is from either Bihar or Odisha.
explanation_text: Reading the floors from the bottom up: Lovish on 1 from Assam, the Odisha man on 2, Rajesh on 3 from Gujarat, Jayesh on 4 from Kerala, Viresh on 5 from Delhi, Tapesh on 6 from Goa, and the Bihar man on 7. Ramesh and Ishant take floors 2 and 7, and nothing in the clues says which of them takes which. Jayesh, Viresh and Tapesh occupy three consecutive floors in that order going up, and with Rajesh on 3 the only room is 4-5-6. Lovish must have exactly one floor between himself and Rajesh, so he takes floor 1. Floor 7 is Bihar and floor 3 Gujarat, so the Kerala-Delhi pair can only be floors 4 and 5, and since Viresh is not from Kerala he is the Delhi man on 5 and Jayesh the Kerala man on 4. Odisha is two floors away from Jayesh, so floor 2 or floor 6; Goa cannot sit below Odisha, so Odisha takes floor 2, Goa floor 6 and Assam floor 1.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Bihar alone would need Ramesh pinned to floor 7, and he may equally be the Odisha man on floor 2.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Kerala is Jayesh's state, on floor 4.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Odisha alone would need Ramesh pinned to floor 2, and he may equally be the Bihar man on floor 7.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Assam belongs to Lovish on floor 1.

key_note: Solved from the direction block that every row of Q.1 to Q.5 carries. The Goa clue has to be read as Goa being nowhere below Odisha; read narrowly as 'not immediately below', a second arrangement survives (Lovish on floor 1 from Kerala, Delhi on 2, Goa on 4, Odisha on 6), which the keys rule out.

short_explanation: Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0, announced in October 2021 for a five-year run, carries an outlay of about ₹1.41 lakh crore and shifts the focus from building toilets to garbage-free cities, faecal sludge management and used-water treatment.
explanation_text: SBM-U 2.0 is the second phase of the urban sanitation mission. Phase one (2014-2019) was built around open-defecation-free status and household and community toilets. Phase two keeps ODF but adds ODF+ and ODF++ targets, legacy-dump remediation, source segregation of waste and treatment of used water in towns below one lakh population. It was launched alongside AMRUT 2.0, which handles drinking water and sewerage; the two outlays are announced together and are easy to swap.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: ₹1.31 lakh crore is not the outlay of either urban mission; the SBM-U 2.0 figure announced was ₹1.41 lakh crore.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: ₹2.64 lakh crore matches no announced urban mission outlay.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: ₹2.54 lakh crore matches no announced urban mission outlay.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: ₹2.87 lakh crore is the AMRUT 2.0 outlay, announced in the same statement, not SBM-U 2.0.

common_traps: ₹2.87 lakh crore belongs to AMRUT 2.0, which was launched on the same day; SBM-U 2.0 is the smaller of the two.

short_explanation: West Bengal is the largest vegetable producing state in the country, and the Second Advance Estimates for 2020-21 kept it at the top of the vegetable table.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Andhra Pradesh leads in some individual crops such as chillies and papaya, but its total vegetable output is well below West Bengal's.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Uttarakhand is a small hill state; its vegetable output is a fraction of the leading states' and it never figures among the major producers.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Odisha is a sizeable vegetable producer but sits below West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Madhya Pradesh is among the top few vegetable states, but its share stays behind West Bengal's.

key_note: West Bengal's lead rests mainly on potato and other winter vegetables; Uttar Pradesh is usually the close second.

short_explanation: Lovish is the only friend who can take floor 1 — he needs one floor between himself and Rajesh on floor 3 — and floor 1 turns out to be the Assam man, so this combination holds.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Tapesh is from Goa, but he is on floor 6, not floor 5.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Kerala is right for Jayesh, but his floor is 4, not 6.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Floor 2 is indeed the Odisha man, but it may be Ramesh rather than Ishant, so this is not fixed.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Delhi is right for Viresh, but he is on floor 5, not floor 4.

key_note: Solved from the direction block that every row of Q.1 to Q.5 carries. The Goa clue has to be read as Goa being nowhere below Odisha; read narrowly as 'not immediately below', a second arrangement survives (Lovish on floor 1 from Kerala, Delhi on 2, Goa on 4, Odisha on 6), which the keys rule out. Option D is the near miss: the floor and the state match, only the name is not pinned down.

short_explanation: CHAMAN stands for Coordinated programme on Horticulture Assessment and MANagement using geoinformatics, run by the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre to estimate horticultural area and production from satellite data.
explanation_text: CHAMAN uses remote sensing and sample surveys to fix the area and yield of selected horticultural crops in the major producing districts, so that the Department of Agriculture's horticulture estimates rest on measured imagery rather than only on state reporting. It runs alongside the older FASAL system, which does the same job for field crops.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: FASAL is the forecasting system for field crops, not horticulture, using space, agro-meteorological and land-based observations.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: MNCFC is the centre that implements CHAMAN; it is an institution, not the programme or portal named in the question.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: CCE means crop cutting experiment, the field method of estimating yield, not a geoinformatics portal.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: No horticulture geoinformatics portal carries this name; the KISAN pilot deals with crop insurance using space technology.

short_explanation: Under the Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana a borrower could take up to ₹10 lakh, the ceiling of the Tarun slab, as a collateral-free loan for a non-farm income-generating activity.
explanation_text: MUDRA loans come in three slabs by ticket size: Shishu up to ₹50,000, Kishore from ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh, and Tarun from ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh. The loan is made by a bank, NBFC or microfinance institution to a micro enterprise in manufacturing, trading, services or allied agriculture; MUDRA, a SIDBI subsidiary, refinances the lender. The credit is collateral-free, and guarantee cover comes from the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: ₹2 lakh is not the boundary of any MUDRA slab.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: ₹5 lakh is the top of the Kishore slab, not the scheme's ceiling — Tarun runs above it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: ₹20 lakh is above the ceiling as it stood; the Tarun Plus slab up to ₹20 lakh came only in 2024.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: ₹2 crore is the kind of limit used for credit-guarantee and infrastructure-fund products, not for MUDRA.

common_traps: ₹5 lakh is where Kishore ends and Tarun begins; the question asks for the scheme ceiling, which is the top of Tarun.

short_explanation: The Second Advance Estimates for 2020-21 put total horticulture production at about 329.86 million tonnes, a record at the time and comfortably above foodgrain production.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 330.98 million tonnes is close to the estimate but not the figure reported in this round; the later revised estimate for the year was higher than this.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 345.68 million tonnes overstates the year's output by a wide margin.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 32.68 million tonnes is out by a factor of ten and would be smaller than a single major crop's output.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 33.98 million tonnes is likewise a decimal slip; national horticulture output is in the hundreds of million tonnes.

common_traps: Two options move the decimal point one place, so a hurried reader can pick 32.68 or 33.98 for 329.86 or 339.8.

short_explanation: After the July 2021 reshuffle Piyush Goyal held Commerce and Industry, Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, and Textiles — statements 1, 2 and 3.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Railways and Labour and Employment were not with him — Railways went to Ashwini Vaishnaw and Labour to Bhupender Yadav.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Commerce and Industry alone understates his charge; Consumer Affairs and Textiles were also his.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Railways was Ashwini Vaishnaw's portfolio from July 2021.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 2 are right but Railways is not; Textiles is the third correct one.

common_traps: Goyal did hold Railways until 7 July 2021, so anyone answering from an older list picks Railways; the question is set after that reshuffle.
key_note: Portfolio questions are date-sensitive. On any reading before 7 July 2021 the answer would have included Railways and excluded Textiles.

short_explanation: Each friend is being matched with the state of the person one floor above him: Lovish on 1 with Odisha on 2, Rajesh on 3 with Kerala on 4, so Tapesh on 6 goes with Bihar on 7.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Goa is Tapesh's own state, not the state of the floor above him.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Assam is on floor 1, which is Lovish's own floor.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Gujarat is Rajesh's own state, on floor 3.

option_rationales.label: D

short_explanation: NEP 2020 replaces the 10+2 structure with a 5+3+3+4 design covering ages 3 to 18.
explanation_text: The four stages are foundational (five years — three of pre-school plus Classes 1 and 2, ages 3 to 8), preparatory (three years, Classes 3 to 5, ages 8 to 11), middle (three years, Classes 6 to 8, ages 11 to 14) and secondary (four years, Classes 9 to 12, ages 14 to 18). The change that matters is at the two ends: three years of pre-school are brought inside the formal structure for the first time, and Classes 11 and 12 stop being a separate stream and become part of a single four-year secondary stage with subject choice across streams.

option_rationales.rationale: 5+3+3+3 gives secondary only three years; NEP's secondary stage spans Classes 9 to 12, four years.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 5+4+3+3 stretches the preparatory stage to four years and shortens secondary; preparatory is three years.

option_rationales.rationale: 5+3+3+2 keeps the old two-year higher-secondary block instead of merging it into a four-year stage.

option_rationales.label: D

short_explanation: MGNREGA obliges the Programme Officer to provide work within 15 days of the application, or of the date from which work is sought if that is later; failing that the applicant is entitled to an unemployment allowance.
explanation_text: The entitlement structure has three numbers that get mixed up. One hundred days is the guaranteed employment per rural household per financial year. Fifteen days is the deadline for providing that work after a valid application. Fifteen days is also the period within which wages must be paid, after which delay compensation runs. Work is to be provided within 5 km of the village, and a travel allowance of 10% of the wage is due beyond that. The unemployment allowance, where work is not given in time, is paid by the state government, which gives states a direct incentive to provide work.

The PMC Bank episode showed the cost of that sequence. The amended Section 45 lets the RBI act on a scheme first and keep the bank running, so depositors are not locked out while the resolution is put together.

short_explanation: Hardening is the stage in which plantlets raised in the nursery or in tissue culture are gradually exposed to outside conditions so that they survive transplanting to the field.
explanation_text: Plants grown in a culture vessel or a protected nursery have thin cuticles, poorly functioning stomata and weak root systems because humidity is high and light is low. Hardening steps the plants down in stages, lowering humidity and raising light and temperature over days or weeks, so that the plant builds the cuticle and root function it needs outdoors. Without it, mortality after transplanting is heavy.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Domestication is the long process of bringing a wild species into cultivation over generations, not the short acclimatisation of raised plantlets.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Agronomy is the branch of science dealing with field crop production and soil management.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Erosion is the removal of topsoil by water or wind and has nothing to do with raising plants.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Genome editing is targeted alteration of DNA sequence in the laboratory.

short_explanation: All three statements hold: the amendment leaves out primary agricultural credit societies and societies whose main business is long-term agricultural finance, it lets the RBI frame a reconstruction or amalgamation scheme without a moratorium, and it does not disturb the state registrars' powers over co-operatives.
explanation_text: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 was the response to the PMC Bank failure. It brought urban co-operative banks and multi-state co-operative banks under the RBI's banking supervision — board qualifications, appointment of the chief executive, capital raising and audit. What it did not do is end dual control: registration, elections, membership and administration of the society stay with the state or central registrar. And it deliberately excluded primary agricultural credit societies and long-term agricultural credit societies, which are not deposit-taking urban banks and remain under co-operative law.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 2 are right, but so is 3 — the registrars' powers under state co-operative law were expressly preserved.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 3 are right, but so is 2 — the moratorium precondition was removed.

option_rationales.rationale: Statements 2 and 3 are right, but so is 1 — PACS and long-term agricultural credit societies are excluded.

option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 is right, but statements 2 and 3 are also correct.

option_rationales.label: E

short_explanation: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers 3 days of pre-hospitalisation and 15 days of post-hospitalisation expenses, intensive and non-intensive care, cashless treatment at any empanelled public or private hospital anywhere in India, and implants where medically needed — so every statement holds.
explanation_text: PM-JAY gives ₹5 lakh of cover per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation to roughly the bottom 40% of households, identified from the deprivation and occupational criteria of the 2011 Socio-Economic Caste Census. The cover is defined by a package rate list, is entirely cashless and paperless at the point of service, and carries no premium for the beneficiary. Diagnostics, medicines, consumables, ICU, implants and the pre- and post-hospitalisation windows are inside the package rate rather than billed separately — which is why all four statements in this question are features rather than a mix.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 2 are right, but so are 3 and 4 — portability to any empanelled hospital and implants are both covered.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are right, but implants are covered too.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are right, but so is 2 — both ICU and non-ICU care are in the package.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 3 are right, but statements 2 and 4 are also correct.

topic_name: Types of forestry and social forestry
short_explanation: Extension forestry is the raising of trees on blank areas away from the conventional forest estate, such as canal banks, roadsides, railway lines and village wasteland, purely to extend the area under tree cover.
explanation_text: Extension forestry is treated as one component of social forestry, so the two terms overlap. The distinction that the examiners want is the location: social forestry is the broad programme of growing trees for the community's fuel, fodder and small timber needs, while extension forestry specifically means pushing tree cover into treeless land outside recorded forests. Agroforestry, by contrast, keeps trees and crops or livestock on the same piece of land at the same time.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Social forestry is the wider programme of raising trees for community needs; extension forestry is the part of it that targets treeless areas away from forests.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Agroforestry deliberately combines trees with crops or livestock on the same land, which the stem does not describe.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Ecological forestry is not a recognised category in this classification.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Mixed forestry means raising more than one species together, usually for fodder and fuel, and says nothing about location.

key_note: Since extension forestry is a component of social forestry, option A is arguably part-right; the stem's insistence on land devoid of tree growth away from conventional forest areas is what settles it on extension forestry.
