option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Z is on Friday — the far end of the four-day gap from A.

key_note: Solved from the instruction block, which is carried in both rows although it is headed 'for Q.11'. The full order is Monday A, Tuesday D, Wednesday C, Thursday N, Friday Z.

short_explanation: NEP 2020 rests on access, equity, quality, affordability and accountability; leadership is not one of its pillars.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Access is one of the five pillars — bringing every child aged 3 to 18 into the system.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Affordability is one of the five pillars.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Equity is one of the five pillars, and drives the policy's treatment of socio-economically disadvantaged groups.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Accountability is one of the five pillars, and underlies the separation of regulation from operation in school and higher education.

topic_name: Soil classification systems and soil orders
short_explanation: Loamy soil is the balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay with organic matter, and that mix is why it drains well while still holding moisture and nutrients, making it the best general agricultural soil.
explanation_text: Soil texture is decided by the proportion of sand, silt and clay particles. Sandy soil drains fast and holds little water or nutrients; clayey soil holds water and nutrients but drains poorly and is hard to work; loam sits between the two. Organic matter improves structure in any texture but is what makes loam particularly productive.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Sandy soil is dominated by coarse particles, drains too quickly and holds few nutrients.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Clayey soil is dominated by the finest particles, holds water to the point of waterlogging and cracks on drying.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Sandy and loamy cannot both be right, since the two are different textural classes.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

common_traps: The stem's list of sand, silt and organic matter tempts a reader towards sandy soil; it is the balance of all three particle sizes that defines loam.
tag_note: The item is about soil texture classes such as sand, silt, clay and loam, not about taxonomic soil classification systems or soil orders.

short_explanation: Some Hero are Actor and all Actor are Dancer, so those Heroes are Dancers; and reversing the same statement, some Actor are Hero, and all Hero are Zero, so some Actor are Zero. Both conclusions follow.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion I does follow, but so does II, through the chain some Actor are Hero and all Hero are Zero.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion II does follow, but so does I, through some Hero are Actor and all Actor are Dancer.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: An either-or pair needs two conclusions that are uncertain and complementary; here both are definite.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Both conclusions are established by definite chains, so neither can be rejected.

short_explanation: Growing a short duration crop alongside sugarcane so that it is harvested before the cane matures, with neither crop cutting into the other's yield, is companion cropping; sugarcane with potato or with onion is the standard example.
explanation_text: Companion cropping is the case where the yield of each of the two crops is essentially the same as it would have been grown alone, because their peak demands fall at different times. Sugarcane takes ten to eighteen months and grows slowly at first, so a short crop can use the wide inter-row space and the early season and be off the field before the cane closes its canopy.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Intercropping is the general term for growing two crops together in a definite row pattern; it does not carry the specific condition that neither crop's yield falls.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A nurse crop is grown to shelter or support the main crop in its early stage, which is not what a short cash crop with sugarcane is doing.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: In relay cropping the second crop is sown into the standing first crop near its maturity, so the second crop is harvested after the first, not before.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Alternate cropping means growing different crops on the same land in successive seasons, not together.

common_traps: Intercropping is the broad family that companion cropping belongs to; the stem's detail about the short crop being harvested before sugarcane matures without loss is what picks the narrower term.
key_note: Several textbooks would simply call sugarcane plus potato an intercrop, so intercropping is a defensible loose answer; companion cropping is the specific term the examiner is testing.

short_explanation: All Pet are Dog and no Dog is Cat, so no Pet is a Cat, and that reverses to no Cat is Pet. The second conclusion only claims a possibility, and nothing in the statements blocks an Animal from being a Dog, so it also holds.
explanation_text: Conclusions phrased with 'can be' or 'may be' are possibility conclusions, and they follow whenever the statements do not rule the situation out. Here some Cat are Animal, and those Cats are certainly not Dogs; but the class of Animals is not confined to those Cats, so other Animals being Dogs is left open, and the possibility stands.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion I does follow, but II is a possibility conclusion that nothing contradicts, so it follows too.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion II does follow, but so does I, from all Pet are Dog together with no Dog is Cat.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or applies to two uncertain conclusions that between them cover every case; that is not the relation here.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: I is definite and II is an unblocked possibility, so both stand.

common_traps: 'Some Animal can be Dog' is a possibility, not a claim of fact; testing it as though it asserted that some Animals are Dogs leads to rejecting it wrongly.

short_explanation: NEP 2020 is stated to be aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and specifically with Sustainable Development Goal 4 on inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: There is no UN framework called the 2030 Agenda for Development; the agenda adopted in 2015 is for sustainable development.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Green growth is an economic-policy idea, not the name of the UN agenda NEP cites.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Green development is not a UN agenda title.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The Fifth Technological Revolution is not a UN agenda; the policy's anchor is SDG 4.

short_explanation: No tillage, also called zero tillage, leaves the soil undisturbed between harvest and planting except for the narrow slot opened for the seed or for nutrient injection.
explanation_text: The tillage ladder runs from conventional tillage through minimum tillage to no tillage. Conservation tillage is defined by outcome rather than by operation: any system that leaves at least thirty per cent of the surface covered with crop residue after planting qualifies, so no tillage is one way of achieving conservation tillage. Zero till wheat after rice in the Indo-Gangetic plain is the familiar Indian case, saving a turnaround time and a good deal of diesel and water.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Minimum tillage reduces the number of operations to the minimum needed for a seedbed, but it still disturbs the soil.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Conservation tillage is the wider category defined by residue cover left on the surface; no tillage is the specific system described here.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Sustainable tillage is not a defined tillage class.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Fallowing means leaving land uncropped for a season to restore moisture or fertility; it is not a tillage system. The option text also carries a stray answer fragment.

common_traps: Conservation tillage and no tillage are easy to swap; the stem describes the operation, which is the definition of no tillage.
key_note: Option E in the source paper carries leftover text reading 'Solution - (c)', which leaks the key; the item itself is sound.

topic_name: Education sector market and online learning
short_explanation: All three statements match UNICEF's findings on schooling during the pandemic: hours of online learning do not substitute for the same hours in a classroom, remote learning in India reached urban children far more than rural ones, and civil-society organisations filled part of the gap for children who were cut off.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is correct, but so are the other two — the urban skew of remote learning is one of UNICEF's central findings.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, but so is statement 1 on the quality gap between online hours and classroom hours.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, but so is statement 2.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, but so is statement 3.

key_note: The UNICEF passage this row refers to is not in question_text and no other row in the chunk carries it. The answer is reconstructed from the three statements, each of which matches UNICEF's documented pandemic schooling findings, but the specific report and its wording should be checked before publication.

short_explanation: Some Brown are Red, and no Brown is Key, so those Red things are not Keys; and every Brown is a Horse while no Brown is a Key, so some Horses are not Keys. Both follow.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion I follows, but II follows as well, since the Browns are Horses and none of them is a Key.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion II follows, but so does I, through the Browns that are Red.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or needs two uncertain, mutually exhaustive conclusions; both of these are definite.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Both are drawn by definite chains, so neither can be denied.

short_explanation: 'messy room feels dirty' and 'water save dirty' share only the word dirty, and their codes share only 'op', so dirty is op.
explanation_text: The method is to compare sentences two at a time and match the shared words with the shared codes. Working through all four: the first and third share messy and room, giving the pair ja and sa; the first and second share room and bad, giving ta and sa; the code common to both pairs is sa, so room is sa, messy is ja and bad is ta. That leaves la for looks, ty for senior, nm for feels, and vs and rt for water and save in some order.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: rt belongs to water or save; which of the two cannot be told from the sentences given.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: vs is the other of water and save, again not separable from these sentences.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: ty is senior, the only new word in 'senior room bad'.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

key_note: Solved from the four coded sentences carried in both rows of Q.16 and Q.17.

short_explanation: 'messy room looks bad' and 'messy room feels dirty' share messy and room, whose codes are ja and sa; comparing 'messy room looks bad' with 'senior room bad' shows room is sa, so ja is messy.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Room is sa — the code common to all three sentences that contain the word.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Looks is la, the only code left in 'messy room looks bad' once room, messy and bad are placed.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Bad is ta, the code shared by the first and second sentences besides sa.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Senior is ty, the only new code in 'senior room bad'.

key_note: Solved from the four coded sentences carried in both rows of Q.16 and Q.17.

short_explanation: F = J, so J > B follows at once from B < F. A and F are both greater than B, but nothing links them to each other, so A > F cannot be drawn.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A > F is exactly the conclusion that fails: both A and F stand above B, which fixes no order between them.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or needs two uncertain complementary conclusions; here II is definite.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion II is definite, so 'neither follows' is wrong.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion I does not follow, so the two cannot both be accepted.

common_traps: Two quantities that are each bigger than a common third quantity have no fixed order between them.

short_explanation: B and O sit on separate branches below A, so neither B > O nor O ≥ B can be proved; but between them the two conclusions cover every case, so exactly one of them must be true — the either-or situation.
explanation_text: An either-or answer needs two things at once. First, neither conclusion may be provable on its own: here A > B and A = C > O place both B and O below A without connecting them. Second, the two conclusions must be complements, together covering every possibility: O ≥ B and B > O do exactly that, since if O is not greater than or equal to B then B must exceed O.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: O ≥ B cannot be established on its own; B and O are linked only through A.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: B > O cannot be established on its own either, for the same reason.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 'Neither follows' would be right only if the pair were not complementary; here one of the two must hold.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Both cannot hold together — they are opposites.

common_traps: Check the pair for complementarity before answering 'neither follows': O ≥ B and B > O leave no third possibility.

short_explanation: The chain runs O < F = J < A < I = K in one unbroken direction, so A > O and, since K equals I which is above A which is above F, K > F. Both follow.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion I follows, but so does II: F = J < A < I = K.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Conclusion II follows, but so does I: O < F = J < A.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or applies to uncertain complementary pairs; both of these are definite.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The chain is unbroken, so both conclusions are established.

tag_note: Nothing in this item is coded — it is a plain single-chain inequality. A tag such as 'Single-chain direct inequality' fits; 'coded inequality' belongs to items where symbols stand in for the relations.

short_explanation: The closing paragraph tells India not to beg for a seat and to build economic strength instead: 'If that status is due, the rest of the world shall see that.' On the author's view the seat follows from a strong economy rather than from lobbying.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The author rejects campaigning of every kind, not just undignified campaigning. Applying 'judicious clout' is still asking for the seat, which is what 'nor do we need to beg' rules out.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The passage ties the seat to economic strength, not to nuclear status. On nuclear recognition the author says only that the Prime Minister's declaration is already enough.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This waters the claim down to a possibility. The author is not hedging: he says the world will want to do business with a strong India and will see for itself that the status is due.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Nothing in the passage has other countries pressing India's case, and 'consternation' is nowhere in the argument. The author's point is that India should stop asking.

common_traps: D says almost the same thing but with 'may'. The tone of the last paragraph is settled rather than tentative, which is what separates the two.
key_note: D is the cautious reading of the same lines and would fit a question asking what the passage proves; the question asks for the author's position, which is the confident version.

topic_name: Vocabulary from context within a passage
short_explanation: 'Lingering vestiges' are the surviving scraps of something fading, and what is fading here is the 'myth of nuclear superiority' guarded by a cartel of five powers. 'Fragile dated beliefs about superiority' keeps both the frailty and the outdatedness.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The unipolar world is a separate idea in the passage, the balance of power built by the sole superpower. The phrase in question is about a belief in nuclear supremacy, not about the structure of world power.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Nuclear capability is a fact, and India's test did not shatter anyone's capability. The passage is explicit that what was demolished is a 'myth'.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The five powers themselves were not shattered; their claim to exclusivity was. A vestige is a remnant of a thing, not the thing.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 'Stout' means sturdy, which contradicts 'lingering vestiges' - the point is that these beliefs are worn out. 'Not to be inferior' also reverses the sense of dominance.

common_traps: E copies the 'dated beliefs' half correctly and flips the adjective. Test the modifier, not just the noun: vestiges linger, so they cannot be stout.

short_explanation: The author writes as an Indian arguing India's case - 'India has no option but to meet the nuclear blackmail of China', 'Let us concentrate on building up our economic strength.' That partisan pride in the national interest is a nationalistic attitude.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: An objective writer would weigh the costs he promises at the start to take note of. He never does; the whole piece argues one side.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: He is critical of China and the USA, but in passing and in service of the larger claim about India's position. Criticism is one strand here, not the attitude of the piece.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Ambivalence means being pulled two ways. The author shows no doubt at all about the tests or about India's course.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Confidence in one's country is not arrogance. He claims nothing beyond India's right to deter and its capacity to grow, and belittles no one's worth.

common_traps: 'Critical' feels right just after the paragraph on China and the USA. Attitude has to be judged from the whole passage, and the closing exhortation is pro-India rather than anti-anyone.

short_explanation: The passage says the USA 'looked the other way' and legislated to help build up Pakistan, that is, it eased the violations rather than holding them back. An inference that the USA retarded such violations runs against the text.
explanation_text: Each of the other four can be traced to a line. China's help to Pakistan came 'violating commitments under agreements and against the spirit of non-proliferation measures like NPT, CTBT, FMCT and MTCR'; 'It is now established that India can produce nuclear warheads and the means of delivering them'; and the last paragraph promises that economic strength will bring both business and, in due course, the seat. In a CANNOT-be-inferred question the answer is the option the passage contradicts or never touches, not the one that is merely hard to prove.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The passage states this almost directly - China built Pakistan against India 'violating commitments under agreements and against the spirit of non-proliferation measures like NPT, CTBT, FMCT and MTCR'.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 'It is now established that India can produce nuclear warheads and the means of delivering them' settles this, and the author adds that the myth of the five-power monopoly has been demolished.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The last paragraph makes exactly this link: build economic strength, and the world will see that the status is due.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The author takes India's economic rise as given - 'Let us concentrate on building up our economic strength. The world will, then, want to do business with us.'

common_traps: 'Retarded certain international violations' means slowed the violations down. A hurried reader sees 'USA' and 'violations' in one line and treats the option as matching the passage, when it reverses what the USA did.

short_explanation: The last paragraph rests on self-sufficiency: 'we are not dependent on others for anything basic', and little is lost if the world does not buy Indian goods. If globalisation has made self-sustenance a myth, that foundation goes.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A Security Council that rarely settles disputes supports the author, who says India need not beg for a seat there. It cannot weaken him.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The order in which countries acquired warheads has no bearing on whether India can stand alone economically.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This attacks the deterrence argument earlier in the passage, not the claim about economic self-reliance in the last paragraph.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Willing recognition by the permanent members makes the author's advice - stop asking, the world will come round - easier to follow, not harder.

common_traps: Several options attack the passage somewhere. The question fences the target to the last paragraph, which is about economic independence alone.

short_explanation: 'A threat to' is the fixed pairing, and the sentence needs a word for a danger that is spreading: the totalitarian philosophy endangers mankind and civilization.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A plague is a disease or an infestation, and idiom wants 'a plague on' or 'a plague of', not 'to'.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Torment is suffering already being felt. The sentence is about what endangers mankind, not about pain inflicted.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A burden is a weight to be carried. A philosophy that must be understood and fought is a danger, not a load.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Gehenna means hell or a place of torment, so it cannot be 'the greatest ___ to mankind'.

short_explanation: The passage answers itself two sentences later - 'No tyrant has ever lasted long by force of arms alone' - and the argument is about rulers who seize power on a claim to represent the common good.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A sovereign holds power by lawful title. The sentence is about rising to power on a claim, which is the tyrant's route.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A baron is a rank of nobility, not a ruler who climbs to power on a claim about the common good.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: An emperor holds an inherited or conquered throne, and the word carries none of the illegitimacy the paragraph is describing.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A suzerain is an overlord to whom a tributary state answers - a relation between states, not a ruler on the rise.

common_traps: All five words name rulers. The deciding evidence is the passage's own repetition of 'tyrant' in the very next sentence.

short_explanation: Perpetrate is the verb English reserves for crimes and atrocities, and the subject here is 'Horrors'. Perpetrated with a clear conscience is precisely the charge being laid against the 'altruists'.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Interpreted means explained or construed. Horrors are committed here, not read.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Executed fits orders, plans and sentences and is neutral about wrongdoing, so it loses the moral weight 'horrors' demands.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Wreak takes havoc, vengeance or destruction as its object rather than 'horrors', and it suggests fury rather than the calm conscience the sentence insists on.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Elucidated means made clear, the wrong sense entirely.

common_traps: 'Wreaked' sounds destructive enough to pass. Its collocation is narrow: one wreaks havoc, one perpetrates a horror.

short_explanation: The 'altruists' defend their own conduct by appealing to the common good, and 'justify themselves by' is the idiom for that.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Propitiate means to appease someone who is angry. A person does not appease himself by the common good.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Sustain would mean keeping themselves going, a physical or financial sense; the sentence is about excusing horrors.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: To establish oneself is to become settled or recognised, which has nothing to do with the clear conscience under discussion.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Bespeak means to indicate or to order in advance, and it does not take a reflexive object here.

short_explanation: The paragraph explains how tyrants hold men down without arms: the collectivist doctrine of state supremacy is the spiritual weapon, so men have been enslaved by it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Enriched reverses the sense. The spiritual weapons here are instruments of subjugation, not of gain.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Embittered names a mood, not the hold the paragraph is explaining; the line continues the point about tyrants lasting without force of arms.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Empowered is the opposite of the argument, which is that the doctrine puts the state above the individual.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Emancipate means to set free, and the form is wrong after 'have been'.

short_explanation: Inalienable rights are rights that cannot be taken away or signed away, which is exactly the clause that follows: rights 'of which they cannot be deprived for any cause whatsoever'.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Ineluctable means impossible to escape, said of fate or of a conclusion, not of rights held against others.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ineffaceable means impossible to rub out, used of marks and memories rather than entitlements.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Intangible means having no physical form. Rights may be intangible, but that says nothing about their being beyond deprivation.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Inexpungible is not standard English; the settled phrase in rights language is 'inalienable rights'.

short_explanation: The phrase pairs an obvious villain with a hidden one - 'neither by evildoer nor supposed benefactor' - and the whole passage warns against 'altruists' who do harm in the name of the common good.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A reprobate is an unprincipled person, so it repeats 'evildoer' instead of contrasting with it. 'Neither ... nor' needs two different kinds of threat.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A prude is merely straitlaced. Prudishness is no danger to rights and has no link to the common-good argument.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A debauchee is a person given to vice, again on the same side as the evildoer, so the contrast collapses.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A delinquent is an offender, which once more duplicates 'evildoer'.

common_traps: Three distractors are near-synonyms of 'evildoer'. The word 'supposed' is the signal: the second figure only appears to be good.

short_explanation: Sentences 1 and 2 stand on their own and break no rule. Sentence 3 needs 'among themselves' for a group acting on itself, 4 is a fragment beginning with 'or' that also misuses the idiom (robberies are pulled off, not pulled out), and 5 runs one verb across a noun phrase and an adjective - 'are constituent parts ... and detrimental'.
explanation_text: Three separate tests decide this set. A reflexive is required when the doers and those acted on are the same people, so a band of robbers keeps a sense of justice among themselves. A clause that opens with a coordinating conjunction and has no subject of its own is a fragment, and sentence 4 is that continuation of sentence 3. And after a single 'are', the items joined by 'and' must be of the same kind: 'are constituent parts of American civil society and are detrimental to the health of the broader society' repairs sentence 5.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Adds sentence 3, which needs 'among themselves' rather than 'among them'.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Keeps sentence 5, whose two complements after 'are' do not run parallel, and drops sentence 1, which is sound.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: These are the two flawed items - 3 for the reflexive and 4 for being a fragment with the wrong idiom.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence 4 cannot stand alone: it opens with 'or' and has no subject of its own.

key_note: The row carries only the five sentences; the instruction line asking which are grammatically correct is missing from the question text, and this explanation assumes it.

short_explanation: Sentences 2 and 5 are not sentences at all. 'In that where the 1986 explosion of the nuclear reactor dramatized the risks of nuclear power' has no main clause, and 'and the withdrawal of the state and privatization increases vulnerability' opens with 'and' and continues sentence 4.
explanation_text: A fragment is easiest to catch by reading the item alone, away from its neighbours. Sentence 2 is a subordinate opening left hanging, and sentence 5 is a second half that belongs to sentence 4. Sentence 5 carries an agreement fault as well: 'the withdrawal of the state and privatization' is a compound subject and takes 'increase'. Of the remaining items, sentence 1 needs only a closing comma round the parenthetical - 'was, Beck says, the' - and sentence 3 is complete, though 'promise of salvation' would be better than 'promise for'.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence 1 is a whole sentence with a punctuation slip, and sentence 3 is complete; neither is defective in the way 2 and 5 are.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Adds sentence 3, which stands on its own and makes sense.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence 3 is complete; the item that belongs beside 5 is 2, the hanging subordinate clause.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence 1 is a full sentence despite the missing comma, so it does not belong with the defective pair.

key_note: The instruction line is missing from the row. The set is answerable only as a pick-the-defective-sentences task, because sentence 4 is plainly sound yet appears in no option, so the question cannot be asking which sentences are correct.

short_explanation: 'Ideally' qualifies the providing, so it belongs immediately before 'provides', and the pair 'a group as well as an individual identity' has to be left intact. Only the first version does both.
explanation_text: Place a comment adverb next to the verb it comments on, and never between a verb and the object that completes it. 'Corporate culture ideally provides an individual worker with ...' reads as intended; moving 'ideally' rightwards makes the reader hold the verb open while an adverb intervenes, and parking it at the end of the clause leaves it drifting with nothing definite to attach to.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 'Provides an individual worker ideally with' splits the verb from the phrase 'with a group as well as an individual identity' that completes it.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 'Provides ideally an individual worker' wedges the adverb between the verb and its object.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: An 'ideally' tacked on at the end reads as an afterthought and attaches loosely to the whole clause rather than to what corporate culture does.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 'As well as ideally individual identity' breaks the parallel pair and loses the article before 'individual identity'.

short_explanation: Grade inflation is the subject, the description 'characterized by the increasing assignment of higher grades for the same academic achievement' belongs beside it, and the rise in GPA averages is the result. The keyed version puts all three in that order.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Placing the 'characterized by' phrase after 'GPA averages' makes it describe the rise rather than grade inflation.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is grammatical, but it front-loads the long description and delays the subject, so the cause and effect land less cleanly.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 'Led to a rise in overall GPA averages, the Grade inflation is characterized ...' leaves the opening participle dangling; it would need 'Having led'. 'The Grade inflation' is wrong as well.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This drops the defining feature, the same academic achievement, which is the whole content of the term, and substitutes the debate the paragraph raises only afterwards.

common_traps: C carries the same information as the keyed version and is not ungrammatical. The item asks for the tightest rewrite, so the near-miss has to be judged on order and emphasis.
key_note: C is defensible as a correct sentence; the key is preferred because it keeps the subject first with its description attached.

short_explanation: The passage ends by preferring real bad air to a harmless imitation, because 'knowing that the fumes are harmless may detract from the urgency of the situation'. The people who need to feel it are the delegates at the climate conference, that is, those who can act and are delaying.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The writer allows that the fake version has a point. The complaint is about what harmless fumes do to the sense of urgency, not about simulation failing as simulation.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This repeats the suggestion without the reason for it, and keeps the focus on the occasion rather than on the people whose complacency the last line targets.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is the supporting observation in the final sentence, not the conclusion the writer draws from it.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

key_note: C is a loose paraphrase of the same suggestion, so the two are close; the key is preferred because it names the decision-makers and the dithering that the closing line blames on harmless fumes.

short_explanation: Reading one article and running one search was enough to bring insurance pitches by email and by phone. What that shows is that the reading and searching trail was visible to others.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The episode points to an obvious route, what was read and what was searched, so this is not a case of the source being unknowable.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: No details were handed over. The writer only read an article and typed a search, so nothing was disclosed to an entity that could pass it on.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The passage records what happened, not what the law is. Whether privacy law is adequate is brought in from outside the paragraph.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

common_traps: B describes the familiar trade in customer data, which is true of the world but not of this incident, where nothing was disclosed to anyone.

short_explanation: Sentence 3 opens by naming conditional cash transfer in full, 5 picks it up as 'this strategy', 1 turns to the Latin American evidence, 4 continues with 'In those countries', and 2 closes by bringing the argument home to India: 3-5-1-4-2.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 32514 sends the India sentence to second place before the strategy has been explained, and it separates 1 from 4 although 'In those countries' needs the Latin American reference immediately before it.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 35214 puts India in the middle and ends on 'In those countries ... showed improvements', leaving the India thread hanging.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 31245 breaks the 1-4 pair with the India sentence, so 'In those countries' points at India, and it closes with the core principle, which belongs with the introduction.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 54321 opens with 'The core principle of this strategy' when no strategy has yet been named.

common_traps: 'In those countries' in sentence 4 is the strongest link in the set: it can only follow sentence 1, which is where Latin America enters.

short_explanation: Sentence 3 introduces the universities as what Britain still has, 5 adds their standing in the rankings, 2 turns with 'But ... also under threat', 4 presses the point with 'In fact, they have been dying a slow death', and 1 explains what lies at the heart of that crisis: 3-5-2-4-1.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 52341 begins with 5, which speaks of 'major British universities' before 3 has introduced them, and it drops 3 in after the turn to the threat.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 52314 has the same wrong opening and ends on 4, leaving the crisis named in 1 stranded in the middle.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 32145 skips 5 in the run-up and closes on the praise in 5, after the paragraph has already said the universities are dying.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 45321 opens with 'In fact, they ...' when 'they' has nothing to refer back to.

common_traps: Sentence 4's 'In fact' and sentence 2's 'But' are both continuation signals, so neither can open the paragraph; that leaves 3 or 5, and 5 already assumes the topic.

short_explanation: Lexis is a person's stock of words and a logomachy is a dispute about words. 'In spite of' needs that mismatch: he has the vocabulary for verbal battles yet rarely picks one.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Deportment is bearing or conduct and eugenics is selective breeding. The two are unrelated, and an enviable bearing has nothing to do with indulging in eugenics.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Epistemology is the theory of knowledge and prologues are introductions to works, so no contrast arises between possessing one and avoiding the other.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Polemics follow from egotism rather than contrast with it, so 'in spite of' collapses, and egotism is not something called enviable.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Both words are verbs, so neither can follow 'an enviable', and disgorging and regurgitating say much the same thing.

common_traps: D reads smoothly because both its words are combative. 'In spite of' demands opposition between the blanks, and egotism and polemics point the same way.

short_explanation: To lucubrate is to study hard, especially by night, and a luminary is an eminent figure. The studious childhood explains the eminence, which is what 'it is no accident' calls for.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Amnesia is memory loss and explains nothing that follows; an alumnus is also not what the largely self-taught Lincoln is remembered as becoming.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Perspicuity is clearness of expression, not an activity of childhood, and a protagonist is a role in a story rather than a standing in life.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Ergophobia is a dread of work, which would make what followed an accident rather than no accident.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Both words are verbs meaning to explain, so the second blank, which follows 'a/an' and needs a noun, cannot take 'explicate'.

common_traps: The second blank follows 'a/an' and must be a noun. That test alone removes the option offering two verbs.

short_explanation: The passage states it outright: revivals reject mass culture and look to the past, yet they are 'both a reaction against and a product of modernity'. That double character is the paradox.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The passage never compares how folk audiences and modern-music audiences receive revivals.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Being liked and hated at once is claimed nowhere; the paradox in the passage is about modernity, not about approval.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Authenticity is treated as a key criterion throughout. Its fading is offered as a reason revivals end, not as a sign that originality is sometimes dispensable.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Revivals are described as connecting present activity with the past, so a failure to present past incidents reverses the text.

short_explanation: The core revivalists are described as using 'their connections with institutions, the recording, radio or television industries, the media, non-profit organisations or the government' to promote the revival. That reach across many spheres is what carries it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: They learn from sources they believe to be authentic, but the passage never says that no one else can reach those sources.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Government is one channel among several, and the passage ranks none of them, so a claim that political connections make revivals more successful goes beyond it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The passage says the opposite: working from historical sources, the core group creates 'a new ethos, musical style and aesthetic parameters'.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Revivals are called natural allies of political and social movements, including nationalism, and the core group's channels include the government.

short_explanation: Serving musical and social movements is what revivals are, not a reason they end. The passage ties their limited lifespan to authenticity ceasing to guide them, to the aesthetic parameters coming to feel too constraining, and to the break-up into traditional and modern post-revival styles.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is one of the stated reasons: the revival may end 'when authenticity is no longer a guiding principle'.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This matches the post-revival split into traditional and progressive or modern styles, which displaces the revived form.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The passage names exactly this - the parameters set by the core revivalists come to be seen by revivalists themselves as too constraining.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Since the first of the two is a stated reason, a pairing that includes it cannot be the option that is not a reason.

common_traps: The stem asks which is NOT a reason, and option E bundles a genuine reason with the answer. Checking that first option on its own settles the item.

short_explanation: The passage calls revivals 'a product of specific historical circumstances and general intellectual and social trends' and natural allies of political and social movements. A revival whose progression is independent of social change is the one trait it does not claim.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Stated as a hallmark: activities in the present are positioned 'within a discourse of historical continuity and authenticity'.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Stated: institutions, the recording and broadcast industries, the media, non-profits and the government are all used to promote the revival.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Stated: a core group of dedicated revivalists formulates the repertoire, the stylistic features and the history.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This is the passage's own wording - revivals are 'a potent force in contemporary society'.

common_traps: The passage does say revivals 'maintain independent dynamics centred on music'. That means the music keeps its own momentum inside the alliance, not that the revival is sealed off from social change.

short_explanation: Revivalists are said to position themselves against the mainstream and to offer a cultural alternative, which is a stance towards mass culture. Turning that into a clash between the objective of revivals and the objective of contemporary mainstream music attributes an aim to mainstream music that the passage never discusses.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The passage gives the core revivalists 'an overt cultural and political agenda' aimed at broad social and cultural change.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The passage says the political agenda of some folk revivals may include asserting one ethnicity over another or backing a national agenda.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The passage has revivals ending when authenticity stops guiding them or when their parameters come to feel too constraining, which is the objective losing its hold.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The passage says the core group derives its musical style and aesthetic parameters from historical sources; the option's 'cosmetic' stands in for 'aesthetic'.

common_traps: 'Position themselves in opposition to the mainstream' looks like a direct match for the keyed option. It describes a cultural stance against mass culture, not a contest of objectives with another kind of music.
key_note: The keyed option is the one that travels furthest beyond the text rather than one the passage flatly contradicts, which is what makes the item close.

short_explanation: A lector is the reader who delivers the lesson at a service, which fits a weekly homily, and jetsam is cargo thrown overboard. The caution is against treating any part of creation as something to be discarded.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A progenitor is an ancestor, and congenial means agreeable; being warned against treating creation as agreeable makes no sense with the reason the sentence gives.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A nestor is a wise old counsellor, which could fit the first blank, but stygian means hellish or gloomy and has nothing to do with a thing being purposeless.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: An inductor is not the person who gives a homily, and 'defunct' would say the thing no longer works rather than that it is fit to be thrown away.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A doyenne is a senior woman in a field, and salvage means rescue, the opposite of what the sentence needs.

common_traps: 'Nestor' and 'doyenne' are tempting as people who might preach. The second blank decides the item: only a word for discarded matter fits 'since every creation of God has a definite purpose'.

short_explanation: 'But' asks for opposition. Docile means yielding and compliant, doctrinaire means rigidly insisting on a doctrine - the job forces a naturally pliant man into inflexibility.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 'A native nature' says nothing, and insouciant means carefree, which is not something a job requires.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Caddish means dishonourable and judicious means sound in judgement. A job may want judgement, but it is not the counterpart of caddishness, and one person can be both.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Gregarious means sociable and prescient means able to foresee. The two are unrelated, so the contrast 'but' promises never arrives.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Sapient and shrewd are close in meaning, which leaves the sentence contradicting itself at 'but'.

key_note: B reads as a contrast on a quick pass, so the item turns on how exact the opposition is: docile and doctrinaire sit on the same axis of flexibility, caddish and judicious do not.

short_explanation: Bated breath, appraise the damage, balmy weather and a serial killer, so the picks run A, A, B, A.
explanation_text: Four pairs, four tests of sense. 'Bated' is shortened from 'abated', so bated breath is breath held back, while 'baited' belongs to hooks and traps. To appraise is to assess the value or extent of something; to apprise is to inform someone, and it needs a person as its object. 'Balmy' is mild and soothing, while 'barmy' is British slang for crazy. And 'serial' means one after another, while cereal is grain.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Opens with 'baited breath', which puts a hook in the sentence, and takes 'apprise the damage', which would need a person to inform.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Every pick is the wrong member of its pair, ending with a 'cereal killer'.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Takes 'apprise the damage' in the second sentence and 'barmy weather' in the third, which would make the countryside's weather insane rather than mild.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Takes 'apprise' and 'barmy' wrongly and ends with 'cereal killer'.

common_traps: Barmy and balmy differ by one letter and both sound plausible next to 'weather'. The sentence says the weather soothed frayed nerves, which only balmy can do.

short_explanation: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator — the address that tells the browser which protocol to use and exactly where the page or file sits on a server.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Universal Resource Locator was the wording in the earliest web drafts; the standard that settled the term (RFC 1738) uses Uniform, and that is the expansion exams accept.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No part of the expansion is 'Union', and the web address locates a resource, not research.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The first word is Uniform, not Union.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Uniform is right, but the middle word is Resource — the thing being located — not Research.

common_traps: Universal and Uniform both read plausibly; the accepted expansion is Uniform Resource Locator.

short_explanation: The Share tab of File Explorer collects the ways of sending a file out — Email, Zip, Burn to disc, Print and Fax — so Print & Fax is the option that lives there.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Sorting and arranging folder contents is on the View tab (Layout and Current view groups).

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The preview and details panes are switched on from the View tab's Panes group.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Properties of a document is opened from the Home tab.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Rename is a Home tab command, in the Organise group.

key_note: In Windows 10 the Share tab's Send group carries Email, Zip, Burn to disc, Print and Fax; the stem's 'Print & Fax' is that pair.

short_explanation: A VGA port is a DE-15 connector — three rows of five holes, fifteen in all, carrying the analogue red, green and blue signals plus sync.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Nine holes is the DE-9 connector, the old serial or COM port.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: No standard display connector has eleven holes.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No standard display connector has thirteen holes.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: No standard display connector has seventeen holes; VGA stops at fifteen.

topic_name: MS Word ribbon, tabs and shortcuts
short_explanation: The Quick Access Toolbar is the small strip above the File tab holding Save, Undo and Redo, and anything else the user pins to it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The document area is the white space where text is typed, not a command strip.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The Ribbon sits below the tabs, not above the File tab.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The title bar shows the file name; the Quick Access Toolbar rests on it, but the bar itself gives no command access.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The ruler sits under the ribbon and is used for margins, indents and tab stops.

topic_name: MS Excel cell references, shortcuts and display behaviour
short_explanation: Ctrl + End moves to the last cell of the used range — where the lowest used row meets the rightmost used column.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl + T converts the selected range into an Excel table.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl + W closes the workbook window.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl + ] selects the cells whose formulas refer directly to the active cell.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl + E runs Flash Fill.

common_traps: Ctrl + End stops at the last cell that holds data, not at the physical end of the sheet.

short_explanation: Truncate empties the file's contents — its length drops to zero — while the file itself, its name and its attributes stay in place.
explanation_text: Delete and truncate are close cousins in an operating system's file operations. Delete removes the directory entry and with it the file's attributes; truncate keeps the entry and the attributes and throws away only the data, which is why a log file can be truncated and written to again without being recreated.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Close ends a process's access to an open file; the contents are untouched.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Seek moves the read/write pointer to a given offset in the file.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Delete removes the file including its attributes — exactly what the stem excludes.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Append adds fresh data at the end of the file.

common_traps: Delete looks like the obvious fit; the phrase 'except deleting the attributes' is what rules it out.

short_explanation: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, written as four 8-bit numbers separated by dots, as in 192.168.1.1.
explanation_text: Thirty-two bits allow about 4.3 crore-times-100, roughly 4.3 billion, distinct addresses. That pool ran short, which is why IPv6 was defined with 128-bit addresses and why techniques like NAT stretch the IPv4 space in the meantime.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: No IP version uses a 64-bit address.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 128 bits is the IPv6 address length.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 256 bits is not an address length in any IP version.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 16 bits is the size of a TCP or UDP port number, not of an address.

short_explanation: Of the items listed only the router is a device every machine on the network connects through — the central point that also passes traffic on to other networks.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Distributor is not a networking device; no such class of hardware exists.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: USB is a port and cable standard for attaching peripherals to one computer.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A network card sits inside each individual machine and connects only that machine.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A network cable is the medium that carries the signal, not a device that anything connects through.

key_note: The textbook 'central point' of a LAN is a hub or a switch; neither is offered, and the router is the only central device in the list, so the key stands.

short_explanation: Starting a computer is called booting: the firmware runs its power-on self-test and then loads the operating system into memory.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Signing in means authenticating to an account, which happens after the machine has started.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Logging in is again an account action, not the start-up of the machine.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Spoofing means faking an identity or an address — a security term.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Threading is splitting a process into separate threads of execution.

short_explanation: Second-generation computers were built on transistors and were programmed in assembly language, which replaced binary codes with mnemonics such as ADD and MOV.
explanation_text: The generations are worth fixing once: first generation used vacuum tubes and machine language; second used transistors and assembly language; third used integrated circuits and high-level languages such as FORTRAN, COBOL, ALGOL, BASIC and later Pascal.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: BASIC is a high-level language of the third-generation era.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Pascal was designed around 1970, well after the transistor machines.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Machine language — raw binary — belongs to the first generation.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: ALGOL is a high-level language, again third generation.

common_traps: Machine language is first generation; assembly is second. The two are easy to swap.

topic_name: MS Word ribbon, tabs and shortcuts
short_explanation: Header & Footer is a group on the Insert tab of MS Word, alongside Page Number.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The Mailings tab holds mail-merge commands.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The Home tab holds clipboard, font, paragraph and styles commands.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The File tab opens the backstage view — Save, Print, Options.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The Review tab holds spelling, comments and track changes.

short_explanation: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, and is stepped forward after every fetch.
explanation_text: Keep the fetch cycle straight: the program counter holds the address of the instruction, the instruction register holds the instruction once fetched, and the memory address register holds whichever address is being read or written at that moment. During a fetch the program counter's value is copied into the memory address register, which is why the two are confused.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A temporary register holds intermediate operands while an instruction executes.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The accumulator holds the result of arithmetic and logic operations.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The address register holds whatever memory address is currently being accessed, whether for an instruction or for data; it is not the register that tracks where the program has reached.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The data register holds the word just read from memory or about to be written to it.

common_traps: 'Address register' is the near miss — it holds an address, but only the program counter keeps the instruction address.

topic_name: Operating systems, utilities and system software
short_explanation: Response time is the gap between a process arriving and the moment it first gets the CPU — how quickly the system reacts, not how long the whole job takes.
explanation_text: Four scheduling times are worth separating. Arrival to first CPU is response time; arrival to completion is turnaround time; the CPU time a process actually needs is its burst time; and the total time it spends sitting in the ready queue over its whole life is waiting time. Interactive systems are tuned for response time, batch systems for turnaround.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Turnaround time runs from arrival all the way to completion, not to the first CPU allocation.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Event time is not a scheduling metric.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Burst time is the length of CPU time a process needs in one stretch of execution.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Waiting time is the total time spent in the ready queue across the whole run, which includes the waits after the process has already had the CPU once.

common_traps: Waiting time and response time coincide only if the process is never preempted; response time stops at the first CPU allocation.

short_explanation: Excel's DAYS function returns the number of days between two dates: =DAYS(end_date, start_date).
explanation_text: DAYS was added in Excel 2013; before that the usual method was to subtract one date cell from the other, since Excel stores dates as serial numbers. DAYS360 exists for a different purpose — bond and accounting calculations that assume twelve 30-day months.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: GAP is not an Excel function.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: DATES is not an Excel function.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: DAYS360 is a real function, but it counts on a 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, so it does not give the true number of days.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: SPAN is not an Excel function.

solution_steps: Take the tank as LCM(36, 45) = 180 units, so pipe A fills 180 ÷ 36 = 5 units a minute and pipe B 180 ÷ 45 = 4.

That leaves 180 - 120 = 60 units for pipe A.
A needs 60 ÷ 5 = 12 minutes, so X = 12.
formula_used: Work = rate × time; taking the tank as 180 units, A fills 5 units a minute and B fills 4.
common_traps: Pipe B stays open for the whole 30 minutes; only pipe A is shut early.

option_rationales.label: A

option_rationales.label: B

option_rationales.rationale: 78 needs a smallest number of 35, again odd.

solution_steps: Let the five consecutive even numbers be n, n+2, n+4, n+6, n+8.
The last three are n+4, n+6 and n+8, whose average is the middle one, n+6.
Smallest 32 and largest 40, so their sum is 72.
formula_used: (n + 6)² - n² = 420, where n is the smallest even number.
common_traps: It is the average of the last three that is squared, and that average is the middle of those three (n+6), not the largest (n+8).

short_explanation: With the triangle's base equal to the rectangle's breadth b, the rectangle is 18b and the triangle 10b, so 8b = 96 and b = 12, giving a perimeter of 2 × (18 + 12) = 60 m.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 72 is 4 × 18, the perimeter of a square on the length; the breadth works out to 12, not 18.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 54 needs a breadth of 9; 8b = 96 gives 12.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 64; the working gives a breadth of 12 and a perimeter of 60.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 48 needs a breadth of 6, which comes from 16b = 96 — halving the rectangle's area as well as the triangle's.

solution_steps: Let the breadth of the rectangle be b metres; the triangle's base is the same b.
Rectangle area = 18b; triangle area = ½ × b × 20 = 10b.
Perimeter = 2 × (18 + 12) = 60 m.
formula_used: Rectangle area = length × breadth; triangle area = ½ × base × height; perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth).
common_traps: The ½ belongs to the triangle only; dropping it makes the triangle the larger figure and the equation gives no positive breadth.

short_explanation: The nominal group technique has members write their ideas silently and alone, then read them out one at a time in a round with discussion held back until every idea is on the board. That is what gives it both full participation and a stage with no interaction.
explanation_text: The sequence is the whole point: silent individual generation, round-robin recording with no comment allowed, then discussion, then a private ranking or vote. Holding the talk back protects the quieter and the junior members, because nobody has heard a senior view before committing an idea, and the private vote means the group settles the matter without a debate that the loudest voice can carry. The principle is to separate generating options from judging them, so that judgement never suppresses the options.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Delphi keeps the experts apart altogether, through rounds of anonymous questionnaires with feedback between rounds. There is no meeting, so there is no behavioural participation of members in a room.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Brainstorming is open interaction from start to finish. Nothing is held back at any stage, which is why a dominant member can steer it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Fish bowling seats a small group to discuss while the rest observe and then swap in. It is a discussion format, not a structured method of generating ideas with a silent phase.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Consensus mapping organises and clusters ideas a task force has already produced, so it works on the output of generation rather than structuring the generation itself.

short_explanation: A decision can be judged only once it has been made and put into effect: the closing step of the process reviews both the result and the way the choice was reached, and that review is what improves later decisions. Evaluating alternatives comes earlier, before the choice, when no outcome yet exists to assess.
explanation_text: The standard sequence runs: define and understand the problem, identify alternatives, evaluate them, choose one, implement it, and then evaluate the decision's effectiveness. The last step has two objects, and both matter. The outcome answers whether the problem actually went away. The process answers whether the problem was correctly defined, whether real alternatives were generated, and whether the decision was taken at the right level and with the facts to hand. Keeping the two apart is the discipline: a good outcome can follow a careless process by luck, and a sound process can still meet a bad outcome, so judging only by results teaches the wrong lesson next time.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Analysing the alternatives belongs to the run-up to the decision. At that stage no outcome exists to be assessed.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This is the defensible answer. Both the outcome of a decision and the process by which it was reached can be assessed only after the decision has been made and implemented.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Identifying alternatives comes earlier still, well before there is anything to review.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Defining and understanding the problem is the first step of the process, not the point after which a review is carried out.

key_note: The keyed option, evaluating alternative courses of action, precedes the choice, so at that point there is no decision outcome to assess; the stem describes the post-implementation review. Option B is proposed instead. The official NABARD 2021 key should be checked before publication.

topic_name: Types of decisions and decision levels
short_explanation: In the standard account of managerial intuition, decisions that rest on skills, knowledge and training are the cognitive-based ones: trained expertise reaching the answer quickly, without a formal analysis being written out.
explanation_text: This framework separates five sources of intuition. Experience-based decisions come from having lived through the situation before. Affect-initiated decisions are driven by feelings about it. Cognitive-based decisions rest on skills, knowledge and training. Subconscious mental processing is data being worked on below the level of awareness. Values- or ethics-based decisions turn on what the manager holds to be right. Naming the source is not an academic exercise: trained expertise can be tested, taught and audited, whereas a decision driven by mood or by a hunch the manager cannot explain offers nothing to check.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Value or ethics based decisions rest on the manager's sense of right and wrong, not on training.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Experience based decisions draw on what the manager has lived through. The question names skills, knowledge and training, which is the schooled side rather than the lived one.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Subconscious mental processing is data being worked on below the level of awareness; the manager cannot say how the answer arrived.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Environment based decisions is not one of the categories in this framework.

common_traps: Experience and training sit close together in ordinary speech. This classification keeps them apart: experience is what happened to the manager, training is what the manager was taught.

topic_name: Individual and organisational factors affecting decisions
short_explanation: Personal values belong to the decision maker, so they are an individual level factor. The other four sit either in the organisation or outside it altogether.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Economic conditions are an external factor that the organisation does not set and cannot control.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Organisational politics works between people and groups inside the organisation, not within a single person.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Organisational policies are rules laid down by the organisation and bind every decision maker alike.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Government legislation is an external constraint that applies to the organisation as a whole.

topic_name: Root cause analysis and problem-solving tools
short_explanation: Fault tree analysis starts from the undesired top event and works downwards, linking causes through AND and OR gates into a branching tree. Those Boolean gates are the feature no other tool on this list has.
explanation_text: The two neighbours are worth keeping apart. Fault tree analysis is top-down and deductive: state the failure, then break it into the combinations of causes that could produce it, with AND and OR gates that let a probability be worked out for the top event. Failure mode and effects analysis is bottom-up and inductive: list each component's ways of failing, trace what each would do, and rank them by severity, likelihood and detectability. One asks what could have caused this failure; the other asks what this part's failure would cause.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Failure mode and effect analysis works upwards from each component's possible failures to their effects and ranks them. It uses no logic gates and draws no tree.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The eight disciplines method is a team problem-solving routine with defined steps, not a diagram built on Boolean logic.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The fishbone diagram also branches, but its branches are categories of possible causes grouped for discussion. There are no AND or OR gates and nothing is computed from it.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Five Whys is repeated questioning down a single chain of causes; it produces a line, not a tree.

common_traps: The fishbone diagram is the near-miss, because it too is a branching picture of causes. Boolean gates and a single stated top event are what identify a fault tree.

short_explanation: Representativeness bias is judging a case by how closely it resembles another case or a stereotype, so that two different situations get treated as one and the base rates and the differences are passed over.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Overconfidence bias is over-rating the accuracy of one's own judgement. It is about certainty, not about resemblance.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Confirmation bias is seeking out and over-weighting evidence that supports a view already held.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Time sight bias is not a standard name; the recognised bias about judging events once they are over is hindsight bias.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Availability bias is judging how likely something is by how readily examples come to mind, usually because they were recent or vivid.

short_explanation: Predispositioning theory came out of the study of chess, where a strong player builds a position that keeps good options open instead of calculating one forced line, and it carries that idea over to deciding under uncertainty.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The rational model assumes a clearly defined problem, full information and a choice that maximises value, which is the opposite of playing a position under uncertainty.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Prospect theory came from experiments on how people weigh gains and losses against a reference point, not from chess.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Bounded rationality describes deciding within the limits of information, time and mental capacity, and settling for a good enough answer.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Intuitive decision making is deciding by feel and pattern recognition. It is a mode of deciding rather than a theory built on chess and uncertainty.

common_traps: Chess is also the setting of well-known work on expertise and bounded rationality, which pulls readers towards that option. The deciding phrase is the individual's relationship with uncertainty, which is what predispositioning theory is about.

short_explanation: The stepladder technique brings members into the discussion one at a time, and each newcomer states a view formed alone before hearing what the group has already concluded. Every member therefore contributes an uninfluenced position.
explanation_text: Two members start and reach a preliminary view. A third joins, gives a view formed alone, and only then hears the pair; a fourth follows in the same way, and the full group decides at the end. Staggering entry works against conformity and against social loafing, because nobody can quietly fall in behind a position they have already heard. The intent is the same as the nominal group technique's - protect the independent view - but there the independence comes from writing ideas down before any discussion, here from the order in which people enter the room.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Cost benefit analysis weighs a proposal's costs against its gains. It is an appraisal tool and says nothing about who speaks when.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Simulation training builds skill by practice in a modelled situation; it is not a way of running a group decision.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Star bursting is a brainstorming variant that generates questions about an idea rather than answers, and it does not stagger individual contributions.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Heuristic methods are rules of thumb for cutting a problem down to size, not a structure for group participation.

short_explanation: The status quo trap is the pull of leaving things as they are, because doing nothing feels safer than acting, even when the present arrangement is plainly worse than the alternatives.
explanation_text: The familiar list of hidden traps in decision making - anchoring, status quo, sunk cost, confirming evidence, framing, overconfidence, prudence and recallability - reserves the status quo trap for the bias towards inaction. It is worth separating from the sunk cost trap: one keeps the present arrangement because change feels risky, the other keeps a failing course because of what has already been spent on it. The practical test for the status quo trap is to ask whether the present arrangement would be chosen today if it were not already in place.

option_rationales.label: A
