option_rationales.rationale: The Ministry of Minority Affairs runs no sanitation campaign of this kind.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is not the implementing ministry for this campaign.

short_explanation: The description matches the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, which gives every rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled manual work a legal right to at least a hundred days of wage employment in a financial year.
explanation_text: What sets MGNREGA apart from every earlier programme is that it is an Act and the employment is a legal entitlement, demand-driven rather than allocation-driven: work must be given within fifteen days of the demand, within five kilometres if possible, and an unemployment allowance is payable if it is not. At least a third of beneficiaries must be women, and the assets created are meant to be durable ones such as water conservation structures and rural connectivity.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The Rural Employment Generation Programme was a KVIC credit-linked subsidy scheme for rural enterprises, later merged into PMEGP.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The Employment Assurance Scheme of 1993 offered a hundred days of work in the lean season, but as an administrative scheme without a legal guarantee, and it was merged into SGRY.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme of 1983 targeted landless households and was merged into the Jawahar Rozgar Yojana.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana is a skilling and placement programme for rural youth, not a wage employment guarantee.

common_traps: The Employment Assurance Scheme also promised a hundred days of unskilled work; only MGNREGA makes it an enforceable legal right.

short_explanation: Catla is the fastest growing of the Indian major carps, which is why it is stocked as the surface feeder in composite carp culture.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Rohu is a major carp too, but a column feeder and slower growing than catla.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Labeo is the genus to which rohu belongs, so it names a group rather than a distinct competitor here.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Mrigal is the bottom feeder in composite culture and grows more slowly than catla.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Tilapia grows fast but is an exotic species, not an indigenous Indian fish.

common_traps: Tilapia's speed of growth attracts the eye, but the stem asks for an indigenous fish.
key_note: Options A and C overlap, since rohu is Labeo rohita; the item is loosely framed but the intended answer is still clear.

short_explanation: Haryana falls in the Trans-Gangetic Plains, the agro-climatic zone that covers Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Chandigarh and the Ganganagar area of Rajasthan.
explanation_text: The Planning Commission divided the country into fifteen agro-climatic zones on soil, climate, rainfall and cropping pattern. The Gangetic plains are split into three of them from west to east: Trans-Gangetic covering Punjab and Haryana, Upper Gangetic covering western and central Uttar Pradesh, and Middle Gangetic covering eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The Trans-Gangetic zone is the rice-wheat belt of the green revolution, with high irrigation and falling water tables.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The Middle Gangetic Plains cover eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The Central Plateau and Hills zone covers parts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh in the plateau region.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The Upper Gangetic Plains cover western and central Uttar Pradesh.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The Western Himalayan region covers Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

common_traps: Three Gangetic zones sit next to each other; Haryana lies west of the Ganga plain proper, which is what trans refers to.

short_explanation: A male sheep kept for breeding is a ram; the female is a ewe.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A boar is a male pig.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A buck is a male goat, and the term is also used for rabbits and deer.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Dam means the mother of an animal, of any species.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A ewe is the female sheep, not the male.

short_explanation: The livestock sector contributed about 4.19 per cent of total gross value added in 2018-19 according to National Accounts Statistics, which is roughly 28 per cent of agricultural GVA.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 5.50 per cent overstates the share for that year.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 1.24 per cent is far too low for a sector of this size.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 7.28 per cent is closer to the share of agriculture as a whole in some earlier accounting, not of livestock.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 2.51 per cent understates the reported contribution.

common_traps: Livestock's share of agricultural GVA is around 28 per cent; the question asks for its share of total GVA, which is a far smaller number.

short_explanation: Pomology is the study and cultivation of fruit crops.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Olericulture is the study and cultivation of vegetables.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Horticulture is the parent discipline covering fruits, vegetables, flowers and plantation crops together, so it is too broad for this stem.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Edaphology is the study of soil in relation to plant growth.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Floriculture is the cultivation of flowers and ornamental plants.

short_explanation: In the quincunx system the trees stand at the four corners of a square with one more tree planted at the centre of it, so a square orchard carries an extra tree in every square.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The hexagonal system places six trees at the corners of a regular hexagon with one at the centre, so its base figure is a hexagon, not a square.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The rectangular system sets trees at the corners of rectangles with wider row spacing than plant spacing, and adds no central tree.

option_rationales.label: D

short_explanation: PM-KUSUM, run by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, promotes solar energy in farming through standalone solar pumps, solarisation of existing grid-connected pumps, and small grid-connected solar plants on farmers' barren land.
explanation_text: The scheme has three components. Component A supports decentralised ground-mounted solar plants of up to 2 MW whose power the discom buys, Component B gives standalone solar pumps to off-grid farmers, and Component C solarises existing grid-connected pumps so the farmer can sell surplus power. The point is twofold: cut the diesel and subsidised grid power used for irrigation, and give the farmer an income from the panel.

option_rationales.label: B

short_explanation: Urea carries 46 per cent nitrogen, the highest nitrogen content among solid straight nitrogenous fertilisers, which is why it dominates Indian fertiliser use.
explanation_text: The figure follows from the formula CO(NH2)2: two nitrogen atoms weighing 28 in a molecule weighing 60, which is about 46.6 per cent. Urea is hygroscopic and, once applied, is hydrolysed by the soil enzyme urease to ammonium, so losses by volatilisation are high if it is left on the surface rather than worked in or applied before irrigation.

option_rationales.rationale: 24 per cent is close to the nitrogen content of ammonium sulphate at about 20 to 21 per cent, not urea.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 52 per cent is the phosphorus content of DAP, not the nitrogen content of urea.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 33 per cent is near the nitrogen content of ammonium nitrate, at about 34 per cent.

short_explanation: Operation Greens was launched in November 2018 by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, with a five hundred crore rupee outlay, to stabilise the supply and price of tomato, onion and potato and raise what growers of these crops realise.
explanation_text: The scheme has a short-term part and a long-term part. The short-term part subsidises transport and storage when prices crash, so produce can be moved from a glut area to a deficit one or held instead of dumped. The long-term part funds value chain infrastructure, farmer producer organisations, processing capacity and market linkage. During the pandemic it was widened from the three TOP crops to all notified fruits and vegetables, which is where the phrase TOP to TOTAL comes from.

option_rationales.label: B

short_explanation: Cereal crops leave the largest quantity of residue after harvest, with rice and wheat straw making up the bulk of India's annual crop residue.
explanation_text: India generates roughly 500 to 600 million tonnes of crop residue a year, and cereals account for around 70 per cent of it, with rice alone the single largest source. Most of it is used as fodder, fuel or bedding, but the surplus in the mechanically harvested rice-wheat belt is burned because the turnaround between harvest and the next sowing is short. That burning is the main reason residue management, happy seeders and zero till are pushed as a package.

option_rationales.label: B

option_rationales.label: E

short_explanation: Karnataka's Unified Market Platform is run by Rashtriya e-Market Services (ReMS), a joint venture of the State government and NCDEX e-Markets. The 2020 integration lets a trader registered on either platform bid on the other through a single login.
explanation_text: e-NAM, launched in April 2016 and run by the Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium under the Ministry of Agriculture, is a pan-India electronic portal that networks existing APMC mandis rather than replacing them. Karnataka had already built its own state-wide electronic market through ReMS, so the work in 2020 was an integration of two live platforms: a Single Sign-On framework widens the buyer pool for the same lot without either side surrendering its own market rules.

short_explanation: Only the two possibility conclusions hold: nothing blocks all lights from sitting inside caps, and lights can overlap the bucket-cap area, but the statements never force some buckets to be outside mugs.
explanation_text: Two forms do the work here. "Only buckets are mugs" means every mug is a bucket; it does not promise that any bucket is left over outside the mugs, so "some buckets are not mugs" is only a possibility, not a certainty. "Only a few buckets are caps" is the one that does give a definite negative, but about caps, not mugs: some buckets are caps and some buckets are not caps. Lights are tied to the picture only through "some caps are not light", which leaves the rest of the caps free, so lights may sit wholly inside caps and may also reach into the bucket-cap overlap.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Some buckets are not mugs is exactly the conclusion that fails; all mugs being buckets still allows every bucket to be a mug.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This keeps the doubtful third conclusion and drops the sound first one.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The second conclusion is a possibility statement too, and nothing in the statements stops lights from touching buckets.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The first two hold, but the third asks for a definite gap between buckets and mugs that the statements never create.

common_traps: "Only X are Y" converts to "all Y are X" and gives no definite negative; that is what makes conclusion III fail.
Possibility conclusions ask only whether a picture can be drawn, not whether it must be.
key_note: Solved on the standard exam convention that "Only A are B" means all B are A, and "Only a few A are B" means some A are B and some A are not B.

short_explanation: Both possibility conclusions can be drawn, but "some splits are not switches" cannot: the statement gives a definite gap on the switches side, not on the splits side.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The first conclusion also holds, since nothing stops styles from reaching the formats that are switches.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Only a few switches are splits" tells us some switches are outside splits; it says nothing about splits lying outside switches.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The third conclusion holds as well, because switches may all be drawn inside styles without contradicting any statement.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Two possibility conclusions do follow, so the set is not empty.

common_traps: "Only a few A are B" gives some A are not B, never some B are not A. Reversing that direction is what makes conclusion II look safe.

topic_name: Sanitation worker welfare and mechanised sanitation
short_explanation: Zero fatalities in sanitation work and all sanitation work being done by skilled workers are both stated NAMASTE outcomes, so statements 1 and 2 hold. Statement 3 fails on the word 'only' - the scheme strengthens supervision at national, state and urban local body level.
explanation_text: NAMASTE, the National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem, was approved in 2022 and is run jointly by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment and the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. It subsumes the older Self Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers and shifts the goal from rehabilitating individuals to re-engineering the work itself: profiling sewer and septic tank workers, capital subsidy for safety devices and cleaning machines, collectivising workers into self-help groups, and a supervisory chain so that no worker enters a sewer unprotected.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 2 is an official outcome as well, so stopping at statement 1 leaves out half of what the scheme commits to.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 3 is wrong as written, and statement 1 belongs in the answer.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Statement 1 belongs, but statement 3 confines the monitoring system to the state level.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Cannot include statement 3, which limits supervision to one tier.

common_traps: Statement 3 is accurate except for 'only at state level'. Monitoring under NAMASTE runs at national, state and urban local body level.

short_explanation: Every other link in the chain from T up to I is a weak one, so the blank must supply the strict step: with a less-than sign the chain reads T at most A at most B, less than C, at most J, equal to I, which makes T smaller than I and J larger than M.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A greater-than sign breaks the chain at C: B above C leaves no path from T up to I or from M up to J, so neither required relation can be read off.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: With another at-most sign the whole run from T to I is weak, so T could equal I and the strict T less than I fails.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: An at-least sign points the wrong way and also allows equality, so the chain is cut in the same way as the greater-than option.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Only one of the two works; the greater-than sign destroys the link rather than preserving it.

common_traps: A chain gives a strict inequality only when every link points the same way and at least one of them is strict.

short_explanation: Sows tend to farrow at night, when the shed is quiet and disturbance is least, which is why a night watch is kept from the expected farrowing date.

short_explanation: B is below W, W is at most O and O is at most A, so B is definitely below A; U and S are both above O but have no link to each other, so U greater than S is unproven.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The second conclusion fails, since U and S are connected only through the common smaller term O.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The first conclusion is sound: the chain B below W, W at most O, O at most A carries all the way through.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Either-or applies only when two conclusions cover the same pair between them. Here the first is definitely true, so the pair is not a complementary one.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The first conclusion is the one that is true; the second is the one left open.

common_traps: Two terms that are each bigger than a common third term cannot be compared with each other. U above O and S above O settle nothing between U and S.

short_explanation: PMAY-Gramin raised the minimum unit size to 25 square metres from the 20 square metres allowed under the old Indira Awaas Yojana, and the added space has to include a hygienic cooking area.
explanation_text: PMAY-G replaced Indira Awaas Yojana in November 2016 and changed both how a house is defined and how it is funded. Beneficiaries are drawn from the Socio-Economic and Caste Census 2011 deprivation data and verified by the gram sabha rather than picked by officials; assistance is released in instalments against geo-tagged evidence of construction; and the scheme converges with others so the household also gets a toilet under Swachh Bharat, 90 to 95 days of unskilled wage employment under MGNREGA, an electricity connection and an LPG connection.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: No intermediate size was notified between the old 20 square metres and the revised 25.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the revised floor is 25 square metres.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the revised floor is 25 square metres.

short_explanation: F is A's son, and C is married to B, who is A's sister, so C is the husband of F's mother's sister, which makes him F's maternal uncle.
explanation_text: Walk it in two steps. F's mother is A. A's sister is B, so B is F's maternal aunt. C is B's husband, which puts C on the mother's side of F's family and makes him male. A brother-in-law of the mother is addressed in this question family as the maternal uncle, the mama side of the tree, rather than the paternal uncle.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A plain uncle would put C on the father's side of F; C is linked to F only through F's mother's sister.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: C is male, being the husband of B, so an aunt relation cannot apply.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: F's mother is A, not C.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Maternal uncle describes the link exactly, so the fallback option is not needed.

common_traps: Uncle and maternal uncle are separate options here; the side of the family, not the word uncle, is what is being tested.

short_explanation: A pullet is a female fowl in her first laying year, so the birds contrasted with her in the passage are those over one year old.
explanation_text: Egg output peaks in the first laying year and falls in the second, so commercial cage units are stocked with pullets coming into lay at about 18 to 20 weeks. A bird older than a year is either force-moulted for a second cycle or culled, which is why the text draws its line at one year.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Six months is still within the pullet stage - such a bird is the one being caged, not the one being contrasted with.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Eight months is likewise a bird in her first laying year.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Ten months is under a year and still a pullet.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Two years is a second- or third-cycle hen, well past the boundary the passage draws.

short_explanation: Pawan sits in the south-facing row second from that row's far end and looks straight at Girish, who sits second from the left in the north-facing row.
explanation_text: The five who face south are Vaibhav, Sumit, Raman, Pawan and Naman; the five who face north are Dev, Girish, Hitesh, Karan and Naresh. Read the north-facing five from their own left to right and the order is Karan, Girish, Dev, Hitesh, Naresh. Across the gap the pairs are Vaibhav opposite Karan, Pawan opposite Girish, Raman opposite Dev, Sumit opposite Hitesh and Naman opposite Naresh. Three deductions fix this. Naresh being third to Girish's right and Dev second to Naresh's left can only be placed with Girish second, Dev third and Naresh last in that row; Karan and Hitesh then need two people between them, and since Hitesh may not sit beside Girish, Hitesh takes the fourth seat and Karan the first. Next, Dev faces the person sitting immediately to Sumit's right, so Sumit sits directly beside that person, and the single gap between Pawan and Sumit plus Vaibhav's ban on sitting next to Sumit pushes Vaibhav to the end of the south-facing row. Finally, Raman and Naman must have one person between them, and Naman is not allowed to face Dev, so Raman is the one opposite Dev and Naman takes the remaining end seat.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Dev is opposite Raman, not Pawan.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Hitesh sits opposite Sumit.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Naresh sits at the end of his row and faces Naman.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Karan sits at the other end of his row and faces Vaibhav.

key_note: Arrangement taken from the direction block printed with this question, which is shared across the four questions of the set. The seating comes out unique.
tag_note: This is a two-parallel-rows puzzle with the rows facing each other, not a single linear row whose members face opposite ways. Suggested tag: parallel rows facing each other.

short_explanation: From Z, Mr Wasan moves 7 km east to R and then 24 km north to S, so Z and S are the ends of a right triangle with legs 7 and 24, giving a straight-line gap of 25 km.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 21; the legs from Z to S are 7 and 24, and the working gives 25.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Adding the two legs outright gives 31, not 30, and in any case the question asks for the straight-line gap, not the walked distance.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 41 comes from adding the opening 17 km eastward leg to the 24 km northward leg, but the 17 km is walked before Z and plays no part in the Z-to-S gap.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: No likely slip gives 18; the right triangle with legs 7 and 24 gives 25.

solution_steps: Track the turns: heading east to Y, a right turn faces south, so the 52 km run to Z is southward.
At Z he is facing south; a left turn faces east, so the 7 km to R is eastward.
At R he is facing east; a left turn faces north, so the 24 km to S is northward.
S therefore lies 7 km east and 24 km north of Z.
Distance = square root of (7 squared + 24 squared) = square root of (49 + 576) = square root of 625 = 25 km.
formula_used: straight-line distance = square root of (east-west gap squared + north-south gap squared)
common_traps: Only the legs walked after reaching Z matter. The 17 km and the 52 km are both spent getting to Z.
Left and right turns must be read from the direction he is already facing, not from the page.

short_explanation: BPKP promotes natural farming, which runs on on-farm inputs such as dung and biomass. Certified organic farming allows bought-in permitted inputs and turns on third-party certification, so it is the odd one out.

Organic farming substitutes chemical inputs with certified organic ones - compost, bio-fertilisers, approved bio-pesticides - which are usually purchased, and recovers the cost through a certified price premium. Natural farming as BPKP defines it aims at near-zero purchased input: cow dung and urine preparations, mulching, intercropping and on-farm residue recycling. key_note: BPKP sits inside PKVY, an organic-farming umbrella, so 'organic farming' is loosely related. The item turns on the narrower distinction between certified organic farming and input-free natural farming.

Both Bing and Yahoo therefore sit inside browser, but nothing says where inside, so they may overlap or stay apart; that leaves the first conclusion unproven. Google meets browser only through "some Google are browser", and that shared part may or may not reach the Yahoo region, so no definite separation of Google from Yahoo can be claimed either. What is safe is the drawing question: since some browsers are already Yahoo, nothing stops the whole of Yahoo from lying within browser.

short_explanation: November is the month shared by three people, A from Agra, G from Patna and M from Dehradun, and A is the one named in the options.
explanation_text: One assignment fits everything. L from Lucknow was born in January, O from Pune in March, R from Ranchi in April, K from Nainital in July, T from Kolkata in September, and A from Agra, G from Patna and M from Dehradun all in November, which is the month shared by three people. Three deductions pin it down. The Kolkata person needs a thirty-day month after July and before November, which leaves only September for T. Patna's person is born in November like Agra's, and Patna cannot be T, L, R, K, A or M, so Patna is G or O. If O held Patna, then G and M would take Dehradun and Pune between them, but Pune needs a thirty-one-day month before April while Dehradun needs a month shorter than thirty-one days, and G and M share a birth month, so that branch dies. G is therefore from Patna and born in November, M shares that month, and since Pune's month cannot be November, M is from Dehradun and O from Pune. That leaves the last three months: K already holds July, so L, who needs a thirty-one-day month that is not March, takes January, and O takes March.

option_rationales.rationale: The Kolkata person is T, born in September, the only thirty-day month falling after July and before November.

option_rationales.rationale: The Lucknow person is L, born in January.

short_explanation: The 1991 package carried conditions from two lenders: an IMF standby arrangement for the balance of payments crisis, and an IBRD structural adjustment loan for the reforms that followed.

Without a state-wide licence a trader has to register afresh in every mandi he wants to bid in. Without single-point levy the same lot pays market fee again at each mandi it passes through, which kills inter-mandi trade. That is why the Centre treats them as a package rather than a menu.

explanation_text: One assignment fits everything. L likes Rio and presents English, M likes Frozen and presents Physics, N likes Up and presents Geography, O likes Lion King and presents Chemistry, P likes Finding Nemo and presents History, Q likes Shrek and presents Civics, and R likes Cars and presents Biology. Three deductions pin it down. Start with Up: Q, M, R and P are each told they do not like it, L likes Rio and O likes Lion King, so N likes Up. Next take L: Finding Nemo carries History and Cars carries Biology, neither of which is L's film, Civics is Q's and Physics is M's, and L is barred from Geography and Chemistry, so L presents English. That forces N onto Geography, since the Up person is barred from Chemistry and the other subjects are taken. Finally, O likes Lion King, so O can hold neither History nor Biology and takes Chemistry; of the two subjects left, R is barred from History, so R presents Biology and therefore likes Cars, and P presents History and therefore likes Finding Nemo. Frozen and Shrek remain for M and Q, and Q does not like Frozen.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: N presents Geography; the Up fan is expressly barred from Chemistry, which goes to O.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: R is expressly barred from History and ends up with Biology.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: P presents History, having taken Finding Nemo.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Three of the four combinations are wrong, so they cannot all be correct.

key_note: Solved from the direction block printed with this question, shared across the three questions of the set. The assignment comes out unique.

topic_name: Direction of one point relative to another
short_explanation: U, T and Y all sit on one east-west line, because T is due east of U and Y stands the same 5 metres above W as U stands above V.
explanation_text: Lay the six points out from the clues. Put V at the bottom left. U is 5 metres straight north of V. T is 11 metres east of U, so T sits on the same east-west line as U. S is 9 metres straight south of T. W is 15 metres east of V, on the same east-west line as V. X is 4 metres straight south of W, and Y is 5 metres straight north of W. Two checks make the picture firm. U is 5 metres above V and Y is 5 metres above W, and V and W lie on one east-west line, so U and Y lie on another east-west line directly above it. T was placed 11 metres east of U on that same upper line, which puts T between U and Y, 4 metres short of Y since the V-to-W gap is 15 metres.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: W lies 5 metres below the U-T line, level with V, so it cannot be collinear with them.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: S is 9 metres below T while Y and W are on a north-south line further east; the three do not line up.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: V and W do share an east-west line, but S sits 4 metres below it and short of W.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: W and X share a north-south line, but T stands 4 metres west of that line.

common_traps: Each clue names the second point's direction from the first. Reading "the distance from U to T, which is in its east" backwards flips half the figure.
key_note: Solved from the direction block printed with this question, shared across the two questions of the set.

short_explanation: Group A ends up as M, I and N, and since M and N are boys while I is a girl, that group holds two males.
explanation_text: Nine friends into three groups with at least three in each means exactly three in each. One split fits everything: group A is M, I and N; group B is J, K and G; group C is F, L and H. Three deductions pin it down. J is in group B, K works with J and G is with J, so group B is full at once with J, K and G. F and L are together, and L cannot be with M, who is in group A, so F and L go to group C. M's group must contain F or I, and F has gone to C, so I joins M in group A. I, H and J are in three different groups, and with I in A and J in B, H goes to C, which fills C with F, L and H. The only person left, N, completes group A. The remaining conditions hold: F and G are apart, and each group has a boy, M and N in A, K in B, L in C.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Group B is J, K and G, of whom only K is a boy.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Group C is F, L and H, of whom only L is a boy.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Group B is settled with one boy, so there is nothing open between A and B.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Both B and C are settled with one boy each.

key_note: Solved from the direction block printed with this question, shared across the three questions of the set. The split comes out unique.

short_explanation: U stands 5 metres north of V and Y stands 5 metres north of W, so the gap between U and Y is the same as the gap between V and W, which is 15 metres.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 7 metres matches no leg in the figure; the U to Y gap works out to 15.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 9 metres is the T to S drop, which runs south and plays no part in the U to Y gap.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 11 metres is only the U to T part of the line; T is 4 metres short of Y.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 12 metres matches no leg; the working gives 15.

solution_steps: U is 5 metres due north of V, and Y is 5 metres due north of W.
V and W lie on one east-west line 15 metres apart, with W to the east.
Equal northward shifts from both ends keep the separation, so U and Y are 15 metres apart.
The same answer comes from adding along the upper line: U to T is 11 metres and T to Y is the remaining 4 metres, giving 15.
key_note: Solved from the direction block printed with this question, shared across the two questions of the set.

short_explanation: The second and third statements together settle it: B is the wife of D, D is the father of N, and S is the wife of N, so S is B's daughter-in-law.
explanation_text: Take the third statement first. It gives B as D's wife, D as N's father and D as having two children, which makes B the mother of N. The second statement adds that T is the son of N and S is the mother of T. Since S is T's mother and N is T's parent too, N is T's father, and S is N's wife. A son's wife is the daughter-in-law, so S is the answer. The first statement cannot help in the same way: it introduces I and J, and J is never linked to B or D, so "S is the wife of J's nephew" leaves S floating outside the family the question asks about.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Without the second statement nothing connects S to D's family; J's nephew is never identified.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The first statement is not needed once the second and third are in hand.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Two of the three statements are enough, so the question is answerable.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Neither of those two mentions B, so the daughter-in-law of B cannot be picked out.

common_traps: A data sufficiency item asks only whether the person can be named, not who it is. Statements that add unplaced people such as I and J add nothing.

short_explanation: I has to join M in group A, because M's group must contain F or I and F is tied to L in group C, so I and F can never share a group.
explanation_text: Nine friends into three groups with at least three in each means exactly three in each. One split fits everything: group A is M, I and N; group B is J, K and G; group C is F, L and H. Three deductions pin it down. J is in group B, K works with J and G is with J, so group B is full at once with J, K and G. F and L are together, and L cannot be with M, who is in group A, so F and L go to group C. M's group must contain F or I, and F has gone to C, so I joins M in group A. I, H and J are in three different groups, and with I in A and J in B, H goes to C, which fills C with F, L and H. The only person left, N, completes group A. The remaining conditions hold: F and G are apart, and each group has a boy, M and N in A, K in B, L in C.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: L and H are both in group C, along with F.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: G and K are both in group B, along with J.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: I and N are both in group A, along with M.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: K and J are expressly told to work on the same project, and both sit in group B.

key_note: Solved from the direction block printed with this question, shared across the three questions of the set. The split comes out unique.

short_explanation: F and L go together and cannot be with M, so they take group C, and H joins them because I, H and J must land in three different groups.
explanation_text: Nine friends into three groups with at least three in each means exactly three in each. One split fits everything: group A is M, I and N; group B is J, K and G; group C is F, L and H. Three deductions pin it down. J is in group B, K works with J and G is with J, so group B is full at once with J, K and G. F and L are together, and L cannot be with M, who is in group A, so F and L go to group C. M's group must contain F or I, and F has gone to C, so I joins M in group A. I, H and J are in three different groups, and with I in A and J in B, H goes to C, which fills C with F, L and H. The only person left, N, completes group A. The remaining conditions hold: F and G are apart, and each group has a boy, M and N in A, K in B, L in C.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: M is in group A and J is in group B, so the two cannot share group C.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: I sits with M in group A and K sits with J in group B.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: L is in group C but G is with J in group B.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: F and H are in group C, but I is in group A with M.

key_note: Solved from the direction block printed with this question, shared across the three questions of the set. The split comes out unique.

short_explanation: The second statement alone fixes the order enough: J is tallest, G is fourth with two below, and H is above G but below F, so F takes second place.
explanation_text: Work the second statement. J is the tallest. G is taller than only two people, so among six G stands fourth. H is taller than G, so H is second or third, and F is taller than H, so F sits above H. That leaves the second and third places for F and H in that order, making F the second tallest. The first statement stops short: E is shorter than only two, so E is third, and H is taller than only one, so H is fifth. That leaves the top two places to be shared by F, G and J with nothing to separate them, so the second tallest cannot be named.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The first statement places E third and H fifth but leaves F, G and J unranked at the top.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Only the second statement works, so the either-or case does not arise.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The second statement on its own is sufficient, so the pair together certainly is.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The first statement is not needed at all.

common_traps: "Shorter than only two" and "taller than only one" fix positions from opposite ends; the first statement looks complete but never touches the top two places.

short_explanation: Part 4 has the wrong preposition: animals walk ON land, not "in land". Everything else in the sentence is sound.
explanation_text: English fixes the preposition by the kind of surface: we walk on land, on the floor, on the road, but in water, in the air, in a field. "In land" would only be possible as the compound noun "inland", which means away from the coast and does not fit a verb of movement here.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Sea Lions are able to" is correct: "be able to" is followed by a bare infinitive, which "rotate" in part 2 supplies.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "rotate their back flippers under" is fine; "under" is completed by "their body" in part 3.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "their body, which allows" is a correct non-defining relative clause referring to the whole action of rotating the flippers.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Part 4 does contain an error, so this cannot be chosen.

short_explanation: The passage defines inappropriate behaviour by its result: markets select against it because "capital seeks to get the more profitable firms", and the individuals "yielding the lowest payoff" are the ones replaced. Behaviour that ends in losses is therefore the inappropriate kind.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Seeking a monopoly raises profit, which is the direction the passage calls appropriate, not inappropriate.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Meeting stakeholder expectations is never discussed in the passage; the test applied there is payoff, not approval.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Corporate social responsibility to improve image is not mentioned, and image-building is not equated with low payoff.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Minimising losses moves towards higher payoff, so studying it is the opposite of the behaviour markets select against.

tag_note: This is not explicit retrieval — the passage never lists examples of inappropriate behaviour, so the answer has to be inferred from the selection mechanism. "Inference and implied meaning", the tag used on the neighbouring rows of the same set, fits better.

short_explanation: Inappropriate behaviour is weeded out because it fails at what economic activity is assumed to aim at — profit or utility maximisation — so capital and selection move away from it.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Behaviour in accordance with Nash equilibrium is what survives in the passage, not what disappears.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Aiming at profit or utility maximisation is the appropriate behaviour; that is precisely why it is not selected against.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The passage never says inappropriate behaviour qualifies or limits Nash equilibrium; it says such behaviour is replaced.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Nothing in the passage treats Nash equilibrium as a myth to be dismantled; the authors test whether outcomes match its prediction.

short_explanation: Part 1 is wrong: after "had" the verb must be the past participle, so "had already begin" should read "had already begun".
explanation_text: Perfect tenses are built with have/has/had plus the third form of the verb. Begin is an irregular verb with three distinct forms — begin, began, begun — and only the third can follow "had". The same trap runs through drink/drank/drunk, ring/rang/rung and sing/sang/sung.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "climbing this year as a" is correct; "begun climbing" takes the -ing form quite properly.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Part 1 contains a clear verb-form error, so "None are incorrect" cannot stand.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "result of the crisis" completes "as a result of" correctly.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Parts 2 and 3 are both sound; the fault lies only in part 1.

short_explanation: Part 1 breaks subject-verb agreement: the real subject is the singular "a rapid transformation", so it must be "There has been a rapid transformation".
explanation_text: In a "there is / there are" sentence, "there" is only a placeholder. The verb agrees with the noun that follows it, so the number of that noun decides everything: There has been a transformation, but There have been transformations. Candidates who look only at the plural-sounding "business scenario" further along the sentence pick the wrong verb.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "transformation in the business" is correct; "transformation in" is the right preposition for a change within a field.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "scenario in the country after" is fine and needs no change.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Part 1 is faulty, so this cannot be chosen. (The paper prints this choice as "None are correct" while the parallel items print "None are incorrect"; the intended sense is the same.)

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "the introduction of digital banking" is correct.

short_explanation: Both forces end in arbitrary behaviour: selection replaces the lowest-payoff individuals "by individuals with arbitrary behaviour", and mutation means "the current behaviour is replaced by arbitrary behaviour". That shared outcome is the link.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The passage describes both forces acting on individuals only; it never sets up an individual-versus-corporate contrast.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The opposite is stated: the game is played "all against all", which the passage calls playing the field as opposed to a pairwise contest.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Darwinian Selection and mutation are the two forces that produce Economic Darwinism in this model, not forces that may fail to.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Individualism in the corporate world is nowhere in the passage.

short_explanation: A pairwise contest is a game in which agents meet two at a time, which the passage contrasts with playing the field, where each individual faces everyone at once. A market with exactly two companies supplying the product is that two-player situation.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Two brands need not mean two contestants — one company can own both — so this does not guarantee a two-sided contest.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Two dominant companies" implies other players are present as well, which makes it playing the field rather than a pairwise meeting.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Two segments of buyers are not two contesting agents; the contest in the passage is between the players of the game, not between customer groups.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: More than two brands competing is exactly the all-against-all case the passage opposes to pairwise contest.

key_note: The keyed option is misprinted as "A market is which" for "A market in which"; read past the typo. B is the closest rival and the reason to reject it is that brands are products, not players.

short_explanation: The sentence is grammatical from end to end, so none of the four parts is wrong.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "An edited version of" is correct; "edited" is a past participle used as an adjective.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "the article was published" is a correct passive: the article receives the action.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "in the newspaper" uses the right preposition for appearing inside a publication.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "to avoid controversy" is a correct infinitive of purpose attached to the main clause.

common_traps: Error-spotting sets condition candidates to expect a mistake, so a clean sentence is often mis-marked. Check each segment against a rule before rejecting the "no error" choice.

short_explanation: Part 2 leaves the sentence without a finite verb: "organization dependent" must be "organization is dependent" (or "organization depends").
explanation_text: Every main clause needs a finite verb, one that carries tense. "Dependent" is an adjective and "depending" is a participle; neither can be the predicate on its own. This is the commonest error type in segment-marked items — a dropped is/are/was that the eye supplies automatically while reading.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "The working environment in an" is correct; "in an organization" simply locates the environment.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "on the nature of communication strategies" is correct — "dependent" always takes "on".

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "to a great extent" is a correct adverbial of degree.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Part 2 is faulty, so this cannot be chosen.

short_explanation: The passage has markets selecting firms, not firms creating markets; capital moves to the more profitable firms and the poor performers are replaced. The keyed option reverses that direction, so it is the one that cannot be inferred.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This restates the selection mechanism in the passage — markets select against those who behave inappropriately — so it is inferable.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Mutation introduces arbitrary behaviour that may survive on payoff, so behaviour not consciously aimed at economics can still pay off. This is inferable.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Payoff differences decide who is replaced, so a firm's economic behaviour does bear on its profitability.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A firm whose behaviour yields a competitive payoff is not selected against, so it keeps its place in the market.

common_traps: The stem is an EXCEPT question: four options are supported and the odd one out is wanted.
The odd one out works by reversing the direction of causation — firms creating markets instead of markets selecting firms. Reversal is the standard way this trap is built.

topic_name: Meaning of an idiom in context
short_explanation: "Under the weather" means slightly unwell, which fits only sentence I, where the child is quiet because he is feeling ill.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: II uses the phrase literally of clouds, which is meaningless, and III is illogical, so neither can be apt.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: III says employees "could come to office as they were feeling under the weather" — being unwell is a reason for staying away, so the sentence needs "could not".

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Sentence I is a correct use, so it is not true that none are correct.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This choice prints the same words as the keyed option; only one of the two identical choices can be credited.

key_note: The paper prints "Only I" twice, as choice A and choice E; A is the marked key. The item is still decidable because the content of that answer is right either way.

topic_name: Sentence completion with a missing part
short_explanation: The Second World War is a finished period, so the simple past "existed" is required, and "the one" needs the relative pronoun "that" to introduce its clause: "like the one that existed during the second world war".
explanation_text: Two rules decide this item. First, a definite finished time (in 1945, during the war, last year) forces the simple past and rules out the present perfect. Second, when a relative clause follows "the one", the pronoun that or which must be present unless it is the object of the clause; here it is the subject, so it cannot be dropped.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "that which had existed" puts the clause in the past perfect, which needs a later past event to be earlier than; there is none here.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "the one existed" drops the relative pronoun, leaving a noun followed by a bare finite verb with nothing to join them.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The present perfect "has existed" cannot be used with a finished time expression such as "during the second world war".

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "one which have existed" breaks agreement — the singular "one" needs "has", not "have".

short_explanation: "Come up with" means to produce an idea, plan or answer, which fits II (renewable energy solutions) and III (an answer to the teacher). Sentence I needs "cope with" or "deal with" — you do not come up with an emergency.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: I is the one misuse in the set: reacting to an emergency is coping with it, not producing it.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: II is correct, but III is equally correct, so this choice is incomplete.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This includes I, which confuses "come up with" (invent, think of) with "cope with" (handle).

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: II and III are both apt uses, so the set is not wholly incorrect.

common_traps: "Come up with" and "cope with" sound close and both take an object, but one supplies something new while the other survives something imposed.

topic_name: Sentence completion with a missing part
short_explanation: After "must surely be" the complement is an infinitive, and the two things the artist does must match: "to challenge the way we see the world and make visible the invisible". The second "to" may be left out because it is understood from the first.
explanation_text: Parallelism means that items joined by and, or or but must have the same grammatical shape: infinitive with infinitive, gerund with gerund, noun with noun. In a chain of infinitives the "to" is usually written once and understood thereafter, so "to challenge ... and make" is correct and "to challenge ... and making" is not.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is parallel, but it misprints "the word" for "the world", which is what rules it out.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "challenging ... and to make" mixes a gerund with an infinitive, so the two halves are not parallel.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "must surely be challenging" reads as a present continuous — the artist is in the act of challenging — which is not the sense of a defined role.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "to challenge way we see" drops the article before "way", and the gerund "making" then clashes with the infinitive "to challenge".

topic_name: Sentence completion with a missing part
short_explanation: The correlative "Just as ... so too ..." requires the second half to echo the tense of the first. The first half is "war has been a part of our civilization", so the second must be "so too has been our age-old practice of exploiting the Earth".
explanation_text: Correlative pairs — just as ... so too, not only ... but also, either ... or, no sooner ... than — work by balance. The structure after the second member should mirror the structure after the first in tense and form. Here the mirror of "has been" is "has been", and the inversion "so too has been X" is the standard order after "so".

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "so too is" shifts to the simple present, which does not answer the present perfect "has been" of the first clause.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "so also is" has the same tense mismatch, and "so also" is the weaker correlative here.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "so too did" is the simple past, which cuts the practice off in the past although the first clause runs up to the present.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "so too had been" is the past perfect, which needs a later past moment to be earlier than; there is none.

short_explanation: "Lay off" in its standard sense means to dismiss workers because there is no work for them, which is sentence III. II confuses it with a layover, the break in a journey.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: I uses "lay off" for giving up a habit; the item treats the dismissal sense as the apt one, so I alone is not the answer.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: II is plainly wrong — a stop on a flight to New York is a layover, not a lay off.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This includes II, which misuses the phrase for a break in a journey.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: III is a correct use, so the set is not wholly incorrect.

key_note: "Lay off" meaning to stop using something is recorded in dictionaries, usually with the article ("lay off the cigarettes"), so sentence I is arguable. The paper takes the employment sense as the phrase's proper use, which is the sense NABARD items test.

short_explanation: The sentence is meant to read: "Every four years, intelligence agencies put out a detailed assessment of where the world seems headed over the next two decades." That needs two swaps — two with years (A-E) and world with detailed (B-C).

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping only two and years repairs "Every four years" and "the next two decades" but leaves "a world assessment of where the detailed seems headed".

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Pairing A with B and C with D puts "two" and "world" together and "detailed" with "headed", which fixes nothing.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This proposes the same two pairs as choice B and fails for the same reason; the paper prints the pairing twice.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping detailed and headed alone gives "where the headed seems detailed", which is not English.

common_traps: Work out the intended sentence first, then read off the swaps. Trying the swaps one at a time against the printed sentence wastes time because two of them interlock.

short_explanation: "Haunts" means the places a particular set of people regularly frequent, which is exactly what exclusive clubs are to the privileged.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Preserve" in this sense is used in the singular — the preserve of the privileged, meaning an activity reserved to them. The plural "preserves of" does not carry that idiom.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A resort is a place people travel to for holidays; these clubs are described as everyday city institutions with prime locations.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A mantlet is a movable shield used in siege warfare, not a place at all.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Intrepid is an adjective meaning fearless and cannot follow "have always been ___ of".

key_note: The passage for this cloze set (blanks 29 to 33) is printed in the stem of this row and of the other cloze rows in the chunk, so the blanks can be read in context.

short_explanation: The intended sentence is: "The feat marked the extraction of natural resources from the environment of another planet for direct use by humans." That needs from swapped with feat (A-C) and direct swapped with another (D-E); extraction stays where it is.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping extraction with feat and from with direct gives "The direct marked the feat of natural resources", which is not a sentence.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Pairing from with another and extraction with feat leaves "the feat of natural resources direct the environment", still broken.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping from with extraction and feat with direct puts a preposition where the subject noun should be.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Pairing extraction with direct and from with another leaves "The another marked the direct of natural resources".

common_traps: "The" at the start of the sentence must be followed by a noun, so the first marked word has to be swapped with a noun — that alone points to feat and settles the A-C pair.

short_explanation: The clubs are described as the resort of the privileged, and diplomats are singled out as a specially revered set within them — "hallowed" carries that sense of being held sacred.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Exasperating means intensely irritating, which describes the writer's annoyance rather than the standing diplomats enjoy inside the clubs.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Galling also means bitterly annoying; the slot calls for the esteem the group is held in.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Impudent means cheeky or insolent, which is a charge against manners, not a mark of privilege.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Complacency is a noun and cannot modify the noun that follows the blank.

key_note: The cloze passage for blanks 29 to 33 is reprinted in this row's stem. The paper prints "an especially ___ tribes"; the plural is a misprint for "tribe" and does not affect the choice, which must be an adjective.

short_explanation: The colonists' clubs are being described as polished, sophisticated boltholes, and "urbane" is the one option that means refined and civilised.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Philistine means hostile to culture and refinement — the opposite of what these clubs claimed to be.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Churlish means rude and surly, a description of bad manners rather than of a refuge.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Indecorous means improper or in bad taste, again the reverse of the sense required.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Eloquent describes fluent speech or writing and cannot sensibly describe a refuge.

key_note: The cloze passage for blanks 29 to 33 is reprinted in this row's stem. Four of the five options are pejorative or apply only to persons, so elimination settles the blank even if "urbane refuges" reads oddly on its own.

short_explanation: The sentence is meant to read: "The report said that the Railways ministry plans to cut down more than it had declared in its clearance application." Only one swap is needed — down with Railways, which is pair B-C.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping said with down gives "The report down that the said ministry", which has no verb in the main clause.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping down with application gives "the application ministry" and "in its clearance down", both meaningless.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping said with application removes the reporting verb and leaves "The report application that".

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping Railways with declared gives "plans to cut declared more than it had Railways".

common_traps: "Cut" needs its particle: cut down is the phrasal verb here, so the word "down" has to end up immediately after "cut". That single observation fixes the pair.

short_explanation: "After meeting with the coach, Riya was encouraged to try out for the team" is already correct and idiomatic, so no interchange is needed.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping coach with encouraged gives "After meeting with the encouraged, Riya was coach to try out", which is not English.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping encouraged with team gives "Riya was team to try out for the encouraged".

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping coach with out gives "meeting with the out" and "try coach for the team".

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping out with team breaks the phrasal verb: "try team for the out" has no meaning.

common_traps: In an interchange set the eye expects at least one swap, so a clean sentence is easy to over-correct. Test the sentence as printed before hunting for pairs; "try out for" is a fixed phrasal verb and is already intact here.

short_explanation: The clubs resist change, so the blank needs a noun for unwillingness to move: "inertia against reform" pairs naturally with "haughty resistance to criticism".

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Tumult means noisy commotion, which is the opposite of the settled refusal to change the sentence describes.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Potency means strength or effectiveness and says nothing about resistance to reform.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Pursuit takes "of", not "against", and would mean chasing reform rather than blocking it.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Deride is a verb; the blank sits in a noun slot joined by "and" to the noun "resistance".

key_note: The cloze passage for blanks 29 to 33 is reprinted in this row's stem. "Resistance ... and ___" signals that the blank must be a noun of the same kind as resistance, which removes two options immediately.

short_explanation: The clubs are going to stay comfortably settled in their colonial habits, and "ensconced" is the word for being firmly and snugly established somewhere.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Abjuring means solemnly renouncing, which is the reverse of clinging to colonial affectations.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Spurning means rejecting with contempt, again the opposite direction.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Abdicating means giving up a position or responsibility, which does not fit clubs that keep their rules.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Decry is a verb in the wrong form for the slot and means to denounce, the opposite of the required sense.

key_note: The cloze passage for blanks 29 to 33 is reprinted in this row's stem. Four of the five options mean rejecting or giving up; only one means settling in, so the sentence's "will remain" decides it.

short_explanation: The sentence should read: "Scientists have found discrepancies in the amount of carbon emission reported by countries and independent agencies." Swapping discrepancies with found (A-B) is the single change required.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping found with amount gives "Scientists have discrepancies amount in the found of carbon emission".

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping amount with emission gives "in the emission of carbon amount", which reverses the sense.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping emission with independent gives "carbon independent reported by countries and emission agencies".

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Swapping discrepancies with emission leaves "Scientists have emission found" and "carbon discrepancies".

common_traps: After "have", the next word must be the past participle. "Scientists have discrepancies" cannot start a perfect tense, so the verb "found" has to move into that slot.

short_explanation: "Tell on" here means to have a harmful cumulative effect, which is exactly what "take a toll on" means: prolonged sleeplessness is sure to take a toll on your health.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A fitting replacement is present among the options, so "None" cannot be chosen.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "To influence" is neutral and loses the sense of damage; it also doubles the "to" already in "is sure to".

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Impacted on" is a past form and cannot follow "is sure to", which needs the base form.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "Shakes up" is in the wrong form for the slot and means to unsettle or reorganise, not to wear down.

key_note: The underlining is lost in this text version; the phrase being replaced is "tell on", which the options make clear.

topic_name: Correct and incorrect usage of a word
short_explanation: "An edge on his voice" uses the wrong preposition — the idiom is an edge in (or to) one's voice, meaning a sharp, irritated tone. The other four sentences use "edge" correctly.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "on the edge of the village" is the plain literal sense, the outer boundary of a place.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "to the edge of disaster" uses edge for the point just before something bad happens; this is standard.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "an edge over the other members" is the idiom for an advantage, and "over" is its correct preposition.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "go over the edge" here is the literal sense of going over a drop, and it is correctly used.

key_note: The stem prints only the headword EDGE without the instruction; from the option set and the parallel GROUND item in this chunk, the task is to find the sentence in which the word is used wrongly.

topic_name: Correct and incorrect usage of a word
short_explanation: The idiom for exhausting oneself is to work or run oneself INTO the ground; "worked herself to the ground" mixes it with "burnt to the ground" and is the wrong use here.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "get off the ground" is correctly used for a venture starting successfully.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "support on the ground" is correctly used for backing among ordinary people, as opposed to among leaders.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "stood her ground" is correctly used for refusing to give way under pressure.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "clearing the ground" is the literal sense and is correctly used of a construction site.

key_note: As with the EDGE item, the stem prints only the headword; the option set shows that the sentence containing the wrong use is wanted.

short_explanation: "Take into consideration" is the formal equivalent of "keep in mind" and slots in cleanly: it is important to take into consideration that this treaty is a national issue for each country.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Thinking about" is a gerund and cannot follow "is important to", which needs the base form.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Be mindful of" cannot be followed directly by a that-clause; it would need "of the fact that".

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Be careful that" shifts the meaning from bearing something in mind to guarding against a risk.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A grammatical and meaning-preserving replacement is present, so the no-change option is not the best answer.

key_note: "Keep in mind" is itself idiomatic, so the no-change option is arguable; the item asks for the closest formal equivalent rather than for a repair of an error.

short_explanation: To clamp down on something is to act firmly to stop it, so the decision is to take strict action to prevent smoking in public places.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Restrict mildly" reverses the force of the phrase; clamping down is severe, not mild.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Facilitate" means to make easier, the opposite of suppressing an activity.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Making an announcement is only words; clamping down implies enforcement action.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Advising against something is far weaker than clamping down, and the option prints the noun "advice" where the verb "advise" is needed.

short_explanation: "Rammed through" describes a law pushed into force quickly over objections; of the options only "enforced" carries the sense of putting the law into effect rather than a physical collision.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Smashed into" is literal impact and cannot describe the passage of tax laws.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A workable replacement is present among the options, so the no-change choice is not the best answer.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "Knocked against" is again physical contact and loses the idea of pushing a measure through.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "Collided against" is both unidiomatic (collide takes "with") and literal.

key_note: "Enforced" is not an exact synonym — to ram through is to force a measure past opposition, which happens before enforcement — but it is the only option in the legislative sense, and the other four are all literal collision verbs.

short_explanation: "Within limits" means up to a point but not completely, which is what "to some extent" says: the trial assessed the effect only partially.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Through and through" means completely, which contradicts the qualification the phrase introduces.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Understandably" comments on why something is reasonable and says nothing about degree.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A correct replacement is present among the options, so "None" cannot be chosen.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "Be degree" is a misprint for "by degrees", and even that would mean gradually, not partially.

common_traps: "Within limits" restricts the extent of a claim. Candidates who read it as "strictly" or "thoroughly" pick the opposite.

short_explanation: To back down is to withdraw from a position or a stated intention, so the authorities retracted their demolition plans.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Supported with irrefutable evidence" confuses back down with back up, which means to support or corroborate.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Asked for help" has no connection with the phrase; that would be to fall back on someone.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Reduced the scale of" is the near miss: backing down means abandoning the plan, not carrying out a smaller version of it.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "Asserted" is the opposite — it means to press a claim rather than to give it up.

common_traps: back up (support) versus back down (withdraw) versus back out (pull out of an agreement) — the particle carries the whole meaning.

short_explanation: To break away from something is to stop being bound by it, so the company wanted to become independent of its traditional, down-market image.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A workable replacement is present among the options, so the no-change choice is not the best answer.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Disentangle" means to free from something knotted or complicated; an image is not a tangle.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "Separate from" suggests a physical or organisational split, not shedding an inherited reputation.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: "Cut loose" is informal and also carries the sense of behaving without restraint, which changes the meaning.

key_note: "Separate from" is the closest rival and fits the frame more smoothly; the item turns on the idea of no longer being defined by an image, which only "become independent" carries. The item is loosely drafted because the underlining is not shown.

short_explanation: Parts 1, 2 and 4 are clean. Part 3 says "where events have removed", which needs an object or a passive ("have been removed") or a different verb altogether, and part 5 prints "off" where the fixed phrase is "remind the reader of".
explanation_text: Remove is a transitive verb: something removes something. "Events have removed" leaves the reader waiting for an object, so the clause never completes. And remind is fixed with of — remind somebody of something — while "off" is a preposition of separation. A one-letter slip of this kind is the standard trap in correctness-selection sets, because the ear hears no difference.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Part 5 is faulty: remind takes "of", not "off", which is a different word meaning away from.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Both parts named here are faulty — 3 leaves "removed" without an object and 5 has "off" for "of".

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Part 2 is correct but part 3 is not, so this pair cannot be the answer.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Parts 2 and 4 are indeed correct, but part 1 is correct too, so this choice is incomplete.

short_explanation: The passage says AI monitors weather patterns and air traffic, "helping airlines to make informed decisions about flight schedules and routes". That is the statement to pick.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The passage never mentions safety measures being formulated by AI or implemented by crew.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says AI is used to monitor weather patterns.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Staff training or work ethos is not discussed anywhere in the passage.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Network problems and the reliability of AI support are not raised in the passage.

short_explanation: Part 1 uses the wrong preposition — divorced FROM, not "divorced with" — and part 2 needs the unreal past after "as if": "as if it presented some objective reality". Only the choice that contains neither part survives.
explanation_text: Divorce takes from when it means separated from: divorced from reality, divorced from its history. And "as if" introducing a hypothetical takes the past form even about the present — as if it presented, as if he were here. Both are fixed patterns, not matters of style, which is why the item can be solved by rejecting parts 1 and 2 without judging the rest.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This includes both faulty parts: "divorced with" in 1 and "as if it presents" in 2.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This includes part 2, whose "as if it presents" should be "as if it presented".

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: These are precisely the two faulty parts of the paragraph.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This includes part 2 with the same "as if" error.

key_note: Part 4 ("which has built the science") reads acceptably on its own, so its exclusion from the answer is arguable. It does not affect the outcome: only one option contains neither part 1 nor part 2.

short_explanation: The order runs 1-D-A-B-C-6: after saying cottage industry needs encouragement, D proposes that every home take up an occupation, A gives them training in the job they like, B says the products must be collected and sold, and C offers co-operative societies to take up that duty.
