option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Starting with A puts government training before any occupation has been proposed, leaving "different jobs" with nothing to refer back to.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Here C follows A, so "this duty" points at training rather than at collecting and selling the produce, which is what co-operative societies are being offered for.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This opens with A before D, so the training arrangement again precedes the proposal it is meant to support.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This puts C before B, so "this duty" has no antecedent at all when the co-operative societies are introduced.

common_traps: C says "take up this duty", which must point back to the duty named in B. Fixing B-C as an adjacent pair settles the item without testing all the orders.

short_explanation: All three points are stated: AI systems adapt to the student's pace, interests and learning style; AI executes skill mapping; and AI helps set question papers according to the curriculum.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This drops the question-paper point, which the passage states directly.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This keeps only skill mapping and drops adaptation to interests and question-paper setting.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This drops adaptation to the student's interests, which the passage lists first.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This keeps only the question-paper point and drops the other two.

short_explanation: In "AI to gauge the best time to buy airline tickets", gauge means to judge or estimate something that cannot be read off an instrument. "Assess" is that word.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Monitor means to watch continuously; it describes the tracking of weather and air traffic later in the passage, not the judgement of a best time.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Analyse means to break data down for study, which is a step towards the judgement rather than the judgement itself.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Measure is the literal dictionary sense of gauge, but "the best time to buy" is not a quantity that can be measured; it has to be judged.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Examine means to inspect closely and stops short of reaching a conclusion.

common_traps: Measure is the textbook synonym of gauge and is the option most often picked; the context decides between the instrument sense and the judgement sense.
key_note: Measure is defensible as a dictionary equivalent, so the item rests on context rather than on definition alone.

short_explanation: The order runs 1-B-D-A-C-6: the general cause comes first (state encouragement is meagre), then the specific hardship (no consideration, insecure jobs), then "Hence, they fail to put up their best", and finally the contrast with sportsmen in other countries.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This puts C before A, which separates "Hence" from the hardships that cause the failure.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Opening with D names the sportsmen's insecurity before the meagre state encouragement that explains it, and leaves "such difficulties" in C pointing at the wrong sentence.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Again D opens, so the specific grievance precedes the general cause it follows from.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This both opens with D and puts C before A, breaking the cause-and-effect link that "Hence" marks.

common_traps: A begins with "Hence", so it must come immediately after the difficulties it explains; C begins with a contrast ("in most other countries"), so it must come after those difficulties are described, not between them and their consequence.

short_explanation: The passage credits AI in healthcare with analysing medical images more accurately and faster than humans (1), giving personalised treatment recommendations (2) and analysing electronic health records (4).

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This drops the analysis of electronic health records, which the passage states in its last sentence.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Points 3 and 5 — drug development and drug administration — do not appear in the passage at all.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This includes point 3, which the passage does not mention, and drops the diagnostic point it does.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This includes point 3; the passage speaks of predicting outbreaks and identifying high-risk patients, not of developing new drugs.

common_traps: Points 3 and 5 sound like plausible things AI does in medicine, which is exactly why they are planted here. The test is what the passage states, not what is true of AI generally.

short_explanation: Part 3 is wrong: after "do anything except", the verb takes the bare infinitive, so it should be "anything except go out", not "except to go out".
explanation_text: When except or but follows a form of the verb do, the verb after it drops its "to": She does nothing except complain. He could do nothing but wait. The full infinitive returns when there is no preceding "do": I had no choice except to wait. Here "do anything except" sets the bare-infinitive pattern, so "to go" is one word too many.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "The wards of the hostel are" is correct; wards here are the residents in the hostel's charge.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "allowed to do" is correct — allow takes the full infinitive, which "to do" supplies.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "on their own at night" is correct and needs no change.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Part 3 does contain an error, so this cannot be chosen.

short_explanation: The passage sets out where AI is being applied — education, airlines, healthcare — without arguing a case, so a title about exploring the applications of AI covers it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Penetration of AI" suggests how far AI has spread and how fast, which the passage never measures.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Using AI to Transform Lives" claims an effect on people's lives that the passage does not argue; it lists industry uses.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Synergy between humans and AI would need a discussion of the two working together, which the passage does not offer.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A case study examines one instance in depth; this passage surveys three sectors briefly.

key_note: B is the tempting near miss because the passage is positive throughout; the deciding point is that a title must cover the whole passage, and what is common to all three sections is the range of applications.

short_explanation: Part 1 is wrong on two counts: a sentence opening with "Hardly" inverts the subject and auxiliary, and the hardly...when pattern takes the past perfect — "Hardly had I finished writing when my brother snatched...".
explanation_text: Put a negative or near-negative adverb at the head of a clause — hardly, scarcely, never, seldom, no sooner, not only — and the subject and auxiliary change places: Hardly had I finished, Never have I seen, No sooner had he left. The partner word matters too: hardly and scarcely pair with when, no sooner pairs with than.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "writing when my brother" is correct; "when" is the right correlative for hardly.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "snatched the fountain" is correct — the simple past is what follows the past perfect in this pattern.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "pen from my hand" is correct; snatch takes "from".

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Part 1 does contain an error, so this cannot be chosen.

common_traps: Two rules are being tested in one segment: the inversion and the past perfect. Repairing only the tense ("Hardly I had finished") still leaves the sentence wrong.

short_explanation: The order runs 3-1-5-2-4: the Jalpaiguri deaths open the paragraph, sentence 1 gives the state-wise picture, 5 introduces the Elephant Task Force report, 2 says "it identified key factors", and 4 lists those factors with "These include".

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Opening with the state-wise statistics leaves "it" in sentence 2 with nothing to refer to, since the report is only named in 5.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ending with the Jalpaiguri deaths turns the news event into an afterthought, and "These include" in 4 comes before the factors are mentioned in 2.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Here 2 follows 3 directly, so "it identified key factors" has no antecedent — the report has not yet been introduced.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This puts 4 immediately after 3, so "These include" points at nothing.

common_traps: Two pronoun links pin the order down: "it" in sentence 2 must follow the report named in 5, and "These" in 4 must follow the key factors named in 2. That fixes 5-2-4 as a block.

short_explanation: The original makes a well-organised training programme, arranged by the management, the thing that brings risk factors down. The reframing that keeps the management as the agent, the programme as the means and the reduction of risk as the purpose is the one to pick.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The original says risk factors are much reduced, not eliminated; "elimination" overstates the claim.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "A training program for risk factors" changes what the programme is about — the original trains people, it does not train risk factors — and drops the reduction altogether.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "A well-trained program" is a misuse: people are trained, programmes are well organised. The qualifier has been attached to the wrong noun.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This is close in sense, but "should conduct" turns the original's assertion about what a programme will achieve into a piece of advice.

key_note: Choice E is a defensible near-equivalent and a candidate could reasonably pick it. The keyed option is preferred because "it is necessary for the management to arrange" keeps the original's force — the programme is what secures the reduction — while E recasts it as a recommendation.

short_explanation: The order runs 3-5-4-1-2: sentence 3 introduces the plan to liberalise the MDA policy in full, 5 says what it will promote, 4 gives the background that the policy was earlier limited to city compost, 1 reports the demands to expand it, and 2 says the expansion will complement Swachh Bharat Abhiyan.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Opening with 1 leaves "this policy" with nothing to refer to; the MDA policy is named only in 3.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This opens with "It will promote", where "It" has no antecedent.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This opens with "This expansion", which presupposes the expansion already described in 1.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This also opens with 5, so "It" again has nothing to point back to.

common_traps: The opening sentence must contain the full name of the policy, not a pronoun or a demonstrative. Only sentence 3 introduces Market Development Assistance in full, which settles the first position immediately.

short_explanation: The order runs 4-2-1-5-3: sentence 4 states the theme (forests turned from wealth into curse this summer), 2 describes this summer's heatwave and fires, 1 gives the yearly background, 5 contrasts previous years in Siberia, and 3 brings it back to this year in European Russia.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Opening with 3 ("This year") assumes a comparison with earlier years that has not yet been made.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This begins with the heatwave before the theme sentence and ends with the general statement about yearly fires, which belongs before the year-by-year contrast.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The numerical order puts "But in previous years" (5) after "This year" (3), reversing the contrast.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This reverses the whole chain, so the contrast words no longer point anywhere sensible.

common_traps: The time markers form a chain that cannot be broken: "wildfires break out every summer" (1), then "But in previous years" (5), then "This year" (3). Fixing 1-5-3 as a block leaves only one workable order.

short_explanation: The right choices are effect, currant, venal and eminent — A, A, B, A. Effect is the noun in "come into effect", a currant is the dried fruit, venal means open to bribery, and eminent means distinguished.
explanation_text: Four pairs worth fixing for good. Affect is normally the verb and effect the noun, except for the rare verb "to effect" meaning to bring about. Currant is the fruit, current is the flow or the adjective meaning present. Venial means a minor, forgivable fault, while venal means corruptible by money — a bribe-taker is venal. Eminent means distinguished, imminent means about to happen, and immanent means inherent.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This takes affect in the first sentence, but affect is the verb; the noun after "come into" must be effect. It also picks venial for the bribe-taking politician.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This picks current for the cake, which is the flow of water or electricity, and imminent for the surgeon, which means about to happen rather than distinguished.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is right except for the second sentence, where a cake is made with currants, not with a current.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This errs in three places: current for the cake, venial for the politician, and imminent for the surgeon.

short_explanation: Only sentences 1 and 5 are sound. Sentence 2 has "hindrances to these" where the reference is to the single work just mentioned, 3 breaks parallelism with "both an opiate and poison", and 4 leaves "believing that what is not" unfinished.
explanation_text: Sentence 3 tests the parallelism that both...and demands: whatever follows "both" and whatever follows "and" must have the same shape, so "both an opiate and a poison" with the article repeated. Sentence 4 tests clause completion: "believing what is not" would work, and "believing that what is not is" would work, but "believing that what is not" starts a that-clause and never supplies its verb.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This includes 2, whose "hindrances to these" does not agree with the singular "this work" it refers back to.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Sentences 3 and 4 are both faulty, so only 5 in this group is correct.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: These are two of the faulty sentences, not the correct ones.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Both sentences named here are faulty — 2 on reference and 4 on an incomplete clause.

short_explanation: The right choices are defuse, oral, discreet and poring — B, A, A, B. You defuse a tense situation, oral hygiene concerns the mouth, discreet enquiries are tactful ones, and to pore over a book is to study it closely.
explanation_text: Defuse comes from removing a fuse from a bomb, hence calming a dangerous situation; diffuse means to spread widely. Oral relates to the mouth, aural to the ear. Discreet means tactful and careful about what one reveals; discrete means separate and distinct. Pore over means to read intently, while pour is what one does with liquid — the spelling difference carries the whole meaning.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This picks diffuse for the tense room — diffuse means to spread out — aural for hygiene, which concerns hearing, and pouring for books, which means tipping liquid.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This is right on the first and fourth but takes aural for hygiene and discrete, meaning separate, for tactful enquiries.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This picks diffuse in the first sentence and discrete in the third, where the sense required is tactful.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This errs in the first two: diffuse for the charged atmosphere and aural for hygiene.

short_explanation: If opinions fall on a spectrum between two camps, the issues must be disputed, so the first blank takes "controversial" and the second takes "opposite", the word for the two ends of a spectrum.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Incontrovertible means beyond dispute, which contradicts a sentence built on divided opinion.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The issues themselves are not contradictory, and inimical means hostile in effect and normally takes "to" rather than describing camps.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Incessant means unceasing, which describes frequency and not the disputed nature of the issues.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Incessant fails in the first blank for the same reason, and relentless describes persistence rather than the two ends of a spectrum.

common_traps: The second blank is decided by "spectrum between two ___ camps": a spectrum runs between opposite poles, so the word must name the two ends, not the temper of the argument.

short_explanation: A dispute that stands in the way of better relations is a bitter one, and the manner of settling it friendly — "resolve the acrimonious dispute in an amicable manner".

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Ambiguous means unclear in meaning, which is not what blocks bilateral relations, and amiable describes a person's friendly nature rather than the manner of a settlement.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Execrable means appalling, the opposite of the goodwill the first step towards better relations implies.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Artful means cunning, which would undercut the improvement in relations the sentence describes.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Flippancy is a noun and cannot fill "in an ___ manner", which needs an adjective.

common_traps: Amiable and amicable are a classic pair: people are amiable, while settlements, separations and agreements are amicable.

short_explanation: The right choices are censured, palate, broach and course — B, A, A, A. To censure is to reprimand, the palate is the sense of taste, to broach is to raise a subject, and a seven course meal has that many servings.
explanation_text: Censor means to suppress parts of a text or film; censure means to criticise formally. Palate is the roof of the mouth and so the sense of taste, palette is the painter's board, and pallet is a bed or a loading platform. Broach is a verb meaning to open a subject or a barrel; a brooch is jewellery. Course is a stage of a meal or a route; coarse means rough or crude.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This picks censored for the reprimand — censoring is cutting objectionable material — and coarse for the meal, which means rough.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is right except for the second sentence, where palette, the board a painter mixes colours on, replaces the sense of taste.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is right except for the third sentence, where brooch, an ornamental pin, replaces the verb broach.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This errs in three places: censored for the reprimand, palette for taste and coarse for the meal.

short_explanation: GDP is arrived at by estimation, not exact counting, and GDP with its growth rate is the standard indicator of how the economy is performing.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Calculation suggests an exact arithmetic result, and "shape of the economy" is loose, informal usage for a formal statement about indicators.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: GDP is measured and estimated from data, never assumed; and GDP is not a measure of the economy's size in the sense this blank needs alongside the growth rate.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "Performance of GDP" is odd — GDP is itself the measure of performance — and the sentence would then repeat the word in both halves.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A target is something set in advance; GDP is a figure arrived at after the fact, and "operations of the economy" is not a usual phrase.

key_note: In Indian official usage the National Statistical Office releases estimates of GDP — advance, provisional and revised — which is why "estimation" is the natural word here. A is the nearest miss.

short_explanation: Phlegmatic — meaning calm and unexcitable — keeps the ph- and the silent g of phlegm and ends in the ordinary adjective suffix -atic.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This adds the invented ending -icisum to an already complete adjective.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This adds the invented ending -icsam; no English word ends that way.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This adds the invented ending -icusim, again on top of a complete adjective.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This has both the invented ending and a transposed stem, "phelg-" for "phlegm-".

key_note: The stem does not print the word to be spelled, but the item is still decidable: only one option is an English word and the other four graft nonsense suffixes onto it.

short_explanation: Moving to a tougher norm is upgrading to it, and the standard verb for dealing with a problem like air pollution is tackle: "Upgrading to stricter fuel standards is one way to tackle air pollution."
explanation_text: The first blank is settled by the preposition rather than by meaning: the sentence prints "____ to stricter fuel standard", and of the five verbs only upgrade takes "to" in this sense — upgrade to a higher version, a stricter norm. Reading the preposition before weighing the meanings saves time on double-blank items.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: "Going to" a standard is not idiomatic, and ward off means to keep something away before it arrives, while the pollution is already present.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: "Viewing to" is ungrammatical, and put off means to postpone, which makes no sense of pollution.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: "Deciding to" must be followed by a verb, not by "stricter fuel standard", and rules are abolished, not pollution.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: "Regulating to" is ungrammatical; regulate takes a direct object.

topic_name: Meaning of an idiom in context
short_explanation: To hit the bull's eye is to achieve exactly what was aimed at, which fits both the archer who wins the competition and the marketing strategy that lifts revenue.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Bite the bullet means to face something painful with courage, which neither sentence describes.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Break the ice means to ease the awkwardness at the start of a meeting, not to succeed.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Caught red-handed means caught in the act of wrongdoing, and it would also need a passive verb in both blanks.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A piece of cake is a noun phrase meaning something very easy; it cannot serve as the verb the blanks require.

common_traps: The archery setting of sentence 1 makes the idiom look literal. Sentence 2 is the check: the same phrase must work figuratively for a sales team.

topic_name: MS Word page setup and formatting
short_explanation: The gutter is the extra space Word adds on the binding edge so that text is not swallowed when the pages are stapled or bound. It is set in Page Setup along with the normal top, bottom, left and right margins.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Word has no 'End Margin'; the margins it names are top, bottom, left, right and gutter.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: No such setting. The space above the body text is the top margin, and the repeating text in it is the header.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Not a Word term. The nearest real idea is the gutter, or the space between columns in a multi-column layout.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

topic_name: File formats, encoding standards and multimedia
short_explanation: TIFF is Tagged Image File Format, a lossless raster image format used for scanning, faxing and printing where quality must not degrade.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The second F is File, not Fax. TIFF is widely used by fax software, which is what makes this the tempting option.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: TIFF stores images, not typefaces; the last word is Format.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Both the third and fourth words are wrong: it is File Format, not Fax Font.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Word order invented; no format is called Tagged Image Front File.

common_traps: TIFF is often handled by fax utilities, so 'Tagged Image Fax Format' reads plausibly. The expansion is File Format.

short_explanation: Phishing is the fraud of posing as a bank, employer or other trusted sender in an email, SMS or web page so that the victim hands over passwords, card numbers or money.
explanation_text: The definition turns on two things together: a fake identity and the victim being persuaded to disclose something. Spoofing supplies only the first half, faking the sender address, caller ID or IP, and is usually the technique that carries a phishing message. Identity theft is what a criminal does afterwards with the stolen details. Keeping the sequence straight is the point: spoof to look genuine, phish to collect, then commit identity theft.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Spoofing is faking an identifier such as the From address or caller ID. It is a technique used inside phishing, not the act of harvesting credentials.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Identity theft is the later misuse of the stolen details, not the attempt to obtain them.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Authentication is the legitimate process of proving who a user is.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Spamming is bulk unsolicited messaging; it need not impersonate anyone or seek data.

common_traps: Spoofing is the close neighbour. Ask whether the stem describes faking an identifier (spoofing) or tricking someone into surrendering information (phishing).

short_explanation: Lynx, released in 1992, is the text-only browser of this group: it renders pages as plain characters in a terminal with no images.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Mosaic (1993) was the browser that popularised inline images, that is, a graphical browser.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Netscape Navigator (1994) grew out of the Mosaic team and was graphical from the start.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Opera first appeared in the mid-1990s as a graphical browser.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Internet Explorer launched in 1995, also graphical.

key_note: Strictly, CERN's line-mode browser (1991) was text-based and earlier; among the options given, Lynx is the intended answer.

short_explanation: F11 toggles full-screen view in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and most other browsers; pressing it again restores the normal window.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: F3 opens the find-on-page box.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: F5 reloads the current page.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: F9 has no standard browsing action.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: F1 opens help.

short_explanation: Excel's function is FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]): the periodic rate, the number of periods and the payment are required, while present value and payment timing are optional.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Drops nper. Without the number of periods Excel cannot compound anything.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Drops pmt, the periodic payment, which is a required argument.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Omits pv and makes type compulsory; in fact pv comes before type and both are optional.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Leaves out type and wrongly brackets pmt, which is required.

topic_name: MS Excel cell references, shortcuts and display behaviour
short_explanation: Ctrl + Spacebar selects the whole column that contains the active cell.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Shift + Spacebar selects the entire row, not the column.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl + Shift + Spacebar selects the whole worksheet, or the current region around the cell.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Alt + Spacebar opens the window control menu of the application.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Fn changes the behaviour of function keys on a laptop; it has no role in selecting cells.

common_traps: Column and row are easily swapped. Ctrl is the taller key and selects the taller block (the column); Shift selects the row.

topic_name: MS PowerPoint views and slide show controls
short_explanation: Slide Sorter view lays every slide out as a thumbnail on one screen, so slides can be dragged into a new order, duplicated or deleted in bulk.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Slide Show runs the presentation full screen, one slide at a time.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Slide Master controls the common layout, fonts and placeholders, not the running order.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Notes Page shows one slide with its speaker notes beneath it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Slide Design applies themes and colour schemes; it is not a view for reordering.

short_explanation: The 1's complement is formed by flipping every bit, so 1000 becomes 0111.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 1100 flips only the first two bits and leaves the rest unchanged.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 1110 is the 2's complement region, not a bit-by-bit inversion; inverting 1000 cannot leave three 1s at the left.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 1101 changes bits arbitrarily; inversion of 1000 gives 0111.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 1001 flips only the last bit.

solution_steps: Take the number bit by bit: 1, 0, 0, 0.
Invert each bit: 1 becomes 0, and each 0 becomes 1.
Read the result in the same order: 0111.
common_traps: The 2's complement is one more than the 1's complement: 0111 + 1 = 1000. The question asks only for the inversion.

short_explanation: A repeater works at the physical layer: it receives a weakening signal, regenerates it to full strength and sends it on, which lets a cable run beyond its normal length limit.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A router forwards packets between different networks using IP addresses; it is not used to stretch one segment.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A gateway translates between networks that use different protocols.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A switch forwards frames to the right port using MAC addresses; extending distance is not its purpose.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A server provides files or services to clients and plays no part in signal strength.

topic_name: MS PowerPoint views and slide show controls
short_explanation: During a slide show, Tab moves the selection to the next hyperlink on the slide; Shift + Tab steps back to the previous one.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Shift alone does nothing here; it only reverses Tab's direction when held with it.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl is used with other keys, for example Ctrl + P for the pen, not for stepping through links.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Alt reaches the ribbon in editing view; it does not move between links in a running show.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Fn only alters what the function keys send on a laptop keyboard.

topic_name: Memory types and the memory hierarchy
short_explanation: ROM is static because its contents do not need refreshing, and non-volatile because they survive a power cut.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: RAM is volatile: switch the machine off and its contents are gone.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: BIOS is the firmware program, not a kind of memory; it is stored in ROM or flash.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Cache is built from static RAM, so it is static but still volatile.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: CMOS memory holds BIOS settings but is volatile, which is why a small battery keeps it alive.

common_traps: Cache is static yet volatile, and CMOS keeps its data only because of a battery. Both halves of the stem must hold.

short_explanation: A warm boot is a restart with the power still on, such as Ctrl + Alt + Del or the Restart command; the machine reloads the operating system without a full power cycle.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Starting a machine that had been switched off is a cold boot.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Pressing the power button on a dead machine is also a cold boot.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: BIOS is firmware that starts the hardware, not an operating system, and this describes no real boot type.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Changing BIOS settings is done by entering setup during startup; it has nothing to do with warm booting.

common_traps: Cold and warm are decided by one thing only: whether power was removed.

short_explanation: A standard CD-ROM holds data in the hundreds of megabytes, so 680 MB is the right order of magnitude; the common retail figures are 650 MB and 700 MB.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 680 KB is about the size of a single photo, far below any CD.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 680 bytes is a few lines of text.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 680 GB is a hard-disk figure; a single-layer DVD holds only about 4.7 GB.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 680 TB is data-centre scale, nothing like an optical disc.

key_note: The 680 MB figure is loose. Standard CD-ROM capacity is quoted as 650 MB (74 minutes) or 700 MB (80 minutes); the option set makes MB the only workable choice.

short_explanation: A light pen is an optical input device: a light-sensitive detector in its tip picks up the screen's glow and reports where on the display it is being held.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Nothing is moved or pressed mechanically; the sensing is by light. A mouse with a ball is the mechanical example.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: All computer peripherals are electronic; that word does not classify the pen's sensing method.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: It sends position data into the computer, so it is an input device, not an output one.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Wrong on both counts: it neither outputs nor senses electrically rather than optically.

short_explanation: The underscore is an ordinary character in a file name; Windows reserves the others for its own use.
explanation_text: Windows forbids nine characters in a file name: \ / : * ? " < > and |. Slashes separate folders, the colon marks a drive, the asterisk and question mark are wildcards in searches, the quote marks group names with spaces, and the angle brackets and pipe redirect input and output at the command line. Anything outside that list, including the underscore, hyphen and space, is allowed.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The forward slash separates folder names in a path.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The less-than sign redirects input at the command line and is reserved.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The question mark is a single-character wildcard.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The asterisk is the multi-character wildcard.

short_explanation: A macro records or scripts a sequence of commands so that a task done repeatedly can be replayed with one click or shortcut.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Office records sound through the audio or media tools, not macros.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Mouse movement may be captured while recording, but replaying pointer motion is not the purpose.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Keystrokes are likewise part of what gets recorded; the reason for recording them is to automate the task.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

common_traps: Recording mouse moves and keystrokes describes how a macro is made. The question asks why it is used, which is automation.

topic_name: Generations of computers and hardware evolution
short_explanation: UNIVAC stands for Universal Automatic Computer, the first commercially sold computer in the United States, delivered in 1951 by Eckert and Mauchly.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The A is for Automatic, not Array.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The first word is Universal, not Unique.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: No such expansion; Unvalued is not part of any computer name.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Both the first and third words are wrong.

topic_name: Pioneers and landmarks in computing history
short_explanation: Vint Cerf, with Robert Kahn, designed TCP/IP, the protocol suite that lets separate networks interconnect, and is therefore called a father of the Internet.
explanation_text: Two titles are regularly confused. Cerf and Kahn built the Internet, the network of networks joined by TCP/IP, in the 1970s. Tim Berners-Lee built the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989: HTTP, HTML and the URL, which are pages and links running on top of that network. The Internet is the road system; the Web is one kind of traffic on it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web, which runs on the Internet but is not the same thing.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Douglas Engelbart invented the mouse and demonstrated hypertext and windowing in 1968.

common_traps: Berners-Lee is the father of the Web, not of the Internet.

topic_name: MS Excel cell references, shortcuts and display behaviour
short_explanation: Excel fills a cell with #### when a number or date is wider than the column; widening the column or shrinking the font shows the value again.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: $$$$ is not an Excel signal; the dollar sign marks absolute references such as $A$1.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: ^^^^ has no meaning in a cell.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: **** is not produced by Excel.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: @@@@ is not produced by Excel.

common_traps: #### appears only for numbers and dates. Text too long for a narrow column spills into the next cell or is clipped, it is not hashed out.

topic_name: Printers, printing metrics and display hardware
short_explanation: DPI is dots per inch, the number of ink dots a printer lays down in one inch, which is the resolution of the printed output.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: It is dots, not discs; nothing about a disc is involved in printing.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: DPI describes the printed output, not the input image. Scanner input is also measured in dpi, but a printer's dpi rates what it produces.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Wrong on both counts, discs and input.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Screen resolution is measured in pixels per inch (ppi), not printer dpi.

common_traps: Read the last few words of each option. A, C and E differ only in output, input and monitor.

short_explanation: In a mesh topology every node has its own dedicated link to every other node, which gives the highest fault tolerance at the highest cabling cost.
explanation_text: A full mesh of n devices needs n(n-1)/2 links and n-1 ports on each device, so six computers already need fifteen cables. That cost is why mesh is used for backbone routers and critical WAN links rather than office floors, where a star built around a switch gives most of the reliability for a fraction of the cabling.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: In a star every device has one link to a central hub or switch, not to each other.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: In a bus all devices share one common backbone cable.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: In a ring each device connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A tree is a hierarchy of stars joined to a root; links are parent to child, not all to all.

short_explanation: A MIDI port connects electronic musical instruments such as keyboards and synthesisers to a sound card, carrying note and control messages rather than recorded audio.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A bus is the internal set of lines that carry data inside the computer, not an instrument connector.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The CPU is the processor.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: USB is a general-purpose port; modern keyboards do use it, but the port named for musical instruments is MIDI.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A UPS is a battery backup power supply.

short_explanation: FORTRAN is short for Formula Translation, the language IBM released in 1957 for scientific and engineering calculation.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Formal is not part of the name; the first word is Formula.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Neither word is right; FORTRAN translates formulas, it does not transmit anything.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The second word is Translation, not Transmission.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The first word is Formula, not Final.

topic_name: MS Excel cell references, shortcuts and display behaviour
short_explanation: Ctrl + ; stamps the current date into the active cell as a fixed value that does not change later.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Excel has no shortcut that inserts memory information.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ctrl + Shift + ; enters the current time.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: There is no location shortcut; the cell reference is shown in the Name Box.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: No shortcut inserts the cell's own address; that needs a formula such as =CELL("address").

common_traps: Date and time differ by one key: add Shift for the time. Both are static stamps, unlike =TODAY() and =NOW(), which update.

topic_name: MS Word page setup and formatting
short_explanation: A template is a ready-made file holding styles, layout and sample content, which Word copies into each new document based on it. Word's default template is Normal.dotm.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Presentation is a PowerPoint file, not a Word style container.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Letters is a category of templates, not the kind of file.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Not a Word term.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: WordArt creates decorative text effects for a single piece of text.

short_explanation: Classic Ethernet was designed as a shared bus: every station taps one common cable, listens before sending and detects collisions (CSMA/CD).
explanation_text: The wiring changed but the textbook answer did not. Early 10BASE5 and 10BASE2 Ethernet ran a single coaxial backbone, a physical bus. From 10BASE-T onwards the cabling radiates from a hub or switch, so modern Ethernet is physically a star; with a hub it still behaves as one shared bus, and with a switch each link becomes its own collision domain. Exams set on Ethernet's defining design expect bus.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Ring is the Token Ring and FDDI design, where a token passes around a closed loop.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Star describes how today's Ethernet is cabled around a switch, but it is not the shared-medium design Ethernet is defined by.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Tree describes hierarchies of hubs or switches in a large building, not Ethernet itself.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Mesh needs a dedicated link between every pair of nodes, which Ethernet does not use.

common_traps: Physically a modern office runs a star. The keyed answer is Ethernet's logical shared-bus design.
key_note: Star is defensible for switched Ethernet as cabled today; the item is asking about Ethernet's classic shared-medium topology.

short_explanation: File compression re-encodes data so it occupies fewer bytes, letting many files fit in less space; ZIP and RAR archives work this way.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Not a computing term.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Copying duplicates files and uses more space, not less.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Compatibility is about whether a file can be opened by a program; it does not change size.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Maintenance covers housekeeping such as defragmenting or deleting old files, not encoding data more tightly.

topic_name: Memory types and the memory hierarchy
short_explanation: Cache is built from static RAM sitting between the processor and main memory, so it is a form of RAM: fast, small and volatile.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Virtual memory is disk space used as an overflow for RAM; it is slower, not faster.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: ROM cannot be written to freely during normal running, which cache must be.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Cache loses its contents when power goes; nothing about it is permanent.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: PROM is programmable read-only memory, written once and then fixed.

common_traps: The stem's wording about strong, fast memory tempts ROM or 'permanent memory'. Speed does not imply permanence; cache is volatile.

topic_name: MS Word ribbon, tabs and shortcuts
short_explanation: F12 is the saving key on the function row: it opens the Save As dialog, so an unsaved document is written to disk exactly as Ctrl + S would do.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: F8 extends a selection in Word.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: F9 updates fields such as a table of contents.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: F10 activates the ribbon's key tips, the same as tapping Alt.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: F6 moves between the panes of the window.

key_note: Shift + F12 is the exact equivalent of Ctrl + S (save in place); plain F12 opens Save As. Among the five options F12 is the only saving key.

short_explanation: A Trojan horse hides inside something the user wants to install, such as a free utility or a cracked game, and runs its harmful payload once the user opens it.
explanation_text: The three malware families are told apart by how they spread. A virus attaches itself to a host file and spreads when that file is run or copied. A worm copies itself across a network with no user action. A Trojan does not self-replicate at all; it relies entirely on the user being persuaded to run it, which is why disguise is its defining feature.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Malware is the umbrella term for all malicious software, so it does not name this particular disguise.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Spyware quietly monitors activity and reports it; the stem is about how the program gets installed.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts traffic between two parties; it is not a downloaded program.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A denial-of-service attack floods a service to make it unavailable.

topic_name: Printers, printing metrics and display hardware
short_explanation: A thermal printer uses heat on specially coated paper instead of ink or toner, which is why it is called inkless; ATM slips and shop bills are printed this way.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: An inkjet sprays liquid ink from cartridges.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A dot matrix printer strikes an inked ribbon with pins.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A plotter draws with pens or ink for large drawings.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A line printer is an impact printer and also uses an inked ribbon.

common_traps: Thermal-transfer printers use a wax ribbon; the inkless label belongs to direct thermal printing on heat-sensitive paper.

topic_name: Memory types and the memory hierarchy
short_explanation: Whatever the processor is currently working on must sit in main memory (RAM), because the CPU can address it directly; disks cannot be executed from.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Disk memory is storage the CPU cannot read instructions from directly; data must be loaded into RAM first.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Secondary memory is the same thing under another name, used for long-term storage.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Not a standard level of the memory hierarchy.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

topic_name: MS Excel cell references, shortcuts and display behaviour
short_explanation: Format Painter, the paintbrush on the Home tab, copies only the formatting of a cell (font, colour, borders, number format) and applies it to whatever is selected next.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: An ordinary copy and paste brings the contents across as well; formatting alone needs Paste Special or Format Painter.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The default font is a setting, not a way to transfer formatting.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The formatting toolbar lets a user apply formats by hand; it does not copy one cell's look to another.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A cross-reference links to content elsewhere in a document.

common_traps: Double-click the Format Painter to keep it active for several targets; a single click applies it once.

short_explanation: A flip-flop is the basic bistable circuit that holds one bit: it stays in whichever of its two states it was set to until the next clock or input changes it.
explanation_text: The hierarchy matters here. Logic gates compute but remember nothing. A flip-flop, built from a few gates with feedback, is the smallest circuit that stores a bit. Registers and counters are then built from several flip-flops, and memory arrays from many more. So the basic storage component is the flip-flop; everything above it is an assembly of them.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A register stores several bits, but it is itself built from a row of flip-flops, so it is not the basic component.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Derived gates such as NAND, NOR and XOR are combinational; their output depends only on the present inputs, with no memory.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: A counter is a chain of flip-flops arranged to count pulses.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A multiplexer selects one of several inputs; it stores nothing.

common_traps: Register is the tempting answer. The question asks for the basic component, and a register is made of flip-flops.

topic_name: File formats, encoding standards and multimedia
short_explanation: ASCII is the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, the 7-bit scheme that assigns a number to each letter, digit and control character.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Standard, not Stable, and Information, not International.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Code, not Case, and Information, not Institutional.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The last two words are reversed; it is Information Interchange.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The second word is Standard, not Stable.

common_traps: All five options look alike. Fix the four words in order: American, Standard, Code, Information Interchange.

topic_name: Operating systems, utilities and system software
short_explanation: A patch is a piece of code issued by the vendor to modify software already installed, usually to close a security hole or correct a defect.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: A hole is the vulnerability that a patch closes, not the correction.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A fix is loose everyday usage; the term for a vendor-issued modification is a patch.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Not a term for software updates.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Antivirus software detects malware; it does not modify the vendor's program.

common_traps: 'Fixes' reads like a synonym. The standard term in this definition is patch.

topic_name: MS Word ribbon, tabs and shortcuts
short_explanation: Ctrl + N creates a new blank document and opens it in its own window, ready to type in.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Incomplete: the new document is not merely created, it is opened for editing straight away.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Word creates .docx documents, not plain text files.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: A new paragraph comes from pressing Enter.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Opening an existing document is Ctrl + O.

key_note: Option A is arguably the same action stated loosely; the key prefers the fuller wording, since Ctrl + N both creates the file and puts it on screen.

topic_name: Generations of computers and hardware evolution
short_explanation: Second-generation computers (roughly 1956 to 1963) replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, making machines smaller, cooler, cheaper and more reliable.
explanation_text: The generations are named after the switching element. First: vacuum tubes, bulky and hot. Second: transistors. Third: integrated circuits, many transistors on one chip. Fourth: the microprocessor, a whole CPU on one chip. Fifth: parallel processing and artificial intelligence. Fixing that ladder answers most generation questions in one step.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Vacuum tubes belong to the first generation.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The microprocessor defines the fourth generation.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Integrated circuits define the third generation.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Artificial intelligence is associated with the fifth generation.

topic_name: Operating systems, utilities and system software
short_explanation: DOS stands for Disk Operating System, the command-line operating system that loaded from disk and ran PCs before Windows.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Neither word is right; the D is for Disk.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Differential is not part of any operating system's name.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Outsourcing has no meaning here; the S is for System.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The D stands for Disk, not Device.

key_note: The option spells it 'Disc'; the standard spelling is Disk Operating System. It is the only option with the right two words.

short_explanation: Colleges A, C and E carry 60% of the applications and average 100 each, so the whole set is 500; E and C together are 175, and 175 x 18/35 gives College X 90 applications.
explanation_text: The whole set of six questions turns on one number. A, C and E hold 25% + 20% + 15% = 60% of the applications, and an average of 100 means they hold 300 between them. So 60% of the total is 300 and the total is 500, which fixes A = 125, B = 80, C = 100, D = 120 and E = 75. Work that out once and every question in the set becomes a single line.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: No step in the ratio gives 85; scaling 175 down in the ratio 35 : 18 gives exactly 90.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it is neither a college figure nor the result of the ratio, which is 90.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is College E's own figure (15% of 500), taken instead of scaling E + C by 18/35.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This is College B's figure (16% of 500), not College X.

solution_steps: A, C and E are 25% + 20% + 15% = 60% of all applications.
Their average is 100, so together they received 3 x 100 = 300.
60% of the total is 300, so the total is 500.
College E = 15% of 500 = 75 and College C = 20% of 500 = 100, so E + C = 175.
formula_used: Total = (sum of known colleges) / (their combined percentage); X = (E + C) x 18 / 35
common_traps: The ratio is written (E + C) first and X second, so X is 175 x 18/35; dividing the other way gives about 340.
key_note: The total of 500 is never printed on the chart. It comes only from the note that A, C and E average 100.

short_explanation: The missing term is the geometric mean of 325 and 145: it squares to 325 x 145 = 47,125, whose square root is about 217, and 216 is the only option anywhere near that.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Roughly twice the true value; no step in the equation doubles the answer, which is about 217.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Roughly half of 325 - halving one side instead of taking the square root of the product of the two numbers.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it sits between the two given numbers, but the square root of 47,125 is about 217.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: About twice 325 - doubling the denominator instead of taking the square root of 325 x 145.

solution_steps: Cross-multiply: ? x ? = 325 x 145.
? = square root of 47,125, which is about 217.1.
Only 216 lies near 217, so the item is asking for the nearest value.
formula_used: a / b = c / a, so a = square root of (b x c)
key_note: The exact value is 217.08, so no option is exact. 216 is the nearest by a wide margin, and the row has to be read as an approximation item.

short_explanation: College D received 120 applications; boys being 40% fewer than girls puts boys and girls in the ratio 3 : 5, so the boys number 120 x 3/8 = 45.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is the number of girls, 120 x 5/8, not the boys.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This splits College D's 120 down the middle; the 40% gap makes the split 45 and 75.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the 3 : 5 split of 120 gives 45.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary. Taking 40% of 120 would give 48 in any case, and the correct reading of '40% less than the girls' gives 45.

solution_steps: A, C and E hold 60% of the applications and average 100, so the total is 300 / 0.60 = 500.
College D = 24% of 500 = 120.
Boys are 40% less than girls, so boys = 0.6 x girls, that is boys : girls = 3 : 5.
Boys = 120 x 3/8 = 45 (and girls = 75).
formula_used: If boys are 40% less than girls, boys : girls = 60 : 100 = 3 : 5
common_traps: '40% less than the girls' is measured against the girls, not against College D's 120 - the total is the wrong base.

short_explanation: The square root of 841 is 29, so the missing term is 863 - 29 - 75 + 93 = 852.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: carrying the three known terms across correctly leaves 852.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: nothing in the line produces it, and the balance gives 852.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Close to what dropping the +75 altogether would give (927); with all four terms kept the answer is 852.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the working gives 852.

solution_steps: Square root of 841 = 29, since 29 x 29 = 841.
The line becomes 29 + ? + 75 - 93 = 863.
formula_used: Move each known term across the equals sign with its sign reversed

short_explanation: Rounding gives 40 x 56 / 7 = 320, 20% of 700 = 140 and 11,479.50 / 7 = about 1,640; with the third term read as 6 cubed the left side is 320 - 140 + 216 = 396, so the missing value is about 396 + 1,640 = 2,036.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the rounded terms come to about 2,036.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it sits nearly 900 above what the four rounded terms produce.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: no combination of the rounded terms lands here.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary. Adding 20% of 700 instead of subtracting it would give about 2,316, and the correct handling gives 2,036.

solution_steps: 20% of 699.81 is about 140.
The third term is 6 cubed = 216 (printed as '63' in this transcript).
Left side is about 320 - 140 + 216 = 396.
The bracket is subtracted on the right, so it is added on the left: ? = 396 + 1,640 = 2,036.
formula_used: Round each term, then reverse the sign of any term crossing the equals sign
common_traps: The bracket is subtracted on the right of the equals sign, so it is added when it moves to the left.
key_note: Read exactly as printed ('+ 63') the left side is 243 and the answer is about 1,883, which is not among the options. Reading the term as 6 cubed = 216 reproduces the keyed 2,036 to the decimal, so the transcript has lost a superscript. Worth a source check before publication.

short_explanation: College C's 100 applications become 110 once the extra 10 are added, and 110 out of College A's 125 is 88%.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is 100 out of 125 - the original College C figure, with the extra 10 never added.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This subtracts the 10 instead of adding it: 90 out of 125 is 72%.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This adds 10 to the percentage (80% + 10) instead of adding 10 applications before dividing.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 110 out of 125 is 88%.

solution_steps: Total applications = 300 / 0.60 = 500.
College C = 20% of 500 = 100 and College A = 25% of 500 = 125.
College C revised upward by 10 = 110.
formula_used: Percentage = (part / whole) x 100
common_traps: The 10 is added to College C's count before the division, not to the percentage afterwards.

short_explanation: A full pie is 360 degrees, so College B's 16% share is 0.16 x 360 = 57.6 degrees.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is 24% of 360 - College D's slice.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is 20% of 360 - College C's slice.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is 15% of 360 - College E's slice.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This is 25% of 360 - College A's slice.

solution_steps: College B's share of applications is 16%.
16% of 360 degrees = 0.16 x 360 = 57.6 degrees.
formula_used: Central angle = percentage share x 360 degrees
common_traps: Every wrong option is another college's angle, so the share has to be read off the correct row before multiplying.

short_explanation: The gaps should rise 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, which makes the fourth term 135 + 75 = 210; the printed 220 is the term that breaks the run.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 85 is 60 + 25, the first step of the ladder - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 435 is 310 + 125, the last step of the ladder - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 310 is the corrected 210 + 100, and it also leads correctly to 435 - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 135 is 85 + 50, the second step - it belongs.

solution_steps: 135 + 75 = 210, but the series prints 220.
210 + 100 = 310 and 310 + 125 = 435, both of which match the printed series.
formula_used: Differences rising by a fixed 25 each step: 25, 50, 75, 100, 125

short_explanation: Colleges A and B together are 125 + 80 = 205 and College E is 75, so the difference is 130 - the same as 26% of the 500 total.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 120 is College D's total, not this difference.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This is College A's own figure of 125, with College B never added and College E never taken off.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: taking E's 75 from A and B's 205 gives 130.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the working gives 130.

solution_steps: Total applications = 300 / 0.60 = 500.
College A = 25% of 500 = 125 and College B = 16% of 500 = 80, so together 205.
College E = 15% of 500 = 75.

short_explanation: The gaps run 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, so the second term should be 110 + 7 = 117; the printed 118 is one too many.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 131 is the corrected 117 + 14, the second step of the multiples-of-7 ladder - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 152 is 131 + 21 - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 180 is 152 + 28 - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: 215 is 180 + 35 - it belongs.

solution_steps: The last three gaps are 21, 28 and 35 - successive multiples of 7.
Reading backwards, the earlier gaps are 14 and 7.
110 + 7 = 117, but the series prints 118, so 118 is the wrong term.
formula_used: Differences are 7, 14, 21, 28, 35 (successive multiples of 7)
common_traps: The wrong term is off by only 1, so the gaps have to be tested against a clean pattern rather than eyeballed.

short_explanation: The gaps are the squares of the even numbers - 16, 36, 64, 100 - so the last gap should be 12 squared = 144 and the final term 235 + 144 = 379, not 380.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 235 is 135 + 10 squared - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: 71 is 35 + 6 squared - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: 135 is 71 + 8 squared - it belongs.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 35 is 19 + 4 squared, the first step - it belongs.

solution_steps: The next gap is 12 squared = 144, so the last term should be 235 + 144 = 379.
formula_used: Differences are 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 squared
common_traps: The last term is wrong by only 1, so the gaps must be tested as squares rather than scanned for a big jump.

short_explanation: College E received 75 applications; 40 boys at Rs 100 is Rs 4,000 and the remaining 35 girls at Rs 75 is Rs 2,625, giving Rs 6,625 in all.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This charges the boys Rs 75 and the girls Rs 100 - the two fees the wrong way round.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This takes 40 girls as well as 40 boys; College E has only 75 applicants, so the girls number 35.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it corresponds to only 32 girls, while College E's 75 applicants leave 35.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: with 35 girls at Rs 75 the total is Rs 6,625.

solution_steps: Total applications = 300 / 0.60 = 500.
College E = 15% of 500 = 75.
Boys = 40, so girls = 75 - 40 = 35.
formula_used: Total fee = (boys x 100) + (girls x 75)
common_traps: The girls are 75 - 40 = 35, and College E's 75 has to be worked out from the chart before anything is charged.

short_explanation: The 25 litres poured over carry 20 litres of milk and 5 of water, so Jar B ends with x + 20 litres of milk against 50 of water; (x + 20)/50 = 7/5 gives x = 50.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 70 is the milk in Jar B after the pour. It is also what you get by writing x/50 = 7/5, leaving the 20 litres of poured milk out of the numerator; the question asks for the milk before the pour, which is 50.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it is 1.25 times 50, and no step in the problem scales by 1.25.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is the water Jar B already held, copied across as the milk; solving the ratio gives 50 litres.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the equation gives exactly 50 litres.

solution_steps: Jar A is milk : water = 4 : 1, so 25 litres holds 25 x 4/5 = 20 litres of milk and 5 litres of water.
Jar B then holds (x + 20) litres of milk and 45 + 5 = 50 litres of water.
5(x + 20) = 350, so x + 20 = 70 and x = 50 litres.
formula_used: Milk poured = 25 x 4/5; final ratio (x + 20) : (45 + 5) = 7 : 5
common_traps: The 5 litres of water that come across with the mixture join Jar B's 45 before the final ratio is applied.

short_explanation: Downstream the ferry does 32.4 / 1.8 = 18 km/h; with still water seven times more than the stream, that is nine stream-speeds, so the stream is 2 km/h, the ferry 16, and upstream it covers 14 x 6.4 = 89.6 km.
explanation_text: 'Seven times more than' is read in these papers as eight times as much - the stream's own speed plus seven more of it. That makes the downstream speed 8s + s = 9s. Had the phrase meant simply seven times as much, downstream would be 8s = 18, the upstream speed 13.5 km/h and the answer 86.4 km, which is also on the list. The key takes the first reading.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is 14 km/h taken over 5.4 hours; nothing in the question gives 5.4 hours, and over the stated 6.4 hours the ferry covers 89.6 km.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary - 14 km/h for 4.2 hours. The stated 6.4 hours gives 89.6 km.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary - 14 km/h for 4.4 hours, again not a time the question supplies.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This reads 'seven times more' as exactly seven times, making the stream 2.25 km/h, the ferry 15.75 and the upstream speed 13.5 km/h. The key takes the phrase as eight times the stream speed.

solution_steps: 108 minutes = 1.8 hours, so the downstream speed is 32.4 / 1.8 = 18 km/h.
Still water speed = 8 x stream speed, so downstream = 8s + s = 9s.
9s = 18, so the stream is 2 km/h and the ferry 16 km/h in still water.
Upstream speed = 16 - 2 = 14 km/h.
Distance in 6.4 hours = 14 x 6.4 = 89.6 km.
formula_used: Downstream = b + s, Upstream = b - s, Distance = speed x time
common_traps: 108 minutes is 1.8 hours, not 1.08 hours.
'Seven times more than' is taken as eight times as much in this paper.
key_note: Both readings of 'seven times more' appear in the options: the key uses boat = 8 x stream (89.6 km), while boat = 7 x stream gives 86.4 km.

short_explanation: Pipes A and B fill 4% an hour, so 24 hours leaves 4% to go; with C draining 100/35 of a percent per hour the net rate falls to 8/7 % an hour and the last 4% takes 3.5 hours, making 27 hours 30 minutes.
explanation_text: The stem gives a part-tank rate, not a full-tank time, and converting it first keeps the rest simple: 32% in 8 hours is 4% per hour, so A and B alone would need 25 hours. C's 35 hours to empty is 100/35 = 20/7 % per hour. Net rates are only needed for the final stretch, because C is shut for the first 24 hours.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: after 24 hours only 4% is left and the net rate of 8/7 % per hour clears it in 3.5 hours, not 6.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is C's emptying time copied straight from the stem.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is how long A and B alone would take, with C ignored altogether.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary, and shorter than the 24 hours A and B have already run.

solution_steps: A and B fill 32% in 8 hours, so 4% per hour - a full tank in 25 hours.
C empties the tank in 35 hours, so it drains 20/7 % per hour.
In the first 24 hours A and B fill 24 x 4 = 96%, leaving 4%.
With C open the net rate is 4 - 20/7 = 8/7 % per hour.
4 divided by 8/7 = 3.5 hours.
Total = 24 + 3.5 = 27.5 hours, or 27 hours 30 minutes.
formula_used: Net rate = filling rate - emptying rate; time = work left / net rate
common_traps: C is opened only after 24 hours, so it never touches the first 96% of the filling.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: x comes out as -2/3 or -2 and y as -1/4 or -1/2; the largest x, -0.67, still sits below the smallest y, -0.5, so x is less than y in every pairing.
explanation_text: In these root-comparison items the strict sign is used when no pairing of roots can be equal, and the 'or equal to' sign only when at least one pairing ties. Here the four values are -2, -0.67, -0.5 and -0.25, all distinct, so x < y is the exact statement and x is less than or equal to y understates it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This reverses the comparison. It comes from ranking the roots by their digits and ignoring the minus signs - 2 and 0.67 do look bigger than 0.5 and 0.25.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Wrong direction, and no pairing of roots is equal in any case.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The direction is right but the 'or equal to' is not earned: -2/3 is strictly below -1/2, so the strict form is the answer.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A relation does hold - all four x values fall below both y values.

solution_steps: The largest x is -0.67 and the smallest y is -0.5.
-0.67 is below -0.5, so every x falls below every y.
formula_used: Factorise both quadratics, then compare the largest x with the smallest y and the smallest x with the largest y
common_traps: All four roots are negative, so the root with the larger digits is the smaller number.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: x squared = 25 gives x = 5 or -5, and y squared + 11y + 30 = 0 gives y = -5 or -6; x is never below y, and x = -5 ties with y = -5, so x is greater than or equal to y.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This misses the tie: x = -5 and y = -5 are equal, so strict 'greater than' fails.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Reversed - 5 is above both y values.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Reversed - x is never the smaller of a pair.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A relation does hold: x is greater than or equal to y in every pairing.

solution_steps: x squared - 12 = 13 gives x squared = 25, so x = 5 or -5.
y squared + 11y + 30 = (y + 5)(y + 6) = 0, so y = -5 or -6.
5 beats both y values; -5 beats -6 and equals -5.
No pairing puts x below y and one pairing ties, so x is greater than or equal to y.
formula_used: Compare each root of the first equation against each root of the second
common_traps: x squared = 25 carries the negative root -5 as well; dropping it hides the tie with y = -5 and makes strict x > y look right.

short_explanation: Putting p at 3% and the rest at 5%, 0.03p + 0.05(7,800 - p) = 320 gives p = 3,500, so the two parts are Rs 3,500 and Rs 4,300.
explanation_text: Every option splits Rs 7,800 correctly, so the split alone settles nothing - the interest has to be tested. A quick sanity check first: the whole sum at 5% would earn Rs 390 and at 3% only Rs 234, and Rs 320 sits nearer the 5% end, so the larger part must be the one earning 5%.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: These do add to Rs 7,800, but they yield 72 + 270 = Rs 342, not Rs 320.

option_rationales.label: C
