option_rationales.rationale: This pair yields 132 + 170 = Rs 302 - short of Rs 320.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This pair yields 123 + 185 = Rs 308.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This pair yields 90 + 240 = Rs 330.

solution_steps: Let the part at 3% be p, so the other is 7,800 - p.
The other part is 7,800 - 3,500 = Rs 4,300.
formula_used: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time / 100, added over the two parts

short_explanation: Setting 0.9(X + 480) = 1.2X + 90 gives X = 1,140, so article B costs Rs 1,620 and sells for Rs 1,458; undoing the 10% discount makes its marked price 1,458 / 0.9 = Rs 1,620.
explanation_text: Three prices sit in a chain here and they have to be taken in order: cost, then selling price, then marked price. The 10% loss connects cost to selling price, and the 10% discount connects marked price to selling price. The loss is already inside the Rs 1,458, so only the discount is undone at the last step.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This divides by 0.9 twice, once for the 10% loss and again for the 10% discount, starting from B's cost of Rs 1,620. The loss is already built into the Rs 1,458 selling price, so only one division is due.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the chain from X = 1,140 ends at Rs 1,620.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it is roughly double the marked price the working gives.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: undoing the 10% discount on Rs 1,458 gives exactly Rs 1,620.

solution_steps: Selling price of A = 1.2X; selling price of B = 0.9(X + 480).
Cost of B = 1,140 + 480 = Rs 1,620, and its selling price = 0.9 x 1,620 = Rs 1,458.
Marked price x 0.9 = 1,458, so the marked price is Rs 1,620.
formula_used: SP = CP x (1 + profit or - loss); SP = MP x (1 - discount)
common_traps: Article B's marked price happens to equal its cost price of Rs 1,620 - a coincidence of these numbers, not a shortcut to reuse.

topic_name: Quadratic equations — root comparison (x vs y)
short_explanation: x is 7 or 1/3 and y is 2 or 4/5; 7 sits above both y values while 1/3 sits below both, so the comparison flips and no single relation holds.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Fails at x = 1/3, which is below both y values.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Fails at x = 7, which is above both y values.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Fails for the same reason as 'x greater than y', and there is no tie to rescue it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Fails because x = 7 exceeds both y values.

solution_steps: 7 is above both 2 and 0.8, but 1/3 is below both.
Because the direction changes between pairings, no relation can be fixed.
formula_used: A relation exists only when every x compares the same way against every y

short_explanation: Both partners stay in for the same six years, so the profit splits 2 : 3; A's Rs 7,056 is two-fifths of the 70% left after the donation, which puts the total profit at Rs 25,200.
explanation_text: Time only enters a partnership share when the partners are in for different periods. Here both run for six years, so the years cancel and the split is simply 2 : 3. The donation comes off the top, so the ratio is applied to 70% of the profit, not to the whole of it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary. Skipping the donation would give Rs 17,640 and swapping the 2 : 3 shares would give Rs 16,800 - neither is 24,200, and the correct total is Rs 25,200.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: A's Rs 7,056 is 28% of the total, which fixes it at Rs 25,200.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 28% of 27,200 is Rs 7,616, not Rs 7,056.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 28% of 26,200 is Rs 7,336.

solution_steps: Equal periods, so the profit ratio is the investment ratio 2 : 3.
30% is donated, leaving 70% to be shared.
A's share = (2/5) x 0.7 x Total = 0.28 x Total.
0.28 x Total = 7,056, so the Total is Rs 25,200.
Check: 70% of 25,200 is 17,640, and two-fifths of that is Rs 7,056.
formula_used: Share = ratio part x distributable profit, where distributable = 70% of the total
common_traps: Both partners invest for the same six years, so the period drops out of the ratio entirely.

topic_name: Number series — multiplicative and mixed patterns
short_explanation: Each term is the previous one multiplied by 2, then 3, then 4, then 5, with 1 added each time, so the next is 446 x 6 + 1 = 2,677.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This reuses the multiplier 5 (446 x 5 + 1) instead of moving on to 6.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This jumps to 7 (446 x 7 + 1); the multipliers run 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: no multiplier in the run produces it, and the sixth term is 2,677.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

formula_used: Next term = previous term x multiplier + 1, with the multiplier rising by one each step

topic_name: Number series — multiplicative and mixed patterns
short_explanation: The jumps are the squares of 30, 25, 20 and 15 with alternating signs - +900, -625, +400, -225 - so the next jump is +10 squared and the term is 546 + 100 = 646.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Right size of jump, wrong sign - the signs alternate, and a minus is followed by a plus, giving 646.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This adds 150; the bases fall 30, 25, 20, 15, 10, so the last jump is 100.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This subtracts 150 - wrong sign and wrong size.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This adds 50 rather than 10 squared = 100.

solution_steps: The next jump is +10 squared = +100, so the term is 546 + 100 = 646.
formula_used: Alternating jumps of +30, -25, +20, -15, +10, each squared
common_traps: The bases fall 30, 25, 20, 15, 10, so the jumps shrink while the signs flip.

short_explanation: Society D has 200 in the public sector and, at 5 : 3, 200 x 3/5 = 120 in the private sector, a difference of 80.
explanation_text: The two tables work together: the first gives the public-sector count outright, the second gives public against private. So the private figure is always the public figure scaled by the second number of the ratio over the first - 200 x 3/5 for D - and the society's total is the two added. Building that one line for every society first makes the rest of the set quick.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the 5 : 3 split of Society D leaves a gap of 80.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 200 against 120 is a difference of 80.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it would need 110 in the private sector, while 5 : 3 gives 120.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This uses Society C's 4 : 3 row against D's 200, giving 150 and a gap of 50. D's ratio is 5 : 3.

solution_steps: Society D: public = 200, with public : private = 5 : 3.
Private = 200 x 3/5 = 120.
formula_used: Private = public x (private part / public part)

short_explanation: Society E holds 100 public and 150 private, 250 in all, while Society B's private sector is 80 x 2 = 160, and 250 : 160 reduces to 25 : 16.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The second term is right, so the first must be 25 - Society E's total is 250, not 230.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Society E's 250 is right, but Society B's private sector is 160, not 170.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The right pair of numbers the wrong way round; the question names Society E's total first.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: Society E's 250 against Society B's private 160 gives 25 : 16.

solution_steps: Society E: public 100 at 2 : 3, so private = 100 x 3/2 = 150 and the total is 250.
Society B: public 80 at 1 : 2, so private = 80 x 2 = 160.
250 : 160, divided through by 10, is 25 : 16.
formula_used: Total = public + private; reduce the ratio by the highest common factor
common_traps: The first term is Society E's whole population, not just its public sector.

topic_name: Number series — arithmetic and difference patterns
short_explanation: The gaps grow by consecutive odd numbers, running 10, 13, 18, 25, 34, so the first gap is 10 and the missing term is 7 + 10 = 17.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This makes the first two gaps 13 then 10, so the gaps would shrink before growing; they only grow.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This gives gaps of 8 then 15 - a rise of 7 where a rise of 3 is due.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This gives gaps of 11 then 12 - a rise of 1 where 3 is due.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This gives gaps of 9 then 14 - a rise of 5 where 3 is due.

solution_steps: The known gaps are 48 - 30 = 18, 73 - 48 = 25 and 107 - 73 = 34.
These rise by 7 and then 9, so the earlier rises must be 3 and 5.
Working back, the gap before 18 is 13 and the one before that is 10.
7 + 10 = 17, and 17 + 13 = 30 - the series holds.
formula_used: Second differences are 3, 5, 7, 9 - consecutive odd numbers

short_explanation: The whole job is 192 man-days, equal to 240 woman-days; twelve men do half of it in 8 days and the six who stay add 24 man-days more, leaving 72 man-days, which is 90 woman-days and needs 22.5 women over 4 days - not a whole number, and no total on the list follows from it.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Forty-five women working 4 days would do three-quarters of the job, against the three-eighths that is actually left; the stem's own figures call for 22.5 women, so this total is not reachable.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Thirty-nine women over 4 days come to 0.65 of the job against the three-eighths remaining; nothing in the stem produces this count.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Nothing in the stem produces 57. With the women needed working out at 22.5, no whole-number total on this list can be reached.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Forty-eight women over 4 days would finish four-fifths of the job; the stated rates call for 22.5 women.

solution_steps: Whole work = 12 x 16 = 192 man-days = 10 x 24 = 240 woman-days, so 4 men match 5 women.
12 men for 8 days = 96 man-days, exactly half the work.
The 6 who remain add 6 x 4 = 24 man-days over the next 4 days, leaving 72 man-days.
72 man-days = 72 x 240/192 = 90 woman-days, spread over 4 days, so X = 22.5 women.
A count of women cannot be 22.5, and neither 12 + 22.5 nor 6 + 22.5 appears among the options.
formula_used: Total work in man-days = men x days; here 192 man-days = 240 woman-days
key_note: Solved as written the answer is X = 22.5 women, so the count is not a whole number and no option matches either 12 + 22.5 or 6 + 22.5. The keyed 51 would be the 6 remaining men plus 45 women, which needs the women's rate to be half of what is printed - 10 women in 48 days rather than 24. The stem needs a source check before publication; as printed, no option is reachable.

short_explanation: Societies A, B and D total 250, 240 and 320, which add to 810.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the three public figures alone add to 430 and the three private ones to 380, giving 810.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the three society totals of 250, 240 and 320 come to 810.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it overshoots the three totals by 30.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 250 + 240 + 320 is 810.

solution_steps: Society A: public 150 at 3 : 2, so private 100 and total 250.
Society B: public 80 at 1 : 2, so private 160 and total 240.
Society D: public 200 at 5 : 3, so private 120 and total 320.
formula_used: Total per society = public + public x (private part / public part)

short_explanation: Society E totals 100 public plus 150 private, that is 250, and half as much again is 375.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 1.5 times 250 is 375.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it is not 1.5 times any figure in Society E's row.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is 30% more than 250; the stem says 50% more, which gives 375.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the working gives 375.

solution_steps: Society E: public 100 at 2 : 3, so private = 150 and the total is 250.
formula_used: 50% more than N = 1.5N
common_traps: The base is Society E's whole population of 250, not its public 100 or its private 150.

short_explanation: Abhi's age X years ago matching Bhim's age 3X years ago makes Bhim older by 2X; the second condition forces X = 6, so the gap is 12 years.
explanation_text: When two people's ages are matched at different look-back points, the age gap is the difference between those two points. Abhi at X years ago equals Bhim at 3X years ago, so Bhim reaches that age 2X years later than Abhi does - Bhim is 2X years older. The second sentence is then only needed to pin down X.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the gap is 2X with X = 6, that is 12 years.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: neither condition produces 15.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is 3X, read off the '3X years ago' phrase instead of derived; the gap is 2X = 12.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: X itself is 6 and the gap is twice that.

solution_steps: Abhi - X = Bhim - 3X, so Abhi = Bhim - 2X: Bhim is older by 2X.
Abhi + 3X = Bhim + 6.
Substituting Abhi = Bhim - 2X gives Bhim + X = Bhim + 6, so X = 6.
The difference in ages is 2X = 12 years.
formula_used: Write both conditions as equations in the two present ages and eliminate one age
common_traps: The age gap is the difference between the two look-back periods, 3X - X = 2X, not 3X.

short_explanation: The 2 : 1 split puts Rs 12,000 in Scheme A for 3 years and Rs 6,000 in Scheme B for 5 years, so 360Y = 0.48 x 300(Y + 15), which gives Y = 10.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: At Y = 12 the two interests are Rs 4,320 and Rs 8,100, and 4,320 is about 53% of 8,100, not 48%.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: At Y = 15 they are Rs 5,400 and Rs 9,000 - a ratio of 60%.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: At Y = 8 they are Rs 2,880 and Rs 6,900 - about 42%.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: At Y = 7.5 they are Rs 2,700 and Rs 6,750 - exactly 40%.

solution_steps: The sums are 2 : 1 of Rs 18,000, so Rs 12,000 in A and Rs 6,000 in B.
Interest from A = 12,000 x Y x 3 / 100 = 360Y.
Check: A earns Rs 3,600 and B earns Rs 7,500, and 3,600 is 48% of 7,500.
formula_used: Simple interest = P x R x T / 100
common_traps: The 2 : 1 follows the order the schemes are named, so the larger Rs 12,000 goes to Scheme A.

short_explanation: Society A's public figure of 150 is a count and stands; at the true 5 : 4 the private sector is 150 x 4/5 = 120, so the society holds 270 people.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 150 public plus 120 private is 270.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This is the figure under the wrong 3 : 2 ratio, 150 + 100 - the very number the question asks you to correct.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the 5 : 4 split puts 120 in the private sector, not 80.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This applies a 5 : 3 split (150 + 90), which is Society D's ratio row, not A's corrected one.

solution_steps: The public count of 150 is given directly and the ratio error does not touch it.
With the correct 5 : 4, private = 150 x 4/5 = 120.
formula_used: Private = public x (private part / public part)
common_traps: Only the private side moves; the public 150 is a headcount, not a share of the ratio.

short_explanation: Four years hence the three ages total 88, so today they total 88 - 12 = 76; with A at 35 and B at 25, C is 16 now and 21 five years from now.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: C is 16 today, so five years on he is 21.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it would need C to be 17 today, while the present total of 76 leaves him 16.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary, and below C's present age of 16, when the question asks for five years later.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This takes the four years off the total only once instead of once for each of the three people, making C 24 today - and then never adds the five years either.

solution_steps: Four years hence each of the three is 4 years older, so the group total rises by 3 x 4 = 12.
Present total = 88 - 12 = 76.
C's present age = 76 - 35 - 25 = 16.
C five years hence = 16 + 5 = 21.
formula_used: Total age of n people t years hence = present total + n x t
common_traps: Rolling a group total back four years removes 4 x 3 = 12 years, not 4.

short_explanation: The TV costs Ravi Rs 9,000 less 20%, that is Rs 7,200, plus 5% transport, making Rs 7,560; a 25% profit on that is Rs 1,890.
explanation_text: Any charge the buyer pays to get the goods home joins the cost price. So the base for Ravi's 25% is not the marked price and not the discounted price, but the discounted price carrying the 5% transport - Rs 7,560. Getting the base right is the whole question; the percentages themselves are easy.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is 25% of Rs 7,200, with the 5% transport charge left out of the cost.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This takes 25% of the marked price of Rs 9,000, ignoring both the discount and the transport.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is 20% of Rs 7,200 - the discount rate used in place of the profit rate.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This is 20% of the correct cost of Rs 7,560 - again the discount rate standing in for the 25% profit rate.

solution_steps: Discounted price = 9,000 x 0.8 = Rs 7,200.
Transport adds 5%: 7,200 x 1.05 = Rs 7,560, which is Ravi's cost price.
formula_used: Cost to the buyer = MP x (1 - discount) x (1 + extra charges); Profit = cost x profit rate
common_traps: Transport paid by the buyer is part of his cost price, so the 25% is taken on Rs 7,560, not Rs 7,200.

short_explanation: Mixture A holds 378 x 4/9 = 168 ml of milk, so mixture B holds 168 x 1.375 = 231 ml; that is 35% of B, making B 231 / 0.35 = 660 ml.
explanation_text: Two percentage moves sit back to back and they work in opposite directions. '37.5% more than' scales up, so multiply by 1.375. 'Is 35% of the total' works backwards from the part to the whole, so divide by 0.35. Mixing up which is multiplied and which is divided is what wrecks this item.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 35% of 530 is 185.5 ml, not the 231 ml of milk B must hold.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 35% of 502 is about 176 ml, against the 231 ml required.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 35% of 572 is about 200 ml, still short of 231 ml.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This takes 37.5% of A's milk, 63 ml, as B's milk instead of 37.5% more than it, which is 231 ml.

solution_steps: Milk in mixture A = 378 x 4/9 = 168 ml.
37.5% more milk in B = 168 x 1.375 = 231 ml.
That 231 ml is 35% of mixture B.
Mixture B = 231 / 0.35 = 660 ml.
formula_used: Part = whole x ratio share; whole = part / its percentage
common_traps: The 4 : 5 ratio has nine parts, so milk is 4/9 of 378, not 4/5.
'37.5% more than' means 1.375 times, not 0.375 times.

topic_name: Volume and surface area of solids
short_explanation: The cone's volume over the cylinder's is one-third of the squared radius ratio times the height ratio, so (1/3)(9/4)(h/35) = 3/10 and the cone stands 14 cm high.
explanation_text: Comparing two solids is quicker as a single ratio than as two separate volumes. Pi cancels, the radius enters squared, and the cone keeps its factor of one-third: cone over cylinder = (1/3)(r/R) squared x (h/H). With r/R = 3/2 that squared term is 9/4, and one-third of 9/4 is 3/4, so the height ratio has to supply the remaining 4/10.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This forgets to square the radius ratio - using 3/2 in place of 9/4 gives 21 cm.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is simply half the cylinder's height; the volume ratio and the squared radii both have to enter.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the volume equation gives exactly 14 cm.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: nothing in the two ratios produces 16, and the working gives 14 cm.

solution_steps: Cone volume / cylinder volume = (1/3) x (r/R) squared x (h/H).
(r/R) squared = (3/2) squared = 9/4.
formula_used: Cone = (1/3) x pi x r squared x h; Cylinder = pi x R squared x H
common_traps: The radius enters squared and the cone carries the one-third; dropping either changes the answer.

short_explanation: The two speeds come out as 1.8k downstream and 1.4k upstream, a ratio of 9 : 7, and for any boat the still-water speed to the stream speed is (9 + 7) : (9 - 7), that is 8 : 1.
explanation_text: Downstream speed is boat plus stream and upstream is boat minus stream, so adding the two speeds gives twice the boat and subtracting them gives twice the stream. That means any pair of downstream and upstream speeds in the ratio m : n puts the boat and the stream in the ratio (m + n) : (m - n) - no need to find the actual distances at all.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: This is the upstream number from the 9 : 7 speed ratio read off as the answer; halving the sum and the difference gives 8 : 1.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is D1's share of the 6 : 7 distance ratio, not a speed comparison at all.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: This is the downstream number from the 9 : 7 speed ratio, again taken before the sum and difference step.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: it is the midpoint of 7 and 8, while the working gives exactly 8.

solution_steps: Take D1 = 6k and D2 = 7k.
3 hours 20 minutes is 10/3 hours, so the downstream speed is 6k divided by 10/3 = 1.8k.
The upstream speed is 7k / 5 = 1.4k.
Downstream : upstream = 1.8 : 1.4 = 9 : 7.
Boat = (9 + 7)/2 = 8 units and stream = (9 - 7)/2 = 1 unit, so the boat is 8 times the stream.
formula_used: Boat = (downstream + upstream) / 2; stream = (downstream - upstream) / 2
common_traps: 3 hours 20 minutes is 10/3 hours, not 3.2 hours.

topic_name: Area and perimeter — rectangle, square, triangle
short_explanation: With the breadth a quarter of the length, the area is length squared over 4, so length squared = 1,024 and the hall is 32 m by 8 m - a difference of 24 m.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the sides are 32 m and 8 m, a gap of 24 m.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: This is the ratio figure itself - the breadth is a quarter of the length, not 4 m short of it.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary, and close to the square root of 256, which would be the side only if the floor were square.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: the working gives 32 m and 8 m.

solution_steps: Breadth = length / 4, so area = length x length/4 = length squared / 4 = 256.
Length squared = 1,024, so the length is 32 m.
Breadth = 32 / 4 = 8 m.
formula_used: Area = length x breadth
common_traps: Dividing 256 by 4 before taking the root gives a length of 16; the 4 has to be cleared from length squared / 4 = 256, leaving length squared = 1,024.

short_explanation: A and B together do 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 of the work a day, so 12 days between them, and C at 1.25 times that takes 15 days.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: 1.25 times the pair's 12 days is 15.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: nothing in the question gives the 21.6 days that 27 would imply for the pair.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: this doubles the pair's 12 days instead of taking 1.25 times them.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This is the time A and B take together, with the 1.25 factor never applied.

solution_steps: A's rate is 1/20 of the work a day and B's is 1/30.
Together: 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60 = 1/12, so the pair finish in 12 days.
C takes 1.25 x 12 = 15 days.
formula_used: Combined time = 1 / (1/a + 1/b)
common_traps: Adding the two times (20 + 30) or averaging them (25) is not how work combines - add the rates, not the days.

short_explanation: A runs Rs 6,000 for 12 months, B its money for 6 months and C Rs 12,000 for 4 months; B's Rs 8,000 is two-sevenths of the Rs 28,000 profit, and 6x / (120,000 + 6x) = 2/7 gives x = Rs 8,000.
explanation_text: Partnership shares follow money multiplied by the months it stays in, so each partner's weight is a rupee-month figure. The chain of joining dates is the only tricky part here: B joins at the six-month mark and so runs for 6 months, and C joins two months after B, which is eight months into the year, leaving C just 4 months.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: This is A's capital copied across; B's own capital works out at Rs 8,000.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: Rs 9,000 for 6 months would earn B about Rs 8,690, not Rs 8,000.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: Rs 10,000 for 6 months would earn B about Rs 9,333.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary: Rs 7,500 for 6 months would earn B about Rs 7,636.

solution_steps: A: 6,000 x 12 = 72,000 rupee-months.
B joins after 6 months, so B contributes x x 6 = 6x rupee-months.
C joins 2 months after B, that is 8 months in, so C contributes 12,000 x 4 = 48,000.
B's share is 8,000 out of 28,000, which is 2/7 of the profit.
Check: B's 48,000 rupee-months out of 168,000 is exactly 2/7.
formula_used: Profit share is proportional to investment x time
common_traps: C joins two months after B, which is eight months into the year, so C's money works for four months and not six.

short_explanation: The Delphi technique collects expert opinions individually, circulates an anonymous summary of the round, and asks the same experts to answer again, repeating until the estimates converge.
explanation_text: The design exists to strip out group pressure. Because the experts never meet and no answer carries a name, no senior or loud voice can anchor the room, and nobody must defend a first answer to save face. What changes a participant's mind is the argument in the summary, not who made it. The cost is time, which is why Delphi suits forecasting and policy questions rather than decisions needed this week.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Brainstorming is a face-to-face session for generating many ideas with criticism suspended; there are no anonymous rounds.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: In the nominal group technique members write ideas alone but then meet to discuss and rank them in one sitting.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Bounded rationality is a description of how limited decision makers are, not a technique.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Multi-voting narrows a long list by repeated rounds of voting; it does not gather written expert responses.

common_traps: The nominal group technique is the close neighbour. Delphi keeps the experts apart and anonymous across several rounds; the nominal group brings them together after the silent writing stage.

topic_name: Quantitative methods and analytics in decision making
short_explanation: PERT, the Programme Evaluation and Review Technique, schedules a project by estimating activity times and computing the critical path, so it rests on numbers rather than on judgement.
explanation_text: Quantitative techniques share one test: the decision follows from data worked through a model, and a second analyst with the same data should reach the same answer. PERT, linear programming, queueing theory, decision trees and simulation all pass it. Rules of thumb, experience and creativity may be sensible and are often faster, but they are qualitative because the reasoning is not reproducible from the numbers.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: A rule of thumb is a heuristic drawn from experience, with no computation behind it.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Psychological analysis deals with attitudes and behaviour, which are not quantified into a decision model.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Creative methods such as brainstorming generate ideas; they do not measure alternatives.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Following a standard procedure applies an existing rule and calculates nothing.

topic_name: Types of decisions and decision levels
short_explanation: Arranging transport and timings so staff reach a conference is a routine, repetitive task handled by existing rules and past practice, which makes it a programmed decision.
explanation_text: The dividing line is whether the organisation already has a procedure for the situation. Programmed decisions are recurring and structured, so they are settled by rules, policies or standard operating procedures and are usually taken lower down the hierarchy. Non-programmed decisions are novel and ill-structured, with no ready template, and they climb to senior management because judgement has to fill the gap. Scheduling is the textbook example of the first kind.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Non-programmed decisions deal with new and unstructured problems, such as entering a new market.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Strategic decisions set long-term direction and are taken by top management.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The employee is acting in an official role for the organisation, not deciding a private matter.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Major is not a category in this classification, and routine scheduling is minor in any case.

short_explanation: Selective perception is seeing a situation only through one's own chosen frame of interests and experience, so conflicting evidence and other options are filtered out before they are considered.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Availability bias is judging by whatever examples come to mind most easily, usually recent or vivid ones.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Immediate gratification is preferring a quick reward over a larger later one.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Status quo bias is favouring whatever the current arrangement is.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Hindsight bias is believing after the event that the outcome was obvious all along.

common_traps: Selective perception filters what is taken in; confirmation bias is the related habit of seeking evidence that supports a view already held.

short_explanation: Anchoring is letting the first piece of information received, such as an opening price or an initial estimate, dominate the final judgement, with later adjustments made only slightly away from it.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Confirmation bias is hunting for evidence that supports a conclusion already reached, which involves many pieces of information, not one.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Not a recognised bias in this list.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Escalation of commitment is pouring more resources into a failing course of action to justify what has already been spent.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Hindsight bias is the after-the-fact sense that the outcome was predictable.

common_traps: Anchoring is about the weight of the first input; framing is about the way the same information is worded.

topic_name: Root cause analysis and problem-solving tools
short_explanation: A flowchart maps a process as a diagram of boxes and diamonds joined by arrows, showing in order the activities performed and the decisions taken at each branch.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Brainstorming produces ideas in a group; it draws no process map.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Benchmarking compares a firm's performance with the best in the field.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Five Whys digs down to a root cause by repeatedly asking why; it does not show sequence over time.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Force Field Analysis weighs the forces driving and resisting a change.

topic_name: Bounded rationality and limits on information processing
short_explanation: Bounded rationality, Herbert Simon's idea, is that real managers decide within limits of time, information and mental capacity, so they satisfice, taking the first option that is good enough rather than the provably best one.
explanation_text: The rational model assumes a clear problem, all alternatives known, all consequences known and a stable ranking of preferences. None of that holds in an office. Simon's answer was not that managers are irrational but that they are rational within boundaries: they simplify the problem to a workable model and stop searching once an option clears their acceptance standard. That is why two competent managers with the same file can defensibly choose differently.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Not the standard term; behaviour is what the concept explains, but the name is bounded rationality.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Objective rationality is the opposite idea, the fully informed maximising decision the model assumes.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Limited rationality reads like a plain-English paraphrase, but the term fixed in the literature is bounded rationality.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Subjective rationality refers to a choice that is rational given the person's own beliefs; it does not name these constraints.

short_explanation: Frame blindness is setting out to solve the wrong problem because a mental frame was adopted with little thought, so the best option and the real objectives are never brought into view.
explanation_text: This is the first of the decision traps, and the costliest, because every later step inherits it. Careful analysis of the wrong question still produces the wrong answer. The guard against it is to state the problem more than one way before generating options, and to ask who else would define it differently, so the frame is chosen deliberately rather than by default.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Failing to interpret feedback is a later error, in learning from the outcome rather than in setting the problem.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Not keeping track means failing to record and review decisions over time.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Overconfidence concerns the accuracy of estimates, not the framing of the problem.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Short-sighted shortcuts are heuristics such as anchoring that are relied on too readily.

topic_name: Quantitative methods and analytics in decision making
short_explanation: Predictive analytics uses past data and statistical or machine-learning models to estimate what is likely to happen next, such as which loans will default.
explanation_text: The four levels build on one another. Descriptive analytics reports what happened, diagnostic analytics asks why it happened, predictive analytics forecasts what might happen, and prescriptive analytics recommends what to do about it. Each stage needs the one before it, and the value and the difficulty both rise as you move along the chain.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Inferential analysis generalises from a sample to a population; it is a statistical method rather than one of the four analytics levels.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Descriptive analytics summarises what has already happened.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Diagnostic analytics explains why something happened.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Prescriptive analytics recommends the action to take, going a step beyond forecasting.

topic_name: Rational decision-making model and its assumptions
short_explanation: A decision is rational when it follows from reasoning: the objective is stated, evidence is weighed, and the option chosen is the one the analysis supports.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Gut feeling is intuition. It can be valuable where a manager has deep experience, but it is not what makes a decision rational.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Bias is exactly what rational decision making tries to remove.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Emotion may inform what is valued, yet a choice driven by feeling is not a reasoned one.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: This pairs reasoning with gut feeling; adding intuition does not make the decision rational, and the stem asks for the single basis.

short_explanation: Framing bias is being swayed by how information is presented: the same facts described as a 90 per cent survival rate or a 10 per cent death rate pull decisions in opposite directions.
explanation_text: Framing works because people treat gains and losses differently, the finding behind prospect theory: a loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases, so a loss frame pushes towards risk-taking and a gain frame towards caution. The practical guard is to restate the choice both ways, as what is gained and what is given up, and see whether the preference survives.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Commitment bias is persisting with an earlier choice to stay consistent with it.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Confirmation bias is seeking evidence that supports a view already held.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Hindsight bias is the after-the-event belief that the outcome was obvious.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Anchoring bias is over-weighting the first number or fact received, not the manner of presentation.

common_traps: Anchoring and framing are the pair most often swapped. Anchoring is about which figure came first; framing is about the wording of the same figure.

short_explanation: Judgemental problems are the ill-structured ones where no formula settles the matter, so they are handled by applying sound judgement and choosing the course that keeps the chance of bad outcomes low.
explanation_text: Problems sort by how much structure they carry. Routine, well-defined problems go to standard operating procedures; quantifiable ones go to models such as inventory reorder formulas, queueing theory or linear programming. What is left, where the objectives conflict and the data are incomplete, is the judgemental class. There the honest aim is not the optimum but a defensible choice that limits the damage if things go wrong.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Habitual responses and standard procedures answer routine, programmed problems, not judgemental ones.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Inventory models, queueing theory and statistical analysis suit structured problems that can be quantified.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Frequently changing strategy is a reaction to technological change, not a way of solving judgemental problems.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Linear programming and network analysis are computational techniques for well-defined problems.

key_note: The item is loosely worded; the intended contrast is judgemental (unstructured) problems against computational and routine ones.

short_explanation: Brainstorming is a face-to-face session in which a selected group throws out ideas on a problem with criticism held back, so that quantity and openness come first and evaluation comes later.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Delphi keeps the experts apart and anonymous across written rounds; there is no face-to-face discussion.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Multi-voting is a way of shortening a list by successive votes, used after ideas exist.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The didactic method is a teaching approach, used for decisions only where a group must be led through both sides of an issue.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: A decision tree is a diagram of options, chances and payoffs, not a group discussion.

topic_name: Root cause analysis and problem-solving tools
short_explanation: In root cause analysis the human cause is the one where a person did something wrong or failed to do something required, and that lapse then produced the physical failure.
explanation_text: RCA sorts causes into three layers. The physical cause is the item that failed, a seized bearing or a burst pipe. The human cause is the act or omission behind it, such as a lubrication check that was skipped. The organisational cause is the system that allowed it, such as a maintenance schedule nobody owned or a training gap. Stopping at the physical layer replaces the part and lets the failure return; the fix belongs at the organisational layer.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The physical cause is the tangible item that failed, such as a worn component.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The organisational cause is the faulty system, policy or process that let the human error happen.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Not a category in root cause analysis.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Not a category in root cause analysis.

topic_name: Bounded rationality and limits on information processing
short_explanation: Bounded rationality is Simon's term for decision making constrained by limited capacity to absorb and process information, which is why managers simplify the problem and settle for a satisfactory option.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Not a standard term; intuition is contrasted with rational analysis rather than named this way.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Irrationality means deciding against reason altogether. Bounded rationality still reasons, within limits.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Limited rationality is a plain-English paraphrase; the established term is bounded rationality.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Not a term in the literature.

common_traps: 'Limited rationality' appears in both this item and Q.94 as the near-miss. The examiners want Simon's exact phrase, bounded rationality.

topic_name: Communication, conflict and delay in group decisions
short_explanation: Explaining the reasons and the evidence while a decision is being made reduces the resistance and the negative feeling that surround a change people do not understand.
explanation_text: People rarely resist the decision itself; they resist being surprised by it. Communication during the process, rather than an announcement after it, lets those affected raise objections early, see that their concerns were weighed, and understand what changes for them. The other four items in this list, interest, support, harmony and cooperation, are precisely what good communication is meant to increase, so only the negatives belong in the blank.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Interest and receptivity are outcomes communication should raise, not reduce.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Support for change is something to be built, not minimised.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Harmony and agreement are desirable outcomes.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Support and cooperation are also outcomes to be increased.

common_traps: The stem asks what is minimised. Four options are benefits, which makes them wrong here however attractive they read.
key_note: Loosely drafted, but only one option names something a manager would want less of.

short_explanation: The overconfidence trap is rating one's own judgement and forecasts as more accurate than they are, helped along by a memory that keeps the successes and drops the mistakes.
explanation_text: This is one of the hidden traps described by Hammond, Keeney and Raiffa. Its practical damage is in estimating: ranges are set too narrow, contingencies too thin, and deadlines too tight, so a project that was 'certain' to finish in six months runs to nine. The usual correction is to force the extremes first, state the highest and lowest plausible values before settling on a figure, and to look at how similar past estimates actually turned out.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The estimating and forecasting trap concerns faulty reference points in predicting uncertain quantities, not inflated belief in one's own ability.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The anchoring trap is giving too much weight to the first information received.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Gathering more information than can be used is the overload problem, a different failing.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The confirming-evidence trap is seeking support for an option already favoured.

short_explanation: Prospect theory was set out by Daniel Kahneman with Amos Tversky in 1979; it showed that people judge outcomes as gains and losses from a reference point and feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain. Kahneman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics in 2002.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Henry Mintzberg wrote on managerial roles and on how strategy actually forms in organisations.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Herbert Simon gave bounded rationality and satisficing, an allied idea but a different theory.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: W. Edwards Deming is associated with quality management and the PDCA cycle.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Albert Bandura is a psychologist known for social learning theory and self-efficacy.

common_traps: Simon is the other economics-adjacent psychologist in this area. Simon gave bounded rationality; Kahneman and Tversky gave prospect theory.

short_explanation: The analytic style fits this case: it tolerates ambiguity, gathers more information and examines several alternatives before deciding, which is what a problem with more than one workable answer and a hidden cause-effect link needs.
explanation_text: In the decision-style model, styles vary on two axes, tolerance for ambiguity and whether the person thinks in tasks or in people. The directive style has low tolerance for ambiguity and decides fast on little information. The analytic style shares the task focus but has high tolerance for ambiguity, so it investigates before choosing. The stem is the Cynefin complicated domain, where expertise and analysis can uncover the relationship but it is not visible at a glance; that is analysis, not a snap call and not consensus-building.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: The avoidant style postpones and sidesteps decisions, which leaves the cause undiscovered.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: The conceptual style is broad and creative, suited to genuinely novel problems where no right answer is discoverable at all.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: The behavioural style works through people and consensus; it addresses agreement rather than analysis.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: The directive style decides quickly with minimal information, which suits simple problems with one obvious answer.

key_note: The stem paraphrases the Cynefin framework's complicated domain ('good practice', several right answers, analysis or expertise required), mapped here onto the analytic decision style.

short_explanation: Manish already has his three hotels and his criteria; weighing each hotel against cost, facilities and proximity is the evaluation of alternatives.
explanation_text: The steps run in a fixed order: define the problem, set the criteria and their weights, generate alternatives, evaluate each alternative against the criteria, choose, implement, and review the outcome. explanation_text: PM-SYM, launched in 2019, is a voluntary contributory pension for unorganised workers - street vendors, head loaders, rickshaw pullers, domestic workers - earning up to Rs 15,000 a month. A worker joining between 18 and 40 pays a monthly contribution fixed by entry age, from Rs 55 to Rs 200, the Centre pays an equal amount, and an assured pension of Rs 3,000 a month begins at 60. LIC holds the corpus and pays the pension; the bank or Common Service Centre handles enrolment and the auto-debit.

The premium was raised from Rs 12 to Rs 20 a year with effect from 1 June 2022. Its sister scheme PMJJBY is life cover, and life cover carries the narrower entry band of 18 to 50 with cover ceasing at 55.

short_explanation: The Aspirational Districts Programme works on five themes - health and nutrition, education, agriculture and water resources, financial inclusion and skill development, and basic infrastructure - so shelter and housing is the listed item that is not one of them.
explanation_text: Launched in January 2018 and steered by NITI Aayog, the programme picked 112 districts lagging on composite development indicators and ranks them on a delta basis, that is on improvement rather than on absolute level, so a very poor district that moves fast can top the table. The themes carry weights: health and nutrition and education 30 per cent each, agriculture and water resources 20 per cent, and financial inclusion with skill development and basic infrastructure 10 per cent each. Basic infrastructure means all-weather roads, electricity, drinking water, household toilets and panchayat internet.

explanation_text: SECC is separate from the decennial Census. The Census is taken under the Census Act, 1948 and its individual records are confidential and cannot be used to grant or refuse a benefit. SECC was run by the Ministry of Rural Development and the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs precisely so that household-level deprivation data could be used to select beneficiaries, which is how PMAY-G and Ayushman Bharat identify households. The caste enumeration it collected was never published in full.

The 86th Amendment of 2002 split that promise: the 6 to 14 part became an enforceable fundamental right in Article 21A, given effect by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, while the duty towards children below six stayed in Article 45 as a directive. A question asking for education 'under the Directive Principles' is pointing at Article 45.

topic_name: Street vendor credit and livelihood schemes
short_explanation: PM SVANidhi pays a digital-transaction cashback of up to Rs 100 a month, which caps at Rs 1,200 for a vendor over a loan year.
explanation_text: The scheme was launched in June 2020 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs for street vendors whose trade stopped in the lockdown. It lends Rs 10,000 without collateral for a year; repay on time and the next loan is Rs 20,000, then Rs 50,000. Two incentives sit on top of the loan: a 7 per cent interest subsidy credited quarterly, and the cashback, which is structured to build a digital payment record - Rs 50 for the first 50 transactions in a month, then Rs 25 for each further block of 25 - because that record is what allows the vendor to be credit-scored later.

option_rationales.rationale: Rs 1,100 is eleven months at the Rs 100 monthly cap.

short_explanation: Goa has no Regional Rural Bank; Sikkim is the other state without one. Elsewhere RRBs cover the states, with the heaviest presence in the northern and central plains.
explanation_text: RRBs were created by an ordinance in 1975 and the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976, on the Narasimham Working Group's recommendation, to combine a commercial bank's discipline with a cooperative's local reach. Equity is held 50 per cent by the Centre, 35 per cent by the sponsor commercial bank and 15 per cent by the state government; the RBI regulates them while NABARD supervises them and refinances their lending. Successive rounds of amalgamation cut their number from 196 to 43.

topic_name: Employees' provident fund, ESI and statutory social security
short_explanation: ESI applies to employees drawing monthly wages up to Rs 21,000, a ceiling raised from Rs 15,000 with effect from 1 January 2017; for a person with disability the limit is Rs 25,000.
explanation_text: ESI is contributory social insurance rather than a welfare grant: the employee pays 0.75 per cent of wages and the employer 3.25 per cent, and in return the insured person and dependants get medical care at ESIC hospitals and dispensaries plus cash benefits - sickness, maternity, disablement and dependants' benefit. It applies to non-seasonal factories and notified establishments employing 10 or more persons.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 15,000 was the ESI ceiling until the end of 2016 and remains the wage ceiling for statutory EPF coverage - a common mix-up.

option_rationales.label: B
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the ceiling is Rs 21,000.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the ceiling is Rs 21,000.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the ceiling is Rs 21,000.

common_traps: ESI wage ceiling Rs 21,000; EPF wage ceiling Rs 15,000.

topic_name: Employees' provident fund, ESI and statutory social security
short_explanation: The minimum pension under the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 is Rs 1,000 a month, fixed in September 2014.
explanation_text: EPS is funded not by a separate deduction but by diverting 8.33 per cent of the employer's provident fund contribution, calculated on wages up to the Rs 15,000 ceiling, with the Centre adding 1.16 per cent. Because the pension is formula-linked to pensionable salary and length of service, members with short or low-wage service earned far less than Rs 1,000, which is why a floor was set and is met from budgetary support.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the statutory floor is Rs 1,000 a month.

option_rationales.label: C
option_rationales.rationale: Arbitrary figure; the statutory floor is Rs 1,000 a month.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 1,500 is a figure often demanded in revision proposals, but the notified minimum remains Rs 1,000.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

short_explanation: Census 2011 counted 68.84 per cent of India's population as rural and 31.16 per cent as urban.

option_rationales.label: A
option_rationales.rationale: 55.6 per cent is far below the 2011 rural share and matches no census year.

option_rationales.label: C

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: 72.5 is close to the 2001 rural share of 72.2 per cent, not to 2011.

option_rationales.label: E
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

short_explanation: 'Aazadi se Antyoday tak' was run by the Ministry of Rural Development, which used the campaign to saturate its own rural schemes in selected blocks during the Azadi ka Amrit Mahotsav.

option_rationales.label: D
option_rationales.rationale: The Ministry of Cooperation, created in 2021, handles cooperative societies.

option_rationales.label: E

short_explanation: Maharashtra has the largest number of cooperative societies in the country, a legacy of its sugar, dairy and urban credit cooperatives.
